a-catalogue-of-rare-and-valuable-books-i: A Catalogue of Rare and Valuable Books, 1908. The rare book catalogue. This book preserves that catalogue. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
abdul-baha-some-answered-questions-1908:
Abdu'l-Baha, the son of the founder of the Baha'i faith, gave these talks at table in the years before this book of 1908. Laura Clifford Barney heard them, wrote them down, and turned them into English. The book was the first great Baha'i work to come out in English in the West.

Guests asked him hard points on God, on Christ, on science, and on the ways of the soul. He gives crisp, calm replies, each fit to stand on its own as a short essay. The book is the door through which most first readers step to the Baha'i faith.
alexander-locke-1908:
Samuel Alexander wrote this short study of John Locke for the Philosophical Classics series, and it appeared in 1908. Alexander taught at Manchester and later won fame as a thinker in his own right. His subject was the English thinker whose work shaped modern ideas about knowledge, government, and faith.

Readers get Locke's life in brief, then a clear tour of his main claims. Minds start blank, Alexander explains, and all knowledge grows from sense and reflection. In politics, Locke held that rule rests on consent and that people keep rights no ruler may take. The book stays a neat first map of a thinker who helped found liberal thought.
andrewes-devotions-vol1-1908: Volume one of the Devotions of Bishop Lancelot Andrewes, in a 1908 edition. The great Anglican bishop's private prayers, rich in patristic learning. This book preserves those classic devotions. It awaits future readers. The library keeps the document safe.
andreyev-seven-that-were-hanged-1908:
The Seven Who Were Hanged, Leonid Andreyev's story of 1908, reached English in Herman Bernstein's translation of 1909. Five young terrorists who plotted against a minister wait in prison for execution. With them hang two common criminals, a murderer and a horse thief, each facing death in his own way.

Andreyev enters each cell in turn: the brave, the broken, the calm, the terrified. Parents visit, clocks tick, and the state machine moves without haste or hatred. The story made Andreyev famous around the world on its appearance. Tolstoy's circle debated its protest against capital punishment for years. Its quiet, mounting dread has lost none of its force.
angela-foligno-divine-consolations-1908: The Book of Divine Consolations, sayings of the 13th-century mystic Angela of Foligno. After her conversion she recorded visions of Christ's love. This translation preserves her intense spiritual voice. The library keeps the document safe.
aquarian-gospel-of-jesus-the-christ-1908:
Levi Dowling said he read the past from a vast store of all deeds. The Aquarian Gospel of Jesus the Christ came out in 1908. Dowling was a preacher in the States with a love of the East. The book calls its age the Aquarian age, now at its dawn.

The tale fills the lost years of Jesus with trips to India, Tibet, and Greece. Wise men of each land teach him a part of the one truth. His birth, his works, and his death then run in a new dress. The book is a chief text of the New Age line of faith.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-08:
The eighth volume of Burton's Nights, published in 1885, nears the end of Shahrazad's thousand and one nights. Her pardon, when it comes in the frame, will rest on the king's transformed heart. The tales still run the full gamut: high romance, low comedy, pious legend, and sly trickster turns.

Burton's apparatus grows richer as the set proceeds, and volume eight carries his learning lightly over long stretches of story. He translates charms, songs, and riddles that tidier versions drop. The result can daunt new readers, yet it preserves the book as the East knew it. Scholars still cite Burton's notes beside his text. The volume keeps faith with both.
arrhenius-worlds-making-borns-1908:
Svante Arrhenius was a Swedish chemist who won a Nobel Prize for his work on how salts split in water. His Worlds in the Making, in Borns's 1908 translation, surveys the birth and death of worlds for general readers. It is climate science's first popular classic.

Arrhenius calculates how carbon dioxide in the air traps heat and could warm or cool the whole planet. He also proposes panspermia, the idea that life's seeds drift through space from world to world. His greenhouse figures, rough as they were, started a line of research that runs to today's climate models.
arxiv-2511-20108:
Alam, Gizzini, and Clavier squeeze secrecy and energy savings from battery-free wireless devices. Their 2025 paper studies ambient backscatter with multi-user NOMA systems. Backscatter devices reflect ambient radio signals instead of transmitting. NOMA lets several users share one channel simultaneously. A passive eavesdropper threatens the shared downlink.

The goal is secrecy energy efficiency, secrecy rate per unit power. With two backscatter devices, closed-form optima were derived. Reflection coefficients and power splits sit on a Pareto boundary. More devices make the math intractable directly. A grid search benchmarks small cases exhaustively. Particle swarm optimization scales the search upward. A neural network predictor then mimics the optimizer. It matched optimal answers with over ninety-five percent accuracy. Adding backscatter lifted secrecy efficiency by up to 615 percent. Gains peaked in high-noise conditions especially. SHAP explanations showed the network leans on dominant channel features. That matches theory, building trust.
arxiv-2511-20208:
Ashby, Barrenechea, Lukyanov, Pryer, and Trenam build a finite element method for polymer fluids. Their 2025 paper discretizes a reduced Oldroyd-B model. Dilute polymer solutions flow unlike plain liquids. Long molecules stretch and add elastic stresses. Full tensor models are costly to simulate.

The reduction writes the stress using one direction only. A vector outer product replaces the full tensor. Borrowing tricks from magnetohydrodynamics shapes the scheme. The mesh respects the de Rham complex structure. Discrete velocity comes out exactly divergence-free. Interior penalties handle viscosity within elements. Upwind transport tames sharp stress layers. An IMEX time scheme stays linear at each step. A discrete energy law mirrors the true dissipation. Benchmark flows include the classic lid-driven cavity. A four-to-one contraction tested sharp corners. High Weissenberg numbers stayed stable and accurate. Efficient viscoelastic simulation gets a reliable route.
arxiv-2511-20308:
Grendár argues a famous rank test has been misdescribed in textbooks for decades. His 2025 paper reexamines the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test. Textbooks say it tests whether two groups share one distribution. The statistic is the U count behind the empirical AUC. AUC measures how often one group's value beats the other's.

A simple counterexample exposes the textbook claim. Two normal samples with different spreads have different distributions. Yet their empirical AUC still settles at one half. Simulations with ten thousand runs confirm that concentration. The statistic behaves exactly as a true null predicts. So the real null is AUC equals 0.5, not full equality. Grendár derives the limit law under that correct null. Finite-sample bias corrections come along with it. The test is consistent against any AUC different from one half. Van Dantzig had established that back in 1951.
arxiv-2511-20508:
Zhang, Mirallès, Dellacherie, Wu, and Boulet ask which weather data truly drives home electricity use. Their 2025 paper tests causal feature selection for load forecasting. Weather strongly drives residential demand for heating and cooling. Throwing in every weather variable can still hurt accuracy. A principled way to choose inputs is needed.

The case study covers Southern Ontario cities and regions. Hourly consumption data came from the provincial system operator. ERA5 reanalysis supplied the matching weather fields. Three forecasting models were tested: GRU, TCN, and PatchTST. Plain correlation-based selection favored radiation and moisture variables. The causal PCMCI method picked direct thermal drivers instead. It pruned indirect variables that merely correlate with demand. Causal selection kept feature sets compact across nine cities. Accuracy matched or improved against using everything. Robustness held during extreme cold, heat, and heavy rain. The module is model-agnostic and lightweight for operators.
arxiv-2511-20608:
Bzdušek surveys three fast-moving threads in topological band theory. His 2025 perspective covers recent advances for single-particle bands. Topology now guides how electronic states are classified and designed. The first thread is the quantum geometric tensor. Its parts, Berry curvature and quantum metric, are newly measurable with light.

The second thread covers topology beyond the standard classification. Delicate and multigap topology escape the tenfold way scheme. They still leave robust fingerprints in real materials. Bundle gerbes form the third, newest thread. Gerbes capture higher-form topology older tools overlooked. The three threads weave together in recent work. Delicate insulators show odd quantum geometry that gerbes describe neatly. A quantized nonlinear optical response falls out of that view. Crystalline solids may soon realize that response experimentally. Optical probes make the abstract geometry tangible in labs.
arxiv-2511-20708:
Ivan Hetman settles in 2025 a batch of existence questions in design theory, the study of how points can be grouped into perfectly balanced blocks. A Steiner system S(2, k, v) arranges v points into blocks of size k so that every pair of points meets in exactly one block. For block sizes up to 5 such systems are fully understood, but for 6 and above only scattered examples were known.

Hetman's headline result proves that S(2, 9, 369) exists, a system of 369 points in blocks of nine. Alongside it he presents many new unitals of order 6, equivalently S(2, 7, 217), plus fresh examples of S(2, 7, 175) and S(2, 7, 259). He also gives S(2, 8, 120), S(2, 8, 504), and S(2, 9, 513). The constructions lean on symmetry: one known design's automorphism group has 4,200 elements, and its subgroups split the points into orbits of sizes 75, 75, and 25, from which new designs grow. The haul of examples leads Hetman to two conjectures about infinite families.
arxiv-2511-20908:
Mykyta Kliapets and colleagues hunt in 2025 for rare hybrid pulsating stars across the whole TESS sky. Gamma Doradus / Delta Scuti hybrids ring with both pressure modes, probing the star's outer layers, and gravity modes, probing near the core, making them prized laboratories for stellar interiors. Confirmed examples are few. The team trained a positive-unlabelled classifier, which learns from known positives plus unlabelled data, on light-curve features from the TESS-Gaia pipeline.

First they verified the pipeline: variability of known Kepler hybrids matched between TESS-Gaia and Quick Look Pipeline curves, with high recovery of Kepler frequencies. The classifier's smart binning scored an average 93.04 percent out-of-bag prediction on test hybrids. Applied all-sky, it produced a catalogue of 62,026 new candidate light curves, each with per-sector hybrid probabilities. Pressure-mode-dominant hybrids proved commoner among strong candidates, and the catalogue awaits asteroseismic follow-up.
arxiv-2511-21008:
Constantinos Daskalakis, Vardis Kandiros, and Rui Yao unify in 2025 the theory of learning Ising models, the workhorse distributions of statistical physics. The goal is closeness of the whole distribution in total variation distance. Knowing the right number of samples was not the problem: roughly n squared over epsilon squared samples are known to be necessary and sufficient. The gap was an efficient algorithm with guarantees across regimes, instead of separate methods per regime.

The authors analyse the maximum pseudo-likelihood estimator, a classic practical method, for two broad model classes. One class has bounded operator norm and satisfies a modified log-Sobolev inequality tied to fast mixing of Glauber dynamics. The other has bounded width, the standard assumption in structure learning. In both, the estimator runs in polynomial time with optimal or near-optimal sample complexity. Their proofs blend tensorisation inequalities, measure decompositions, and concentration bounds.
arxiv-2511-21108:
Sourendu Gupta reviews in 2025 what is known about the phase diagram of quantum chromodynamics, the map of how quark matter behaves across temperature and density. The review synthesises lattice computations, effective field theories, and chiral models. Several slices through the three-dimensional diagram are now known with good precision for two light quarks plus a heavier strange quark, the 2+1 flavour theory. A decade of lattice advances lets researchers probe regions that were previously out of reach.

Gupta uses the accumulated results, plus basic thermodynamic arguments, to reconstruct the diagram for physical QCD, where up and down quarks differ, the 1+1+1 theory. The payoff is twofold: connecting heavy-ion collision experiments, which briefly recreate early-universe matter, with constraints on the matter inside neutron star cores. The review also covers neutron stars and the chiral transition in the large-colour limit, and names the computations that would most sharpen the picture.
arxiv-2511-21308:
Syamlal Sankaran Kunnath and colleagues demonstrate in 2025 that spin waves can travel across an artificial spin ice, something never shown before. Artificial spin ices are arrays of tiny magnets whose frustrated arrangements host exotic states like magnetic monopoles, but their weak dipolar coupling kept waves trapped locally. The team's hybrid design embeds in-plane magnetised nanoelements, each 200 by 75 nanometres, inside a multilayer film magnetised at right angles to its plane.

Exchange coupling between the two subsystems, plus fading tunnelling waves through the film, carries coherent spin waves over a micrometre. Their decay lengths cross one micrometre and group velocities reach hundreds of metres per second under a modest bias field. In the structure, a waveguide 12.73 micrometres long hosts 30 unit cells, with an edge mode at 3.9 gigahertz and a bulk mode at 5.3 gigahertz. Because the ice stays reconfigurable, the platform opens frustrated spin systems to wave-based analogue signal processing.
arxiv-2511-21408:
Frederico Wieser and four coauthors at University College London teach transformers to spend effort only where it surprises them, in 2025. Standard transformers burn the same computation on every token and layer, wasteful when most text is predictable. Their Subjective Depth Transformer alternates two layer types. Decision layers form a quick prior guess and a full posterior view. Dynamic layers then route only the most surprising work onward, using Bayesian surprise as the signal.

Wieser and his coauthors extend the idea through time with the Subjective Timescale Transformer, which predicts how each token's representation should change and skips blocks when little change is expected. Within each skipping layer, self-attention computation falls by 75 percent and key-value cache needs by 50 percent. Over training, the gating shifts from chasing novelty to confirming predictions, as surprise-based theories suggest. The authors stress the results are preliminary, from one model scale and capacity setting.
arxiv-2511-21608:
Steph Foulds and Viv Kendon design quantum walks for neutral-atom computers, including walkers that can stand still, in 2025. Quantum walks, the quantum cousin of the random walk, can model fluid dynamics, but the fluid applications need lazy walks, whose walker also has a rest state. Neutral atoms suit the task: their Rydberg interactions natively implement gates on three or more qubits, and the atoms can be rearranged mid-computation.

Foulds and Kendon lay out gate sequences and model multiqubit Rydberg gate errors. With projected gate fidelities of 0.9981 for two-qubit and 0.9954 for three-qubit gates, a walk on a four-node ring keeps fidelity above 0.99 after four steps and above 0.90 after twenty steps. Richer walks miss those tolerances until a four-qubit gate at 0.9850 fidelity is added. That rescues both the lazy walk on the ring and an eight-node walk, charting what near-term hardware must deliver.
arxiv-2511-21708:
Matteo Spreafico, Ludovica Tassini, Camilla Sancricca, and Cinzia Cappiello test whether language models can do data janitorial work, in a 2025 feature study. Data preparation, profiling, transforming, and cleaning dirty datasets, consumes up to roughly 80 percent of a data scientist's time, making it a tempting target for automation. The team prompted general-purpose and fine-tuned tabular models with poor-quality datasets and scored their help.

A custom quality model, validated through a user study with 61 practitioners, structured the evaluation. Performance varied sharply with the task and the dataset's dirtiness. Models stumbled on counting tasks and are capped by fixed input length, while traditional tools count flawlessly and swallow unlimited input. The verdict is measured: language models cannot yet replace traditional preparation tools, but they can support them well, especially by exploiting context and user intent. The study maps where that support is real today.
arxiv-2512-00008:
Veeramani Pugazhenthi and co-authors present MOTION, on-device motion recognition with machine learning help. Tiny devices that recognize gestures with low delay are gaining ground in daily interaction. Medical uses, like fall detection and rehabilitation tracking, need fast responses without false alarms.

Running recognition on the device itself avoids network delay and keeps health data private. The system targets efficient tracking of movement on very small hardware. Reliable fall and activity detection could support safer independent living for patients. Fall detection, rehabilitation tracking, and patient supervision are the named medical drivers for fast, low-latency on-device recognition.
arxiv-2512-00108:
Black holes can, in principle, give up energy through magnetic processes near their edges. Bo Zhao, Chao-Hui Wang, and Shao-Wen Wei study energy extraction from Kerr-AdS black holes in a 2025 study. These are rotating black holes in a universe with a negative cosmological constant.

The extraction mechanism they examine is magnetic reconnection, where magnetic field lines break and rejoin, releasing energy. The authors map the parameter regions where extraction can occur and analyze its efficiency and power. Their results add to theoretical work on how the most extreme objects in physics might power energetic outflows. The analysis stays within general relativity, the standard theory of gravity and black holes.
arxiv-2512-00208:
Computer-generated people need to react to others with motion that looks natural over time. Hajra Anwar Beg, Baptiste Chopin, Hao Tang, and Mohamed Daoudi present ReactionMamba in 2025, a framework for generating three-dimensional human reaction motions. The system is built to handle both short and long sequences.

ReactionMamba combines a motion variational autoencoder, which compresses movement efficiently, with Mamba state-space models that decode reactions consistently over time. It can produce brief simple motions and long complex ones, such as dance and martial arts. Animators and game developers could use such tools to populate scenes with believable responsive characters. Reaction generation matters wherever digital characters must respond to a partner's movement. For folks who make games or films, a tool like this can fill a scene with life. The lead cast can then do the scenes that count the most.
arxiv-2512-00408:
At ultra-low bitrates, traditional video codecs collapse into blocky artifacts because they chase pixel accuracy. Lingdong Wang and co-authors propose DiSCo in 2025, a semantic video compression framework. The failure, they argue, comes from a mismatch between pixel fidelity and human perception.

DiSCo transmits only the most meaningful information and relies on generative priors to synthesize the remaining detail. Viewers forgive invented texture more readily than obvious compression damage. If the approach matures, video calls and streaming could stay watchable on connections where today's codecs simply give up. Generative priors know what natural video looks like, which pixel codecs cannot exploit. Ultra-low bitrates matter most on mobile and satellite links.
arxiv-2512-00608:
Feedback can enlarge what a broadcast channel is able to carry, but noise in the feedback path spoils naive schemes. Jacqueline Malayter and co-authors present deep broadcast feedback codes in 2025. Deep learning has renewed interest in codes that use channel output feedback.

In the Gaussian broadcast channel with feedback, capacity can exceed the no-feedback region. Linear analytical codes, though, perform poorly with even small amounts of feedback noise. Learned codes promise robustness where formulas fail, which matters for wireless systems that already feed receiver information back to transmitters. Broadcast channels serve many receivers at once, which is where feedback design gets tricky. Learned codes are found by training, not derived, which suits noisy feedback.
arxiv-2512-00708:
Ming-Hsiu Wu, Ziqian Xie, Shuiwang Ji, and Degui Zhi built a new dataset for drug discovery in a 2025 paper. Models that predict how well a drug candidate binds to a protein are key in early drug hunting. Yet current models often overfit to simplified datasets that miss how real proteins change.

Real proteins carry modifications, such as swapped, added, or missing building blocks, and added phosphate groups. The team rebuilt the widely used DAVIS dataset in a complete, modification-aware form. It adds thousands of kinase-ligand pairs that involve such changes. A harder, more honest test set should show which models truly work.
arxiv-2512-00808:
Wen-Han Zhou, Yun Zhang, Jiamu Huang, and Douglas Lin offer an idea for the flares of Sagittarius A* in a 2025 paper. That object is the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way. It gives off frequent short flares across many wavelengths, and their origin is still unknown.

The authors suggest the flares come from bodies being torn apart and evaporating near the black hole. Some bodies are loose rubble piles, others solid monoliths, and each kind breaks up in its own way. If the idea holds, flare timing and brightness could reveal what kind of debris drifts near the galactic center.
arxiv-2512-00908:
Xinzhu Chen, Xuesheng Li, Zhongxiang Sun, and Weijie Yu refine how reasoning models are trained in a 2025 paper. A leading method rewards models for answers that can be checked, and it improves reasoning step by step. Recent work ties learning to token entropy, a measure of how unsure the model is at each word.

High-entropy tokens were thought to drive exploration and deserve stronger updates. The authors argue that most of a reasoning chain is made of low-entropy segments instead. Those calm stretches carry stable, reusable structure. Their correctness-aware method shapes advantages around such segments, rewarding right answers. Better credit assignment could make reasoning training steadier.
arxiv-2512-01008:
Zhongbin Guo and five coauthors present LISA-3D in a 2025 computer vision paper. Text-driven 3D reconstruction needs a mask generator that understands open-vocabulary instructions, like segment the red chair, while staying consistent across camera views. Most 2D segmenters wobble when the viewpoint changes.

LISA-3D lifts language-image segmentation into 3D in two stages. It retrofits the instruction-following model LISA with geometry-aware low-rank adapters, then reuses a frozen 3D reconstructor built from SAM. Multi-view consistency keeps the same object masked the same way from every angle. Consistent masks would make text-guided 3D editing and scene building far more reliable.
arxiv-2512-01108:
Gabriel Olin, Lu Chen, Nayesha Gandotra, Maxim Likhachev, and Howie Choset tackle fast interception in a 2025 robotics paper. Catching a fast moving object is hard because the time window is tiny. Sensor noise makes it harder, since the robot only gets incomplete information about where the target really is.

That uncertainty leaves a distribution over possible target states, not one position. Their system plans in belief space, reasoning over that distribution, and does so in real time with kinodynamic limits in mind. Real-time belief planning could help robots catch, block, or dock with fast projectiles and vehicles.
arxiv-2512-01208:
Alper Yıldırım and İbrahim Yücedağ propose a new attention scheme for transformers in a 2025 paper. Standard transformers pay what the authors call a semantic alignment tax. That tax is a heavy optimization cost. The model must organize a chaotic starting state into a coherent geometric map, through slow local gradient diffusion.

They hypothesize that this diffusive learning causes catastrophic rigidity. A model organized that way cannot adapt to novel concepts without destroying its pretrained reasoning. Their alternative moves from vector space diffusion toward a spectral phase-locking scheme with far better scaling. If the idea works, models could keep learning new concepts without full retraining.
arxiv-2512-01308:
Da-Sol Joo studies how heat-driven flow is modeled in fluids. When a fluid is heated from below, it churns in rolls. This setup is called Rayleigh-Benard convection. Models of churn must add the push of warm, light fluid, but no set form is agreed on.

Joo works out an exact solution for a common churn model in a flat layer. In that layer, churn is fed by heat push alone. An exact case gives model builders a firm check. It shows where the model holds and where its terms for heat push need a fix.
arxiv-2512-01408:
Jose Blanchet and co-authors revisit the Merton portfolio problem with robust data-driven rules. Merton's model picks trades over time to balance gain and risk. Fast trading helps only if drift can be trusted. Drift is hard to pin down in real markets.

Volatility can be screened from realized or implied data. The team builds robust rules around that split. Nonlinear Wasserstein projections guard against drift error. Robust picks aim to hold up when market models are wrong, a key need for real funds. Short horizons are the focus, where frequent trading pays only if robust rules keep model error from eating the gains alive.
arxiv-2512-01708:
Ghita Fassy El Fehri, Aurelien Bellet, and Philippe Bastien learn Bayesian network structure with privacy and federation. Data sits split across sites that cannot pool it. Privacy rules bind each site. Communication costs also grow fast with dimension.

Their Fed-Sparse-BNSL method targets linear Gaussian networks. It keeps rigorous privacy guarantees for each party. Sparse structure keeps messages small as dimension grows. Joint learning without raw data sharing serves hospitals and banks that must map links in data they cannot merge. Sparse structure priors do double duty, cutting both message size and the risk of spurious links in small local data sets.
arxiv-2512-01808:
Ibrahim Abdurrahman and co-authors study pair transfer in calcium-zirconium collisions below the Coulomb barrier. Sub-barrier fusion probes how pairing boosts neutron transfer. Past BCS-based sums boosted pair transfer over no-pairing sums. They still missed the observed boost between one- and two-neutron transfer.

The team revisits reaction dynamics for those collision pairs. Better pairing treatment is the goal. Matching the observed boost would validate how pairing acts during brief nuclear contact. That insight feeds models of fusion used for new element synthesis. Calcium and zirconium targets are stable and well mapped, which makes them a clean stage for isolating the pairing effect itself.
arxiv-2512-02008:
Letting a language model think longer at answer time, rather than training it bigger, has become a popular route to better reasoning. Aradhye Agarwal, Ayan Sengupta, and Tanmoy Chakraborty survey in 2025 how to scale this test-time compute, comparing the well-known strategies side by side under identical conditions.

A fair comparison had been missing, and so had an account of how the best strategy shifts with model type and problem difficulty. The authors organize the options for spending extra inference compute and examine when each pays off. Their map helps builders decide where an extra moment of machine thought is worth its cost.
arxiv-2512-02208:
Random graph theory studies networks that grow by chance, and its limit objects capture what huge random networks look like from afar. Pim van der Hoorn, Huck Stepanyants, and Dmitri Krioukov connect in 2025 two kinds of limits: projective limits of probability measures and direct limits of their symmetry groups.

They show the direct limit group is exactly the symmetry group of the limit probability measure. That tidy correspondence lets results travel between the finite approximations and the infinite limit. It supplies machinery for random graph limits, a framework used to model real networks from social graphs to the internet.
arxiv-2512-02508:
Marco Cardia and co-authors study how to judge water quality with machine learning. Clean water matters across farming and food work, from crop irrigation and animal care to food processing plants. As farms go digital, automatic quality checks become a valuable part of daily operations.

The team applies multivariate analysis, which reads many water measures at once rather than one by one. Learned patterns can flag water that drifts out of a safe range. Faster, cheaper checks could help farms and food firms catch problems early, before bad water harms crops, animals, or products. Clean water checks like these guard both farm yield and the food on our plates.
arxiv-2512-02708:
S. Bellotti and a large team update a survey of magnetic fields on stars that host planets. The survey uses spectropolarimetry, which reads magnetic signatures in starlight. Its targets sit on the current list for Ariel, a planned space mission to study exoplanet atmospheres.

Knowing a host star's magnetic field helps interpret the planet data Ariel will gather. Active stars can mimic or mask atmospheric signals. The campaign status report tells mission planners which target stars are well characterized, and which still need observing time before launch. Star data of this kind takes years to build, so a shared status list keeps scarce scope time from waste.
arxiv-2512-02908:
Iryna Zabaikina and Ramon Grima show how missed counts distort the speeds that cell studies report. Single cell tests fail to catch many of the molecules in a sample. That loss adds noise on top of the true, random way genes turn on and off.

Capture loss is often cast as a binomial draw, a clean model of imperfect detection. Till now it was worked out only for plain gene expression, with no gene control in play. The pair extend it to networks where genes switch each other on and off. Missed counts shift the rates a study would infer, and their work shows how to correct that shift. Labs that count cells one by one can use the fix to read truer speeds from noisy data.
arxiv-2512-03008:
Charmed baryons are heavy particles that contain a charm quark. A team led by A. Dávila-Rivera studies how three of them decay by emitting light in this 2025 work. The three particles belong to a family of six in the quark model.

The authors use the constituent quark model, which treats baryons as built from a few heavy quarks. They work out rates for these light-emitting decays. Such rates give tests that lab experiments can check in the future. They also help show whether the quark model describes heavy particles well. Future collider data can test these rates, since charmed baryons decay in ways detectors can record.
arxiv-2512-03108:
A crystal called RuO2 has sparked debate about its magnetism. Shubhankar Paul and seven co-authors add new evidence in this 2025 work. Some call the crystal an altermagnet, a new class of magnetic matter, while other studies find it is a plain paramagnetic metal.

The authors study how heat capacity, the heat a material soaks up, behaves in this crystal. They report a correction linked to Fermi-liquid theory, with a non-smooth form. Such details help settle what kind of metal RuO2 is. The answer matters for future devices that may use such materials. Heat measures at low temperature often expose the true nature of a metal's electrons.
arxiv-2512-03708:
Groups of cooperating agents, from drones to mobile robots, must agree on a shared course of action while their communication network misbehaves. Loaie Solyman, Aamir Ahmad, and Ayman El-Badawy address delays and dropped packets in a 2025 control preprint. Messages arriving late or not at all create errors that offline planning cannot remove.

Their framework joins semi-continuous hidden Markov models, which track the network's random behaviour in real time, with Lyapunov-based model predictive control. The controller balances three aims at once: gentle control effort, small network-induced error, and small error caused by the communication graph itself. An incremental learning routine updates the network model online as conditions change. Simulations across several network layouts show the agents still reach consensus and stay near optimal performance, even as the topology varies.
arxiv-2512-04008:
Differential privacy promises people in a training dataset that a released model cannot identify them, but the public must take that promise on faith. Zoë Ruha Bell and colleagues design a private learning algorithm whose guarantees can be checked cheaply, in a 2025 preprint. Until now, verification cost about as much computing as training itself.

The team works on differentially private stochastic convex optimisation, where the best trade-offs are known. Their method privately minimises a sequence of regularised objectives and leans only on the standard composition bound for privacy accounting. That structure keeps utility near optimal while making the guarantee auditable with far less computation than training. On large datasets the saving is significant. The authors call it the first algorithm of its kind whose verification scales better than training, a property that could make privacy claims publicly testable.
arxiv-2512-04208:
The Webb telescope's little red dots look like young active galactic nuclei, yet refuse to behave like any known class. They show red continua, feeble hot dust, and no detectable X-rays. Hiroya Umeda and colleagues test an alternative reading in a 2025 astrophysics letter. Each dot may be a black hole in a gaseous envelope, glowing like a cool star.

The authors refit energy distributions of some four hundred dots from the COSMOS-Web survey under this envelope model. Blackbody emission at a few thousand kelvin reproduces the optical and near-infrared spectra. Inferred luminosities drop by one to two orders of magnitude versus dust-reddened interpretations. The revision dissolves the tension: the luminosity function, accretion density, and mass function now agree with active nuclei at later times. Host masses, from the ultraviolet excess, leave a modest excess in the black-hole-to-stellar mass ratio.
arxiv-2512-04808:
Puria Radmard, Paul Bays, and Máté Lengyel automate the search for brain-like circuits that make the same mistakes people do. Neuroscience wants recurrent network models whose internal dynamics explain behavior, errors included. Building them has meant slow, hand-guided tuning of architectures and training goals. Their 2025 arXiv paper flips the workflow: train networks to reproduce behavior itself, including its characteristic slips and suboptimal choices.

Real behavior data are too scarce to train such networks directly. A nonparametric generative model first expands the data into a large surrogate set with the same error patterns. Networks trained on that surrogate learn mechanisms that produce human-like successes and failures alike. Those mechanisms then become hypotheses about the brain's own circuits. Automating the hunt could speed theories of working memory, decision making, and the slips that reveal how cognition is wired.
arxiv-2512-04908:
Fang Li, Fei Zuo, Gopal Gupta, and co-authors build a log anomaly detector out of logic itself, using answer set programming. Security teams drown in system logs while threats keep mutating. Machine learning detectors can be opaque and brittle. Answer set programming instead reasons with explicit rules written as logical predicates. Their 2025 arXiv paper encodes security knowledge in that declarative style and tests it on real Linux logs.

The system flagged brute-force attacks, privilege escalations, suspicious bursts of connections from single addresses, and assorted system faults. Rules can be edited as threats evolve, without retraining. Correlating events across lines, a strength of logic, helped connect scattered signs into incidents. Each alert comes with the rule trail that fired it, so analysts can audit the call. Explainable detection suits forensics, where a black box verdict is not enough.
arxiv-2512-05808:
Sushmita Bhattacharya and six co-authors send a drone out to meet sperm whales at the surface. Whales dive long and surface briefly, in hard to predict spots. Their platform couples an autonomous aerial vehicle with model based reinforcement learning: an empirical model of whale diving steers the search, updated by live sensor data from the field.

Three hard problems sit at the core. The drone must track whale clicks acoustically even when several whales call at once. Robots must share decisions across a distributed setup. And faint signals from fish-borne trackers must be processed on board and caught at long range. The team evaluated the system three ways: real rendezvous attempts off Dominica, hardware trials on land, and simulations from recorded whale tracks. Meeting a whale where it surfaces is a proving ground for autonomous field robotics, and a gentler way to study these animals.
arxiv-2512-05908:
Amirkia Rafiei Oskooei, S Selcan Yukcu, Mehmet Cevheri Bozoglan, and Mehmet Aktas find software bugs faster by translating whole codebases into plain language first. In microservice systems, a bug report in words must be matched to code across many repositories. Language models choke on raw code at that scale. Their approach builds summaries at three levels: file, directory, and repository.

Search then happens language to language. A report is first routed to the likely repositories, then localization walks downward through directories to files, leaving an auditable path. On an industrial system with forty six repositories, the method placed the true bug location in its top ten answers for about four of five reports. It beat retrieval baselines and agentic coding assistants by clear margins. The deeper claim: engineered natural language can beat the raw code it describes.
arxiv-2512-06208:
Ho Fung Tsoi, Dylan Rankin, Vladimir Loncar, and Philip Harris speed up neural nets on images where most pixels carry no signal. In such images, a normal network still grinds through every pixel, which wastes time and chip space. Their framework, SparsePixels, keeps only the small set of live pixels and runs the math on those alone.

Because the pixel budget is fixed when the chip is built, the run time stays the same no matter what image comes in. The team tests the idea on images from a neutrino detector, where true events light up a tiny share of the frame. Their sparse net ran many times faster than a plain one, with only a small drop in accuracy and a modest chip footprint. The method suits fast triggers that must decide, in real time, which rare events to keep.
arxiv-2512-06508: P Mchedlov-Petrosyan and L Davydov study a combined equation used to model surface processes where two things happen at once: molecules settle onto and leave a surface, while also spreading along it. The combined form joins the Cahn Hilliard and Allen Cahn equations, classic tools for diffusion driven change. The authors add flow to the mix, plus viscosity, and a memory effect, so the surface recalls its past states as it evolves. They obtain exact solutions and discuss how the applied field, dissipation, and memory act together.
arxiv-2512-07008:
Mark Shattuck counts patterns in Catalan words, strings of positive whole numbers that start at one and never jump by more than one. Such words pair naturally with Dyck paths, the mountain-range walks that combinatorics uses to model everything from bracket matching to tree shapes. Shattuck's goal is the total of several statistics added across every Catalan word of a given length, with proofs that explain the counts rather than merely verifying them.

Two of the statistics, symmetric valleys and a family of generalized valleys, had formulas awaiting exactly this kind of explanation, requested by earlier researchers. A related identity about Catalan numbers also gets its missing combinatorial proof. The method translates each statistic to Dyck paths and counts sets of paths with one or more steps specially marked.
arxiv-2512-07108:
Ashutosh Jayant Dikshit and co-authors schedule the matchmaking of a future quantum internet in orbit. Quantum satellites can share entanglement, the fuel of quantum communication, with ground stations across the globe. But satellites and stations are scarce, passes are brief, and the weather interferes. Their framework assigns satellite-to-station pairings while respecting fidelity thresholds for the entanglement and the losses imposed by air, weather, and background noise.

Relay chains through links between satellites are included, so a station can be reached through more than one hop. The scheduling is posed as an integer optimization that can chase different goals: the highest total distribution rate, or a fairer spread across station pairs, or a balance between them. That flexibility turns the framework into a benchmark against which simpler, hand-made scheduling policies can be judged.
arxiv-2512-07208:
Fei Luo and co-authors fix a drift problem in federated learning, where many clients train a shared model without pooling their data. When each client's data skews differently, locally trained prompts, the small steering vectors used to adapt big models cheaply, warp toward local habits. Fixes that adjust how results are averaged treat the symptom, not the cause. This framework corrects the local training itself, using a picture of the whole data's shape as a guide.

The server rebuilds that global geometric prior from covariance information in a privacy-preserving way and shares it with clients. A calibration layer on each client then aligns local feature distributions with the global shape during training. On a label-skewed image benchmark the method beat the state of the art, and under extreme skew it improved far more over the baseline.
arxiv-2512-07408:
Minju Jeon and co-authors wire beehives into the internet of things, watching both the colony's indoor climate and the weather outside it. Bee populations are falling under habitat loss, pesticides, and climate change, with farm productivity in the balance. Existing smart hives mostly monitor the inside only, cost too much, and scale poorly. WaggleNet's worker nodes are cheap, about fifteen dollars each, and carry sensors for temperature, humidity, light, and position.

Nodes sit inside and around the hives and whisper their readings over LoRa, a long-range, low-power radio. To a master node that relays them through a standard messaging protocol to a cloud server and a phone app. Field tests delivered every packet across more than a hundred meters of clear sight, and nearly as far with obstructions, including from inside wooden hives.
arxiv-2512-07508:
Achyut Tiwari, Bruno Gompf, and Martin Dressel wrote this 2025 physics paper on a layered crystal. The crystal, a form of tantalum sulfide named in the title, hosts competing quantum states. Charge density waves, a Mott insulating state, and superconductivity all contend inside it.

Its shifts between states come with a stubborn metal-insulator transition. The role of coupling between the layers in that shift was unclear. The authors probe the crystal with spectroscopic ellipsometry, which reads how it handles light. They track its response from room warmth down to its frozen insulating state. At room temperature the crystal acts as a natural hyperbolic medium in visible light.  As temperature changes, the metallic patches that carry current change shape. They stretch from discs into needles, and a new middle phase appears on heating. The transition, they conclude, is a three-dimensional percolation process driven between layers.
arxiv-2512-07608:
Jing Wang, Jie Shen, Xing Niu, Tong Zhang, and Jeremy Weiss wrote this 2025 paper on fairness in language models. Their test ground is medical question answering, where a model picks among given options. Fairness here means one thing: similar questions should receive similar treatment.

Their method, Metric-Fair Prompting, changes how the model works through the questions. Instead of solving each item alone, it pairs up questions that look alike. Similarity is measured with standard language embeddings. The prompt then forces a shared routine for both members of a pair. The model pulls out the decisive clinical features and scores each option as a confidence value. A Lipschitz-style rule keeps scores for similar inputs close together. On the MedQA benchmark for United States medical exams, the paired approach beats plain single-item prompting. Fairness-guided reasoning, they show, can raise accuracy on high-stakes questions too.
arxiv-2512-07708:
Quentin Vigneron and Hamed Barzegar wrote this 2025 cosmology paper on the shapes the universe can take. Bianchi and Kantowski-Sachs spacetimes describe universes that expand unevenly by direction. Their kinship with Thurston's catalog of shapes in three dimensions runs deep.

The authors study such universes inside a gravity theory built on Thurston geometries. Shape enters the laws of gravity directly in that framework. They focus on non-tilted solutions filled with a perfect fluid. Shear-free fluid solutions and static vacuum solutions exist for every topology. A second result concerns what a positive cosmological constant does. Nearly all these metrics settle into smooth, even expansion over time.  Recollapse, meanwhile, is impossible whenever the weak energy condition holds. General relativity fails both tests for its most tangled topology. The new framework needs no extra parameters to earn those virtues. Simple inflation in any shape becomes possible.
arxiv-2512-07808:
M. A. Farooq, G. Di Guglielmo, A. Rajagopala, N. Tran, V. A. Chhabria, and A. Arora wrote this 2025 quantum hardware paper. Reading a qubit means turning a faint analog response into a definite classical answer. Neural networks read qubits well, but their hardware versions are heavy and slow.

Slow readout chokes the fast loops that quantum error correction needs. Their accelerator, LUNA, attacks both the size and the latency problems. Simple integrators first compress the incoming signal at minimal hardware cost. The classifier itself is built from look-up tables instead of arithmetic units. LogicNets, networks synthesized directly into table logic, make that possible. A search framework based on differential evolution hunts for the best designs. The payoff is a far smaller chip footprint. Latency drops by about a third, with little or no loss in reading fidelity. LUNA points toward readout that scales with the quantum machines themselves.
arxiv-2512-08008:
Sarah V White, Precious K Sejake, Kshitij Thorat, and a large international team of radio astronomers posted a catalog paper on arXiv in December 2025. It is the fourth paper on the GLEAM four jansky sample, a complete set of the brightest radio galaxies in the southern sky. The team presents an updated multiwavelength version of the catalog for public use.

The update adds many new host galaxy identifications and redshift information, plus optical photometry from the DESI Legacy Surveys. With that legacy dataset, the authors study how these radio bright galaxies behave across wavelengths. They present a new diagram linking radio power, size, and spectral curvature, which acts as a proxy for a source age. The results highlight candidate remnant and restarted radio galaxies, and show the sample spans the full range of infrared colors.
arxiv-2512-08808:
Erik Rye and Dave Levin turn Wikipedia edit records into a twenty year history of IPv6 client addressing. Wikimedia sites log the network address of editors who are not signed in, using it in place of a username. Public data dumps therefore contain timestamped client addresses spanning more than two decades, an accidental time capsule for network research.

The authors extract tens of millions of unique IPv6 addresses used by editors over that period. With them, they trace how common IPv6 use is in countries tied to each Wikimedia language edition. They also track how adoption grew over time and across regions. A further question is how often client devices such as desktops, laptops, and phones used a specific addressing scheme derived from hardware identifiers. The study shows how a public editing archive can reveal long term change in internet addressing practice.
arxiv-2512-09008:
N S Mankoc Borsnik presents a theory that aims to unify all fermion and boson fields, including gravity,. Internal spaces of the fields are described by basis vectors built from products of gamma operators. In a fourteen dimensional setting, the picture is claimed to cover all observed fermions in families and all known bosons, from photons to gravitons.

A key condition is that fields carry nonzero angular momentum only in ordinary four dimensional spacetime. Bosons fall into two orthogonal groups in this description. The author notes that, in the allowed dimensions, the count of internal fermion states across families matches the count of boson states. General properties of massless fields and their interactions are presented, which fix the Lagrangian of the theory. Basis vectors are illustrated in detail for fourteen and six dimensional cases. New results are reported, and open problems in the theory are discussed.
arxiv-2512-09508:
Oskar Fiuk, Emanuel Kieronski, and Vincent Michielini study the difficulty of reasoning in two-variable first-order logic for hierarchically structured data. Two-variable logic is a fragment of logic using only two variable names, known for balancing expressiveness and decidability. Their setting models databases where items are organized by nested classifications and orders.

Their first logic adds a linear order and a chain of equivalence relations, each coarser than the last, like broader categories. They show deciding whether such a structure exists for a statement is complete for nondeterministic exponential time. A weaker variant without the linear order keeps the exponential model property, guaranteeing small witnesses. Their second logic uses a chain of total preorders; its satisfiability problem is also complete for nondeterministic exponential time. It jumps to exponential space once the successor relations of the preorders can be accessed. Using two independent chains makes the problem undecidable.
arxiv-2512-09708:
Eugenio Clerico gives a short geometric proof of a recent result about merging statistical evidence. E-values are a modern tool for combining evidence across experiments, even dependent ones. An e-merging function takes several e-values and returns a single valid e-value; listing all such functions is basic to the theory.

A full description was obtained by Wang through involved arguments. Clerico's note reproves it with a supporting hyperplane argument applied to concave envelopes, a picture from convex geometry that makes the structure visible. He also shows the result holds without assuming the merging function is monotone, an assumption the earlier proof needed. That extension matters because it proves any non-monotone merging rule is dominated by a monotone one, so restricting attention to monotone rules loses no generality. The note is a compact example of geometry simplifying a basic statistical question.
arxiv-2512-10108:
Ali Zahra reviews a method for analyzing driven diffusive systems with several particle species and open boundaries. Such systems model traffic, transport in cells, and other flows where particles enter, move, and leave. The method generalizes the extremal current principle known from single species models. Its engine is the Riemann problem for the hydrodynamic equations, the mathematical description of how sharp initial profiles evolve. The case study is a two species exclusion process on a lattice, where two particle types move in opposite directions and swap places when they meet.

Despite its simplicity, the model shows the key phenomena of its class, including phase separation, where the species sort themselves into distinct regions. The review shows how the Riemann invariants, special combinations of densities that travel cleanly through the system, dictate the macroscopic behavior. Boundary conditions at the open ends select among phases through the extremal current rule.
arxiv-2512-10308:
Vasiliki Stoumpou leads a team building an interpretable tool to choose between two ways of replacing a failing aortic valve. For low to intermediate risk patients with severe aortic stenosis, surgery and the catheter based alternative are both viable, and real choices vary with patient differences and hospital habits. The authors combine prognostic matching, which emulates randomization between comparable patients, counterfactual outcome models, and an optimal policy tree. The tree splits patients into clinically coherent groups and prescribes the treatment with the lower estimated five year mortality for each.

Trained on data from one hospital, the policy was tested on another institution's patients. Applying its prescriptions in counterfactual evaluation cut estimated five year mortality substantially at both hospitals relative to the choices actually made. The authors describe the framework as the first transparent, data driven recommender for this choice.
arxiv-2512-10908:
K Hari, Subhajit Barman, and Dawood Kothawala give the twin paradox a quantum retelling. In Einstein's classic puzzle, one twin travels and returns younger than the stay-at-home sibling. The authors replace the twins with quantum detectors, small systems that click when they absorb energy from a quantum field. And couple both to the same field as their worldlines diverge and reunite.

The detectors' transition rates and the entanglement that builds between them carry the memory of the trip. The sharpest finding is that the turns leave marks. Changes in direction of acceleration leave distinctive imprints on both the responses and the entanglement. These features have no classical counterpart. The authors note these effects might matter in black hole spacetimes, where detectors on different trajectories probe the field near the horizon. The ten-page paper keeps the model simple so the imprint stays visible.
arxiv-2512-11108:
Jonathan Kamp, Roos Bakker, and Dominique Blok show that tools explaining language model decisions carry hidden biases of their own. Feature attribution methods highlight which words drove a prediction, yet different methods give very different explanations for the same input. Users who notice may distrust the tools, while others may trust them too much.

The authors organise these biases with three general measures covering which words get credited and where in the text credit falls. They tested two transformer models first on a controlled artificial task, then on a natural causal relation task. Models that scored high on word based bias scored low on position bias, and vice versa. Odd or anomalous explanations were also more likely to be biased. The work argues explanation quality must be audited, not assumed.
arxiv-2601-06908:
Hakan Cebeci and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers note on the matter coupling in exotic general massive 3D gravity. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Within exterior algebra formalism, we revisit and study the matter coupling in Exotic General Massive 3D Gravity (EGMG), previously introduced in [ 11 ] .

Considering that the matter Lagrangian is both metric co-frame and connection dependent in general. We explicitly construct associated source 2-form by algebraically solving auxiliary 1-form fields in terms of gravitational field variables, energy-momentum and hyper-momentum 2-forms. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07308:
Manuel Parra-Royón and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers bringing computation to the data. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Purpose: Serverless computing is a paradigm in which the underlying infrastructure is fully managed by the provider.

Enabling applications and services to be executed with elastic resource provisioning and minimal operational overhead. A core model within this paradigm is Function-as-a-Service (FaaS), where lightweight functions are deployed and triggered on demand, scaling seamlessly with workload. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-08108:
Bowen Li and seven co-authors present a prompting method that aims to cut bias in language models. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that methods like chain-of-thought have improved reasoning. Yet many prompting strategies use too many tokens and generalize poorly across varied reasoning tasks.

The team combines adaptive causal prompting with sketch-of-thought, a compact reasoning style. Causal prompting targets the sources of biased answers rather than surface wording alone. Sketch-of-thought keeps the reasoning trace short, which lowers token cost. For practitioners, the paper offers a route to fairer answers that is also cheaper to run across diverse tasks.
arxiv-2601-08208: Sylvain Crovisier and Enrique Pujals wrote a 2026 arXiv paper that sets out a new sense of a critical set for maps of a surface. The maps are two-dimensional diffeomorphisms, smooth warps that can be run in reverse. The set is built into the map itself. It plays the role that critical points play in one dimension. At such a point, the rate of change drops to zero, and those points block a trait called hyperbolicity. A like set on a surface could sort how wild acts arise.
arxiv-2601-08908:
Anna Biggs builds a quantum toy model that acts like a known wild model, yet has no built in chance. The known model is the SYK model, a set of bits that link in wild ways. It is a prime test bed for black hole like acts in a lab sized system. Its wild links are oft set by random picks, which blur what is law and what is luck.

Biggs gives a clean model with fixed rules. It keeps a spin type symmetry, and its charge is built from a known spin sum sign. At low power it acts like the SYK case with extra symmetry. A reader in theory gets a tidier test bed for wild quantum acts.
arxiv-2601-09008:
Amar Kavuri, Howard Gifford, and Mini Das study how the eye hunts for a faint sign in a noisy image. Such hunts guide care scans, bag checks, and fault checks. The eye does not scan in a flat way. It jumps to zones that look like the sign, and skips zones that look like plain noise. The size of traits in sign and noise steer those jumps.

The team varies trait size in both sign and back noise. They track where the eye goes and how oft the sign is found. The aim is to learn when a sign blends in by size, not just by shade. A reader who designs scan tasks gets facts on eye moves. They can shape an image so a key sign draws the eye.
arxiv-2601-09108:
Yanguang Sun and three co-authors fine tune vast image models to mark things in earth shots from space. Such shots guide farm, flood, and town work. To mark a roof or a road, a model must place it true to the pixel. Past work used mid size models, tuned in full. Vast base models hold more skill, but full tune of them is dear.

The team uses wave expert guides to tune just key parts. Wave tools split a shot by trait size, from broad land to fine edge. Guides steer tune to parts that hold the marks. A reader in earth sight gets a lean tune plan. It seeks vast model skill at a cost a small team can pay.
arxiv-2601-09208:
Miki Ueno gives a character led AI friend named Mikasa, drawn from Japan's oshi culture. Oshi is the fan love for a dear character or star, held with warm zeal. New chat and sight tools let such a friend talk with rich mood. Yet most AI friends lose users in weeks. Talk feels fresh at first, then flat and same.

Mikasa is built to hold zeal over long use. Its character, mood range, and talk style aim to grow a bond, not just fill time. Ueno sets out what was built and why each pick was made. A reader in AI friend work gets a case where culture, not just tech, shapes the design.
arxiv-2601-09308:
Peter Harremoes proves a core law of measure work by way of facts and codes. The law is the Radon-Nikodym theorem. It says one spread law can be set as a rate of a next, when the first can not live where the next is null. That rate is the base for entropy and for gap gauges in facts work. Yet most texts on chance skip its proof as too hard.

Harremoes gives a proof that facts work can own. It builds the rate from code and squeeze ideas that field knows well. A reader in that field gets a key law with a proof in their own tongue, not a loan from a hard text.
arxiv-2601-09408:
R. Turrisi reports for the ePIC collaboration on a detector being built for the future Electron-Ion Collider. The 2026 arXiv paper describes the Silicon Vertex Tracker, a key part of the ePIC detector system. The collider, planned at Brookhaven National Laboratory, will probe the strong force inside matter.

The vertex tracker provides high-precision tracking of particles and reconstruction of the points where they were born. Silicon sensors must sit close to the beam and still survive the radiation there. The paper lays out the design and current status of the subsystem. Its performance will shape how sharply the collider can image protons and nuclei.
arxiv-2601-09508:
Jean C. Peyen shows how to sample powersets at random without a costly helper. The 2026 arXiv paper uses Boltzmann sampling, a method that draws random structures with known chances. For structures whose counting sequence stays bounded, the sampler runs efficiently without ever evaluating the generating function.

An algorithm is given, implemented, and tested. Its runtimes match those of existing Boltzmann samplers in the literature. The author also proposes two extensions for structures with unbounded counting sequences. Random sampling of this kind feeds testing, simulation, and the study of typical shapes in combinatorics.
arxiv-2601-09608:
Arjun Nayak and a large team describe a new attosecond light source at the ELI ALPS facility. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents the SYLOS Compact high-harmonic beamline. High-order harmonic generation is the standard lab route to attosecond pulses of extreme ultraviolet light.

Producing enough flux for nonlinear XUV photoionization has been possible for only a few groups. The compact beamline is designed to supply that flux in a smaller footprint. Attosecond pulses let scientists film electrons moving inside atoms and molecules. A more accessible source widens who can run such experiments.
arxiv-2601-09708:
Chi-Pin Huang and seven co-authors speed up robots that think before they act. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents Fast-ThinkAct for vision-language-action tasks. Such robots must take in a scene, plan in words or thought, and then move with care.

Writing out long chains of thought improves generalization but slows reaction badly. Fast-ThinkAct compresses the plan into a verbalizable latent form: short to run, still readable as words. The robot keeps the benefit of planning without the long pause. Faster reasoning matters when a robot works beside people or handles moving objects.
arxiv-2601-10408:
Luke Mortimer, Leonardo Zambrano, Antonio Acín, and Donato Farina bound traits of large quantum rigs from thin data. Such traits show how new acts emerge in big rigs. Labs can oft read just a few traits, and with few shots. The full state stays out of reach.

Past bounds were set as if shots were vast. The team add the true shot count to the math. They use a class of plans named semidefinite programs. Those plans yield bounds that hold with a set chance. The work makes bounds honest for real labs, where data is thin.
arxiv-2601-10608:
Axel Seifert, Fabian Jakub, Christoph Siewert, Leonie von Terzi, and Stefan Kneifel examine the shape of large snowflakes. Snow and ice shape weather and climate in deep ways. Much of the rain that reaches the ground starts as ice high above. The flakes that fall are rarely the neat six-sided crystals of popular images.

Most large flakes are aggregates, clumps formed when small ice crystals collide and stick. The parts include flat plates, columns, and branched dendrites. The authors study the geometry of these clumps, since shape affects how fast flakes fall and melt. Better shape models feed into sharper weather forecasts and climate simulations.
arxiv-2601-10808:
Mikhail Chernikov and Peter Trifonov speed up decoding for ABS+ polar codes. Polar codes are error-correcting codes that split a channel into good and bad sub-channels. ABS+ codes generalize Arikan's original design and polarize much faster. Decoding them well is the practical test. The authors build the SCL decoder in the LLR domain.

LLRs, log-likelihood ratios, are the natural currency of soft decoding. They also optimize the SCL algorithm to cut the cost of computing those ratios. Faster, leaner decoding matters for 5G-style links and storage systems. The paper helps a strong code family move closer to hardware that must decode at line speed.
arxiv-2601-10908:
Jaime Luisi, John C. Forbes, Heather V. Rusk, and Benjamin Gullick follow brown dwarfs that gain mass and cross into stardom. A brown dwarf that steals mass from a binary partner can pass the hydrogen burning limit. That limit divides brown dwarfs from true low-mass stars. The authors call the crossers pink dwarfs and trace their fates.

Some reach the main sequence and end up looking like ordinary low-mass stars. Others stay brown dwarf-like, unable to burn hydrogen fast enough to power their glow. The split decides what telescopes will see millions of years later. The work helps astronomers read odd stars whose past hides a stolen-mass chapter.
arxiv-2601-11208:
Rodrigo Nicolau Almeida studies a fine point in intuitionistic logic. His 2026 preprint looks at local tabularity and a stronger form. Intuitionistic logic, called IPC, drops some rules of classical logic. Above IPC, local tabularity has proved a hard trait to map.

The stronger form is named uniform local tabularity in the work. It asks that all formulas match some of a fixed depth. Depth here counts how deep implications nest in a formula. The contrast with the logic S4 frames the study. S4 is a modal logic where such traits are better known. The work sharpens the map of where IPC-based logics stay tame.
arxiv-2601-11308:
Ferhat Sindy, Annalisa Buffa, and Marco Picasso flag errors in finite difference runs. Their 2026 preprint gives a new recovery-based error indicator. Finite difference methods solve equations on a grid of points. High-order versions are sharp but still hold some error.

The method works after the run, by post-processing its values. Grid values are moved into a polynomial finite element space. A recovery indicator then reads the gradient error from that form. The indicator keeps a polynomial-preserving trait from past work. That trait keeps the check exact on smooth polynomial cases. Users gain a cheap map of where the grid errs. Such maps guide where to refine the grid next.
arxiv-2601-11408:
Qinlin Chen and eight coauthors build a static analysis frame for Verilog. Their 2026 preprint names the framework Qihe. Verilog is the tongue used to describe hardware designs. Static analysis reads code without running it at all.

In software, static analysis has thrived for decades. It finds bugs, checks security, and aids understanding of code. General frameworks supply the base that such tools share. Hardware code has lacked a like base for Verilog work. Qihe aims to fill that gap for chip design teams. A shared frame cuts the cost of each new check. It could bring software-grade tooling to hardware design.
arxiv-2601-11608:
Ganesh Bikshandi reshapes CNNs to fit specialized AI hardware. The 2026 preprint uses NVIDIA Tensor Cores as the case study. Convolutional neural networks sit at the center of modern AI. Their speed is often capped by hardware constraints, not math.

Tensor Cores demand set shapes for fast execution paths. Input channels must be multiples of 8, for instance. Some paths want multiples of 512 to run at full pace. CPU frameworks like oneDNN impose like rules for blocked formats. Bikshandi reformulates networks to meet those hardware rules. The reform keeps the model's task while easing its layout. Hardware-aware forms can unlock speed that naive forms waste.
arxiv-2601-12208:
Yunzhe Li, Richie Yueqi Feng, Tianxin Wei, and Chin-Chia Hsu grade chat systems in multi-turn talks via co-evolution. Past grading uses fixed rubrics and fixed chat context made by hand. That static form misses the diverse acts that dialogue models show in real talks.

Their frame, called CoReflect in the work, joins simulation and grading in one loop. Chats grow harder as rubrics refine, and rubrics refine as chats reveal gaps. An adaptive loop can catch faults that fixed tests miss. The work aims for more true grades of chat skill.
arxiv-2601-12308:
Anurag Kaushish, Ayan Sar, Sampurna Roy, and their co-authors classify remote sensing images from few labelled cases. Few-shot work in this field is hard for three reasons. Labelled data are scarce, domains shift a lot, and geo objects span many scales.

Their adaptive multi-scale correlation meta-network is built for those three facts. Meta-learning trains a model to adapt fast to new classes. Multi-scale traits catch both small and large land features. The work aims for sound maps from brief labelled sets.  Meta traits must move fast to new land classes.
arxiv-2601-12608:
Himadri Halder introduces a new notion in complex analysis: the second Bohr radius. The classic Bohr radius marks how far a power series keeps a key bound. Halder extends that idea to vector valued pluriharmonic functions. These functions live on complete Reinhardt domains in complex space of several variables.

The work builds on a 2000 study by Lev Aizenberg. Aizenberg treated the corresponding problem for complex valued holomorphic functions. Moving to vector values and pluriharmonic maps adds real difficulty. Radii of this kind give sharp, quantitative control over series. They matter in the theory of function spaces and operator theory alike.
arxiv-2601-12808:
Tong Wu and six co authors rethink how communication systems rebuild images at the receiver. Conventional systems, and even AI driven joint source channel coding, follow Shannon rate distortion theory. Generic distortion metrics fail to capture human visual perception, though. Reconstructions guided by them often come out blurred or unrealistic to the eye.

The team move from distortion oriented reconstruction to semantic consistent generation. Their joint source channel generation coding aims to keep meaning, not just pixels. A generated image can look sharp while staying true to the sent content. That shift suits low bandwidth links where bits are precious. The work bridges information theory and generative modeling.
arxiv-2601-13008:
Jingwei Wang and Ligong Bian set out a way to work out how fast a false vacuum decays. Their method applies to electroweak theories in a general number of space dims, written as D dims. Vacuum decay is a core topic in early universe physics.

The pair give one joined treatment for three kinds of fields. These are scalar fields, fermion fields, and gauge boson fields. The tool kit pairs a WKB method with a way to handle sums that would else blow up. A key plus is fast settling of the sums. The sums still settle fast even when the spin-like index grows large.
arxiv-2601-13808:
Ilaria Svampa, Sonia L'Innocente, Stefano Mancini, and Andreas Winter study qubits built on p-adic numbers in 2026. P-adic quantum mechanics swaps real numbers for an other number system. A single p-adic qubit is a two-dimensional representation of the p-adic group SO(3). The team now asks how to compose such qubits into systems.

They investigate composite systems of p-adic qubits and p-adically controlled logic gates. The work covers entanglement, the linked state of two qubits. It also covers universal quantum logic gates, which can build any operation. The study tests if p-adic quantum theory can support full computing.
arxiv-2601-14008:
Jianing Wang bounds gravitational wave output from a bold early-universe model in 2026. The model has an early phase that violates the null energy condition. That condition is a basic rule on how energy can flow in relativity. Breaking it can drive exotic cosmic histories, like a bounce.

Wang shows perturbative unitarity bounds strongly constrain this scenario. Unitarity is the rule that probabilities must sum to one in quantum theory. The bounds limit both the amplitude and the spectral tilt of primordial gravitational waves. Such limits tell observers if the model's waves could ever be seen.
arxiv-2601-15108:
Oleksandr Gamayun and Miłosz Panfil solve an exact problem for a one-dimensional quantum gas. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with hard rods, particles that cannot pass through each other on a line. They target the dynamical structure factor, a key probe of the gas.

The authors obtain an exact analytic formula for that factor. It holds for any many-body state of the system. They study two cases in detail: the ground state and states at finite temperature. They also report a universal random matrix behavior in the result, a pattern shared with random matrix theory.
arxiv-2601-15408:
Pablo Messina, Andrés Villa, and co-authors teach medical models to point at what they describe. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with radiology report generation by vision-language models. Such models can draft reports, but their grounding is weak: words often fail to match the image.

That mismatch makes reports unreliable. The authors present CURE, an error-aware curriculum learning framework. It improves grounding and report quality with no extra data. The model learns from its own errors in a planned order. Reports thus tie each finding more tightly to the visual evidence in the scan.
arxiv-2601-15508:
Haaris Mian and four co-authors rethink how to measure a character's weight in a novel in a 2026 arXiv paper. Most models score characters by their presence in scenes. They count actions, named mentions, and lines of dialogue. That lens favors the character who shows up most. The main character wins by default under such counts.

The authors argue that presence alone misses much of what makes a character matter. A figure can shape a plot while rarely on stage. Their work builds computational representations of character significance that go further. The abstract frames the flaw more than the fix, so details rest in the full text. For digital humanities, the stakes are clear. Better measures of significance mean better maps of how stories work.
arxiv-2601-15708:
Junseok Kim, Nakyeong Yang, and Kyomin Jung blend prompting styles for language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Role-play prompting steers a model by giving it a persona. It can improve zero-shot reasoning. The gains are inconsistent, though. They vary by task and even by instance. The authors read that inconsistency as a clue. Plain prompting and role-play may hold complementary strengths.

Their method is called Persona Switch. It mixes distinct perspectives at decoding time, per the title. Decoding is when the model picks its words, one by one. Switching personas mid-stream may combine the best of each stance. For users, the promise is steadier reasoning without picking the right persona in advance. The work treats prompt design as a control problem, not a guessing game.
arxiv-2601-15808:
Yuxuan Wan and six co-authors strengthen research agents at test time in a 2026 arXiv paper. Deep research agents automate knowledge discovery and problem-solving. Most work on them improves the policy model through post-training. This team takes another path. They evolve the agent's ability at inference time. The agent iteratively verifies its own outputs. Carefully crafted rubrics guide those checks.

Rubrics spell out what a good answer must do. Verification against them can catch errors before they compound. Inference-time scaling spends more compute at run time for better results. The title names that scaling as the lever. For teams that cannot retrain huge models, test-time methods are attractive. This paper adds a rubric-guided version to that toolbox.
arxiv-2601-15908:
Claudio Bonanno and Sharvari Neetin Tikekar study escape from open dynamical systems in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their maps expand the unit interval non-uniformly. A parabolic fixed point sits at the origin, where motion slows. The maps admit an ergodic invariant measure, finite or infinite. The authors cut a hole around that fixed point. The hole is an interval containing the origin. Orbits that enter it escape the system.

They analyze the escape rate of the open system. Then they track how that rate behaves as the hole shrinks. Intermittent maps model systems that linger, then burst. Escape rates quantify how long trajectories survive before leaking out. Such results apply to chaotic transport and to any system with a slow trap at its heart.
arxiv-2601-16108:
Marzieh Adeli Shamsabad and Hamed Ghodrati build a tool to spot false climate claims in mixed media. Their 2026 preprint notes how false posts now use strong pics and clips. Text checks alone miss tricks that sit in the image. False claims spread fast on social feeds. Late acts on climate can stem from such false posts.

The pair join vision and language models with facts from known sources. The joint check weighs words, pics and source facts as one. Proof from firm sources helps flag claims that clash with known facts. The tool aims to catch false posts that look true at a glance. It serves teams who guard climate facts online.
arxiv-2601-16208:
Shengbang Tong and coauthors scale image spread coders with a new code form. Their 2026 preprint uses Representation Autoencoders as the code base. Those coders train in a rich sense space of high size. On ImageNet they showed clear gains for spread models. The team now scales that path for text to image coders built as spread chains.
