Scale tests check if rich codes keep their gains at big size. Rich codes may let the spread chain learn form fast. They may also lift the grade of pics from text prompts. The work adds a path to strong text to image tools. It tests code choice as a lever for scale.
arxiv-2601-16808:
Huiyun Xiao and a team of six co-authors study drops of quantum fluid that hold their own shape. Such drops form in pairs of cold atom gases. The two gases pull and push on each with unlike force. Their 2026 preprint maps how that force gap warps the drop. Math tools track the drop's ground state and its hums.

As the force gap grows, the drop's form shifts. It moves from a round hump to a flat-top shape. The team also tracks how the drop rings when poked. Such drops test deep rules of quantum fluids. They may serve as clean labs for wave and flow work.
arxiv-2601-17008:
Haochong Xia and a team of nine co-authors build a trade bot that plans for bad days. Trade bots learn from past market runs. They oft shine in tests, then fade in live trade. Live markets shift with news, laws, and crowd moods. Their 2026 preprint trains bots on fake hostile markets. A Bayes frame then weighs doubt as it trades.

Fake foes stress the bot with harsh shifts. The bot learns acts that hold up in rough seas. Doubt marks curb bold bets when signs clash. Such care may cut big loss days for funds. It also shows a path to stress-test trade AI.
arxiv-2601-17108:
Dianxin Luan and a team of six co-authors sharpen how radio nets read their own channels. OFDM waves split a stream in many thin bands. Each band's path traits must be gauged fast and true. Big band counts make that gauge hard work. Their 2026 preprint builds MambaNet, a net that mixes two tools for the gauge. One tool tracks long links twixt bands.

The next tool, self-attention, weighs which bands count most. The mix aims for true gauges at low cost. True gauges keep data streams fast and clean. Next-wave radio nets need such lean skill.
arxiv-2601-17208:
Alejandro R. Urzúa wrote a teaching paper on a well known model in quantum physics. The model is the two-mode Jaynes-Cummings model. It deals with an atom linked to two modes of light. Urzúa works in the dispersive regime, where the atom and field are far off resonance.

Step by step, he derives the first-order effective Hamiltonian for the model. A small-change unitary transform removes terms that do not resonate. What is left shows clear frequency shifts from the atom. Those shifts act like a beam splitter set up between the two field modes. The clear path makes a tough topic easier for students to learn.
arxiv-2601-17408:
Harsharaj Pathak and Vineeth N. Balasubramanian work on source-free domain adaptation. The task moves a trained model to a new domain with no labels. Source data cannot be used at that stage. Most strong methods lean on neighborhood consistency. They trust that near points share labels. Bad neighborhoods can mislead that trust and spread error.

The authors use batch-wise cosine similarity as their guide. Similarity across a batch gives a broader, steadier signal. That should cut the harm from one bad neighbor. Source-free methods matter where data is private or lost. Medical and retail models face that wall often. A steadier method widens where adaptation can work.
arxiv-2601-17508:
Binghong Wu and Pascal O. Vontobel analyze the Bethe permanent for block-structured positive matrices. The permanent sums products over all matchings in a matrix. It is exact but hard to compute at scale. The Bethe permanent gives a tractable approximation. It runs through the sum-product algorithm on a factor graph.

The authors use double covers to study that approximation. Block structure is common in real matrices. Knowing when the approximation is tight guides its use. Permanents arise in counting, physics, and network problems. A fast, trusted approximation widens their reach. The double-cover method gives a lens on error. It tells users where the Bethe value can stand in for truth.
arxiv-2601-17608:
Dong Yoon Lee and four co-authors report field experience with a home health system for older adults. Adult children often care for aging parents from afar. They want remote tools that are plug-and-play. Privacy must hold while activity is tracked all day. The system aims to give real-time, clear, actionable updates.

Deployment experience shows where lab designs meet real homes. Sensors, networks, and family habits all test the plan. Lessons from live use guide the next design round. Aging in place is a growing need worldwide. Tools that families trust can delay costly care moves. The report grounds design claims in homes, not demos.
arxiv-2601-17808:
Alejandro Medina and Mary Lauren Benton look for variety, not just a single best answer, in DNA patterns. Their 2026 preprint deals with motif discovery in liver data from ChIP-seq tests. A motif is a short DNA pattern that tends to appear where proteins bind. The classic way to find motifs seeks one top pattern that best fits the data.

Real biology is messier than one pattern. The same data can hold several good motif readings, each tied to a real process. The authors use MAP-Elites, a search method that keeps many strong but distinct results. That choice gives a map of options, not a lone winner. Such a map can show the range of signals in the data.
arxiv-2601-18408:
Anup Dixit works on a deep guess about how number fields grow. Number fields are sets built by adding roots of whole number rules to the plain ratios. Two counts rule each field: one counts its ideal groups, and one sets the size of its unit grid. An old guess says how the pair of counts should grow as fields get large.

All past proofs shrink the task, by group tricks, to a known hard case for square fields. Dixit takes on fields whose group is close to the full set of swaps of their roots. That near-full case is the hard core of the guess. A proof here would push the guess close to a full proof for all fields. The work thus marks a key step in a long hunt in pure maths.
arxiv-2601-18608:
Fabian Fumagalli, R. Teal Witter, and Christopher Musco speed up a way to grade how much each fact counts in a model's call. The grade comes from a fair-share rule in game maths: each fact gets the share it adds, on mean, to the joint worth of all facts. To get the grade in full takes a huge count of runs, one per set of facts. A famed shortcut samples runs and fits a line to guess the grades.

Their plan adds cross terms to that fit, so pairs of facts can share worth in the guess. Those terms catch cases where two facts count most when they come as a pair. A truer fit could give the same grades for far fewer runs. Staff who must tell why a model made a call need grades they can trust at a cost they can pay.
arxiv-2601-19008:
Jia Xu Wei and Wei Wei redefine what an efficient network is. In network design, talk of efficiency often just means low delay or high total flow. The pair argue that such talk mixes up speed with true efficiency, and they offer a cost based view instead.

Their view counts the hardware cost needed to keep a promise: no flow ever gets blocked. A design that meets the promise with less hardware is, in their sense, more efficient. This lens can change how switch layouts are judged, since the cheapest layout that never blocks may beat a faster but costlier one.
arxiv-2601-19108:
Sharvari Nadkarni-Ghosh and Tanush Reddy Vaka model the messy late stages of a modified gravity theory. In f(R) gravity, an extra field can hide itself near dense objects, a trick called the Chameleon mechanism. The team studies how matter clumps evolve in such models once the clumps grow large and the math turns nonlinear.

Their new step is an iterative fix for the nonlinear equation that governs the field. They show the scheme at work on a spherical case. Sound tools for the nonlinear regime are what let such theories be tested against real maps of galaxies.
arxiv-2601-19208:
Shawn Im and three co-authors open up how transformers learn that certain words belong together. Links like the one between bird and flew let models generalize instead of merely memorizing text. Knowing how such links form is key to a mechanical account of how these models work.

The team studies the leading terms of the gradient, the biggest push in each training step. Those terms, they argue, explain how word links get written into the model. A mechanical story of learning ties deep learning back to language theory and may guide better training.
arxiv-2601-19608:
Louis Dailly works in complex geometry on the stability of special spaces. His setting is a log Fano pair, a geometric space paired with a boundary part. The space carries a singular Kähler-Einstein metric, a notion of perfect balance in its shape. On such a space one can build an adapted tangent sheaf, a tool that tracks directions along the space while respecting the boundary.

Dailly shows that this sheaf, and a related canonical extension, are polystable. Stability here is measured against a class pulled back by any adapted map into the space. Polystability is a strong regularity property with deep consequences. Results like this support the broader program linking stability to the existence of special metrics.
arxiv-2601-19708:
Javier Alonso-García and colleagues present a stellar atlas of our galaxy's plane, seen in near-infrared light. Dust blocks visible light from the galactic plane and the outer bulge. Near-infrared light slips through much of that dust. The atlas comes from the VVVX survey, a public project carried out with the VISTA telescope.

The survey mapped the plane and outer bulge to reveal stars hidden from optical telescopes. An atlas like this is a reference for everyone studying the Milky Way's structure. It supports work on star clusters, variable stars, and the galaxy's history. Catalogues of positions and brightnesses let other teams plan follow-up studies. The result is a clearer census of our home galaxy's crowded heart.
arxiv-2601-20008:
Amitay Sussholz, Tsevi Mazeh, and Simchon Faigler revisit how fast stars spin at their equators. They use line broadening measurements from the Gaia satellite's third data release. Rotation broadens a star's spectral lines, so the broadening betrays the spin. Their sample covers more than a hundred thousand stars, enough to map spin against temperature, mass, and age.

The large sample clearly shows the Kraft break, a sharp change in rotation behaviour near a well-known temperature and mass. Above the break, stars keep spinning fast; below it, they brake with age. A clean map of this transition tests theories of how stars shed angular momentum. Gaia's scale turns an old qualitative picture into precise demographics.
arxiv-2601-20808:
Yifei Li and Glennys Farrar ask how well we truly know the matter around us in space. Their 2026 paper concerns the local large scale structure of the universe. That structure is the map of galaxies and dark matter near the Milky Way. Many studies need this map as a baseline. It feeds models of cosmic ray sources and forecasts of dark matter signals.

The authors compare two sources for that map. One is CosmicFlows, a well-known catalog built from galaxy motions. The other is Biteau's galaxy catalog with cloning, a method that fills gaps by copying known structure. The paper weighs how far the two agree. Gaps between them mark where our knowledge of the nearby universe is still soft. The work matters for any study that starts from the local map.
arxiv-2601-21408:
Xinan He and ten co-authors build a detector for fake videos made by the newest generators. Tools like Veo and Wan now make clips so clean that the old giveaways are gone. Gross errors in meaning and flicker across frames no longer betray a fake.

The team hunts subtler traces instead. Their method reads how a clip sits on the learned manifold of real video, layer by layer. It also tracks tiny wobbles across time that humans miss. Finding reliable traces matters for news, courts, and platforms that must tell real footage from synthetic clips.
arxiv-2601-21508:
Johannes Bertram, Luciano Dyballa, T. Anderson Keller, Savik Kinger, and Steven W. Zucker open up a foundation model of brain activity and inspect its parts. Such models fit visual brain responses well, but their inner workings are opaque. That opacity limits what they can teach about the brain itself.

The authors probe the model the way a physiologist probes real neurons. They test each unit's response over time to controlled stimuli. The check asks how neural the model truly is, unit by unit. Answers could turn these models from mere predictors into tools for understanding vision.
arxiv-2601-21808:
Jörg Weissmüller studies how solute atoms cross the boundary between two crystals. The setting involves two solid solution phases that share an interface, with atoms sitting in the gaps of each crystal's structure. Inside each phase, atoms move fast by diffusion, so each side stays internally balanced.

The 2026 paper derives a rate equation for the thermally activated transfer across that interface. Treating each phase as an ensemble of particles, statistical mechanics predicts how many atoms occupy the transition states at equilibrium. Rates of this kind govern real processes in alloys. These range from aging and hardening to corrosion. A firm equation helps connect atomic jumps to changes engineers can measure.
arxiv-2601-22108:
Shuqi Ke and Giulia Fanti ask whether a little verified feedback can steer a very expensive process. Foundation models are pretrained with fixed proxy goals, such as predicting the next token. Those proxies can waste compute on skills that downstream users never need.

Their 2026 preprint introduces value-based pretraining with downstream feedback. A small amount of verified information about the goal guides where the pretraining effort goes, measured by value rather than by the proxy alone. If steering works, the huge cost of pretraining could be aimed better. It could target capabilities people actually want. It would not be spread evenly over everything a model might ever be asked to do.
arxiv-2601-22208:
Evelien Riddell and co-authors probe where language models fail as cloud troubleshooters. Root cause analysis finds the true source of failures in complex software systems. Modern cloud systems are highly distributed and interdependent, so faults propagate across many hops and symptoms appear far from their causes.

Recent models promise help, but the authors' title names what they found: models get stalled, biased, and confused on these tasks. Their 2026 preprint uncovers specific reasoning failures in cloud-based root cause analysis. Naming the failure modes matters for operators. They must decide how much to trust an AI copilot during an outage. Wrong guidance then wastes the scarcest resource, which is time.
arxiv-2601-22308:
Javier Carnerero-Cano, Luis Muñoz-González, Phillippa Spencer, and Emil Lupu test whether sneaky data attacks can fool regression models. Such models predict a number, and they run plants, labs, and works of all kinds. Their 2026 preprint notes that attack studies often assume powers no real foe would have.

The team craft attacks that stay hidden yet still bend the output. They then check whether known guards can catch them. The result is a sterner, more real test of model safety. It helps owners of key systems judge their true risk. Guards can then be built to match.
arxiv-2601-22408:
Shrey Goel and Pranam Chatterjee design peptide chains by a path that stays in safe chemical ground. Peptides are short chains of amino acids, used as drugs and probes. Their 2026 preprint notes that the space of chains is discrete and tightly ruled, and many mid-steps are not sound.

Old generative tools follow fixed spoil-and-fix paths that can cross poor ground. Their method, built on Schrödinger bridge matching, seeks the least-action path instead. Paths that stay sound yield chains more likely to work in the lab. The work could cut wasted synthesis. It suits drug and materials design.
arxiv-2601-22708:
Haonan He and a large team sort the sprawling family of LoRA variants into one map, with code and tests. LoRA tunes big models by training small add-on matrices, a cheap and strong trick. Their 2026 preprint notes that the flood of variants has fragmented the field.

Their taxonomy, review, shared codebase, and head-to-head tests give users a way to choose. A clear map ends much duplicated effort. It also shows which tweaks truly help. The work is a service to every team that fine-tunes. Order, here, is the contribution.
arxiv-2601-23008:
Saak Gabriyelyan, Alexander V. Osipov, and Evgenii Reznichenko revisit a classic property of topological vector spaces. A Baire space is one where countable intersections of open dense sets stay dense, a mark of completeness-like strength. Earlier results tied this property to a condition called property (K).

Other work showed every sequentially complete Fréchet–Urysohn locally convex space is Baire. The authors examine which Baire-type properties such spaces hold more broadly. These questions sit in functional analysis, the theory behind much of modern applied mathematics. Baire-type properties measure how rich a space's topology is, and they underpin many existence arguments in analysis.
arxiv-2601-23208:
Arie Wortsman, Federica Gerace, Bruno Loureiro, and Yue M. Lu analyze masked self-supervised learning with random matrix theory. Masked training, foundational for transformers, hides parts of the input and predicts them. Training mixes many masking patterns, creating a joint, matrix-valued predictor rather than a single estimator.

That object encodes how coordinates condition on one another, posing new analytical challenges. Random matrix tools are well suited to such large, structured objects. Theory of this kind explains why masked pretraining works as well as it does. How coordinates condition on one another is encoded in that matrix-valued predictor, the new object the theory must handle.
arxiv-2603-01508:
Tony Rost asks a forward-looking question in this 2026 work: could a country cope if AI systems might one day merit moral concern? Science now tests AI designs against leading theories of mind, and none yet counts as a strong case. Still, Rost argues that even a credible chance calls for early planning.

He builds a Sentience Readiness Index that scores nations across six weighted areas. The index covers thirty-one jurisdictions and uses expert scoring with language-model help and repeat review. No place earns more than a partly prepared grade, and the top score still sits below half marks. Research settings score best everywhere, while job-level readiness scores worst, which Rost reads as a clear gap to close.
arxiv-2603-01608:
Wenye Lin and Kai Han improve the reasoning of large language models without erasing what they already know. Their 2026 work targets a known trade-off: extra training boosts thought, but it can wipe prior skills. Past work credits fresh on-policy data, yet the pair find a second, overlooked cause.

They show that a hidden regularizing effect sits inside a popular preference method reward estimate. Their method, SPoT, first fixes wrong steps in training traces with tiny edits from an expert oracle. Those near-native traces then train the model with a simple right-or-wrong score per trace. With just a few thousand fixed math pairs, a mid-size model gains clear accuracy in brief training. Gains hold on both familiar and new task types.
arxiv-2603-01808:
Kaiming Cui, Guang-Yao Xiao, Fabo Feng, and colleagues map where brown dwarfs are scarce between planets and stars. Their 2026 study joins radial velocity and astrometry data to build one large sample of wide-orbit companions. Brown dwarfs sit at the blurry border of planets and stars, so their scarcity pattern tests how each class forms.

The sample holds fifty-five giant planets, brown dwarfs, and low-mass stellar companions around sun-like stars. A rigorous count finds a clear brown dwarf desert near a set mass, with no sign it ends out to wide orbits. A new population of giant planets and light brown dwarfs also appears past the water-ice line. Metal and orbit trends point to two distinct formation routes for the groups. A combined population model reproduces the desert, which backs the dual formation view.
arxiv-2603-02008:
Faisal Mohamed, Catherine Ji, Benjamin Eysenbach, and Glen Berseth teach agents to explore with no outside rewards at all. Their 2026 work argues that good exploration tracks not just visited places, but how the agent represents the world. Temporal representations capture what a state implies about the future across many possible tasks.

Their method guides exploration toward states whose future outcomes are hard to predict. Temporal contrastive learning supplies those representations without full state reconstruction costs. The agent thus seeks states that add the most to its knowledge of the environment. Tests span locomotion, manipulation, and embodied tasks with complex exploratory behavior emerging. Such behavior usually needs hand-crafted extrinsic rewards, which this simpler time-based strategy avoids entirely.
arxiv-2603-02208:
Valentin Lacombe, Valentin Quesnel, and Damien Sileo build a data factory for reasoning in this 2026 paper. Training on tasks with checked answers can stretch what language models can reason about. Old task makers use fixed puzzles, so their data lacks breadth at scale. Their suite, Reasoning Core, makes fresh symbolic tasks on demand.

Tasks span planning, logic with equality, grammar rules, cause chains, and equation sets. Each task pairs with a solver that checks answers with full rigor. Task hardness can be dialed up or down for staged training. Solved traces can also be kept as teaching examples for models. Mixing this data into training lifted later reasoning and kept language skill intact. Even top models found the tasks hard with no examples.
arxiv-2603-02308:
Akshat Pandey, Aditya Mahadevan, A Alan Middleton, and Daniel Fisher study a disordered magnet at low temperature in this 2026 paper. Their model is the two-dimensional random-bond Ising model, a grid of spins with random link strengths. Frustration drives a switch between magnetic and nonmagnetic phases as temperature falls. A zero-temperature fixed point controls that switch and borders a spin glass phase.

The authors explain the point through a step-by-step rebuilding of the ground state. Each step adds frustration to a calm starting model until the target is reached. A mapping turns heat behavior into spectral traits of a linked quantum matrix. Disorder in that spectrum grows without bound along the flow. One exponent ties the spectral gap to system size and the spin stiffness at the fixed point.
arxiv-2603-02408:
Tobias Meier, Claire Marie Guimond, Raymond Pierrehumbert, and colleagues model the inside of a lava world in this 2026 paper. K2-141 b is a rocky planet with a magma ocean on its dayside. Extreme starlight couples its interior, air, and surface evolution. The team runs two-dimensional convection models that track volatile gases with tracers.

With a strong outer lid, mantle upwellings rise under the hottest and coldest points. Downwellings sink near the day-night borders, recycling crust in a one-sided tectonic style. The magma ocean runs a few hundred kilometers deep across models. Steady nightside volcanoes build a basalt crust and slowly drain mantle gases. Over a billion years, outgassing could reach tens of bars. Nightside eruptions stay too faint for current telescopes to detect.
arxiv-2603-02608:
Pavan Adroja and Sujoy Chakraborty wrote this 2026 mathematics paper on the Brauer group of certain moduli spaces. A moduli space is a space whose points stand for whole families of geometric objects. Their setting is a compact Riemann surface, a smooth closed curve, of genus at least three.

The authors compute the Brauer groups for spaces of stable parabolic connections and Higgs bundles. They also prove an equality for the related PGL case, matching a stack with the smooth part of its coarse space. The Brauer group measures whether a universal bundle can exist, so these results settle a basic structural question for these spaces.
arxiv-2603-02908:
Qi Zhang, Yifei Wang, Xiaohan Wang, and colleagues forecast whether fine-tuning a language model will help or hurt other skills. Their 2026 paper uses sparse autoencoders, tools that split a model's internal activity into cleaner features. Extra training shifts those features, and the shifts can spill into unrelated domains in poorly understood ways.

Their score, STS, finds which feature directions move during fine-tuning and matches those moves against target domains before any training happens. Across many models and domains, the score predicted real performance changes with strong correlation. An early extension to reinforcement learning is also reported. Because the features are interpretable, the score can guide training choices rather than merely warn about them after the fact.
arxiv-2603-03208:
Tracy Beck, Stephane Guilloteau, Gail Schaefer, and colleagues watch a young triple star system flare as two of its stars swing closest together. T Tauri South's close pair passed periastron in March 2023, and the ALMA telescope imaged the system before, during, and after. Their 2026 paper resolves the pair directly in the sharpest epochs.

Millimeter brightness rose as the passage heated the primary's disk and the surrounding dust, likely because the close approach triggered extra accretion onto the stars. Extended emission near the pair also changed shape and brightened, hinting at magnetic interaction or gravitational disruption of the disks. Around the northern star, a compact dust disk shows a shallow gap and a crescent of excess emission moving at orbital speed.
arxiv-2603-03308:
Adi Simhi and four colleagues study how a conversation's past can trap a language model. Earlier answers, even hallucinated ones, seem to steer later replies toward repeating the same stance. Their 2026 framework, History-Echoes, measures that pull in two ways at once: as probabilities over conversation states, and as geometry inside the model's hidden representations.

Three model families and six datasets cover varied behaviors, from errors to safety refusals. The two measures track each other closely. Persistence turns out to be a geometric trap: gaps in the model's inner space confine where its trajectory can go next. The finding links what a model does on the surface to the shape of its internal state, and the team's code is public.
arxiv-2603-03408:
G Alencar and three colleagues study black holes in a lower-dimensional version of Gauss-Bonnet gravity, an extension of general relativity with higher-curvature terms. They add quintessence, an exotic matter proposed to drive cosmic acceleration, and take the theory's limit down to three spacetime dimensions.
