The letter is document 208 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Adams was told to deal chiefly with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary. Seward's letters armed him with facts and wording for those meetings. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d308: A letter from a Mr. Wise to a Mr. Stuart, dated 18 October 1862, appears as document 308 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart served at the British legation in Washington, and the paper belongs to the volume's Anglo-American correspondence from the Civil War. The record supplies no first names, so the two surnames and the date are the firm facts.
frus-1863p1-d408:
On 3 March 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It appears as document 408 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Cases in these notes can look small, one ship or one arrested man, yet each tested the rules of neutrality. Both governments treated the precedents as serious business. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d508:
Writing on 12 May 1863, William H. Seward, Secretary of State addressed Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington in an official letter. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d608:
A dispatch dated 12 August 1863 went from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d108: Charles Bohlen, First Secretary at the Moscow embassy, wrote a memorandum dated November 9, 1943, preserved as Document 108 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Bohlen, a Russian speaker, was becoming the American government's sharpest interpreter of Soviet affairs, and his memoranda fed the Tehran briefings. The record gives the author and the date only. The paper is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d208:
Secretary of War Henry Stimson wrote a personal, confidential letter to Harry Hopkins, the President's special assistant, on 10 November 1943. Stimson says he has reflected on their talk of the day before and wants his views on paper, in case they help Hopkins or Roosevelt at the coming conferences.

His first point is Overlord, the planned invasion of France: preparations are on schedule, and any slip to midsummer would cost many thousands of lives, so Roosevelt must hold firm against diversions. Second, General Marshall must command Overlord himself, and soon. Third, no new chief of staff should be named yet; an acting chief can hold the post while Marshall is in London.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d308:
A revised American draft of the Cairo communiqué, dated 25 November 1943, was dictated by Harry Hopkins to Warrant Officer Cornelius that morning. It folds Roosevelt's handwritten changes into the draft of the day before, and it names the conference's members from all three delegations.

In joint-statement form, the text says the leaders have agreed on future military operations against Japan from China and Southeast Asia, promising continuous and ever stronger offensives. Pacific islands seized by Japan will be taken from her forever. Territory stolen from China, such as Manchuria and Formosa, will return to the Republic of China. All lands taken by violence and greed will be freed. Korea, in due time after Japan's fall, will become free and independent.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d408:
A first draft of the Tehran communiqué, undated and apparently an American paper, is printed here with its handwritten changes shown. An editorial headnote states that no evidence has been found of the draft being considered outside the American delegation. The sense of its third paragraph was, though, discussed at the plenary meeting of 30 November.

The draft has the three leaders declare their determination. Their nations are to work together in war and in the peace that follows. Complete agreement is claimed on the scope and timing of operations from east, west, and south. A direct address to the German people follows: We do not seek to enslave you, it says. But we mean to destroy your armies, your submarines, and your war plants from the air, relentlessly. Roosevelt's own hand supplied several of the strongest word changes, and Hopkins added the leaders' names at the end.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d508:
The Combined Administrative Committee reported to the Combined Chiefs of Staff in this paper dated December 15, 1943, a little over a week after the Second Cairo Conference. Administrative officers handled the supply, transport, and services side of the joint war effort. The State Department printed the report in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Grand strategy fails without administration: divisions need ports, fuel, food, and shipping space before they can fight. A committee report of this kind shows the logistical reckoning that followed Cairo's decisions. For readers, it offers the working underside of the summit, where the fine phrases of communiqués were tested against tonnage tables and supply lines.
frus-1944-quebec-d108:
Harry Hopkins, President Roosevelt's special assistant, sent this top-secret memorandum to Admiral William Leahy, the president's chief of staff, on September 7, 1944. It weighs in on a Joint Chiefs of Staff paper about what should happen to lend-lease material once Germany was beaten. Hopkins wrote days before Roosevelt and Churchill met at Quebec.

Hopkins argued the paper should not be approved. He pointed to the lend-lease agreements, which promised return of goods only at the end of the whole emergency, not after Germany alone fell. He also cited the shared munitions pool agreed with Britain. Acting alone, he warned, would stir needless friction with allies while Japan still had to be fought.
frus-1944-quebec-d208:
The Combined Chiefs took up the zones paper, C.C.S. 320/26, on September 16, 1944, and approved it with minor amendments as C.C.S. 320/27. Cunningham secured agreement that naval disarmament in American-controlled ports would sit with the American naval member of the Control Commission. He also suggested the American area include Bremerhaven, downriver from Bremen, where large ships berth.

Somervell noted American troops might also be supplied through Antwerp and Rotterdam, and raised an Inter-Allied commission for the Rhine. Logistics went to the Combined Administrative Committee. The meeting also approved Mediterranean "Rankin" planning and release of amphibious craft from Overlord. Marshall then reported Stilwell's news: Japanese advancing on Kweilin, and Chiang still refusing Stilwell command of all Chinese forces.
frus-1945-50-intel-d108:
Director of Central Intelligence Souers wrote to Quinn of the SSU on 4 April 1946, the day after the War Department's letter to Quinn. The new chief and the old unit were now in direct dealing. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Letters between the rising body and the remnant it would absorb have a special tone: courteous, exact, and final. Souers needed the SSU's stations and officers; Quinn needed terms for his people. Readers can watch the transfer being negotiated chief to chief. Within months the SSU's secret work passed to the CIG, giving the group the operational arm its charter had lacked. This letter is an early instrument of that passing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d208:
A memorandum dated 5 March 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Chief of the Legislative Liaison Division, Central Intelligence Group (Pforzheimer). The reader was the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence (Wright). The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 208 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d308:
A memorandum dated 6 January 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the Director of the Policy Planning Staff, Department of State (Kennan). The reader was the Assistant Director for Policy Coordination, Central Intelligence Agency (Wisner). It stands as document 308 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. It was a season of stock-taking: the CIA was a year old, and its friends and critics were both writing things down.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. The points are stated once and left to stand; the file around it holds the answer they drew. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d408:
Brigadier General John Magruder wrote to Secretary of Defense Louis Johnson on 22 December 1949. His memo is document 408 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Magruder had led the wartime Strategic Services Unit, a bridge between the old OSS and the new CIA. He knew secret work from the inside and spoke with rare weight on it. A memo from him to the Secretary of Defense brings a soldier's view into the debate over the young agency. Magruder's voice carried the memory of wartime secret work into a peacetime fight over its future.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d108:
Three zones and one shared capital: that is the map this protocol draws for beaten Germany. Signed by the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union on 12 September 1944, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It carries out the surrender instrument's article on occupation.

Germany, inside her frontiers of 31 December 1937, is split for occupation into three zones, one for each power. Berlin forms a special area held jointly by all three. The protocol then spells out each boundary in surveyor's detail. The eastern zone's line begins at Lübeck Bay and runs along the old provincial borders, and the matching lines for the other zones follow.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d208:
France claimed a full share in ruling Germany, in five proposals laid before the President on 4 January 1945. Stettinius's memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, passes on the French paper circulated in the European Advisory Commission. Paris approved the three allied drafts but wanted more.

The five asks run as follows. A French part in the supreme authority over Germany. A French hand in signing the surrender instrument. A zone of occupation for the French army, with a share of Greater Berlin. Four-power, not three-power, bodies in the control machinery. And a French text of the surrender paper, equal in standing to the Russian and English. Stettinius recommends approval, subject to the military authorities.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d308:
From Malta on February 1, 1945, Secretary of State Edward Stettinius cabled Acting Secretary Joseph Grew in Washington. He reported a step agreed with Foreign Secretary Eden. After meeting Generals Marshall and Brooke, they had told Ambassador Winant in London that both governments approved the protocol on zones of occupation for Germany. Eden was sending the same word to London.

The short cable, marked secret and sent under the Cricket code name for the Malta talks, shows the zone plan clearing its last hurdle before Yalta. Stettinius also asked that John McCloy at the War Department be told. One wire moved the occupation map from draft to agreed fact.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d408:
Points still before the foreign ministers head this American delegation paper, dated in its text February 9, 1945, though the catalog date reads September 1. Two British officials, Bridges and Cadogan, were redrafting the February 8 report on Dumbarton Oaks matters. Their text might reach the ministers that morning, so a final version could go to the afternoon plenary.

A second item follows: the subcommittee on invitations to the United Nations conference. Jebb, Gromyko, and Hiss had been named the day before and planned to meet that morning. Jebb, as chairman, might report in person. The paper is a morning checklist from the conference's last full days.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d508:
Do not send it — yet. Hiss's memorandum to the Secretary of State of March 19, 1945, attaches a draft message. The draft, from the President to Stalin, follows lines the Secretary had given by telephone. Two senior advisers, Dunn and Pasvolsky, strongly recommended against sending it at this time. Three or four other urgent matters, they argued, would soon need messages of the same kind.

Flooding Stalin with presidential messages, Dunn felt, would rob the method of its true importance. Better that the Secretary take the matter up himself with Ambassador Gromyko, using the attached outline of points. The memo is a small lesson in rationing a president's voice.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d108:
Ambassador John Winant sent Washington the British delegation's Foreign Office roster on June 29, 1945. His secret telegram from London is document 108 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The Foreign Office had given the names that day and asked, in return, for the State Department people who would accompany the American delegation.

The British list is led by Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden, with Sir Alexander Cadogan, William Strang, and Ambassador Clark Kerr. Behind them stand named specialists: Geoffrey Harrison for Germany and Austria, William Hayter for the Balkans, Denis Allen for Poland and Czechoslovakia, L. H. Foulds for the Far East, and Patrick Dean for legal questions. The telegram shows each side matching experts to the agenda the leaders would face.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d208:
Edwin Pauley repeated his demand that reparations join the agenda in a telegram dated July 11, 1945. The urgent message to the Secretary of State is document 208 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It was relayed to Byrnes, then at sea with the President.

Pauley had received a copy of Harriman's note to Molotov listing the six items the President might raise at the Big Three meeting. He is strongly of the opinion, he writes, that the topic of reparations should be added to the agenda. He asks that the President be advised of his views immediately. The message underlines how hard the American reparations chief pushed to get Germany's bill, deadlocked in Moscow, in front of the three leaders themselves.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d308:
General Crane, the American representative on Bulgaria's Allied Control Commission, protested to General McNarney on July 10, 1945. More than two months had passed since the fighting with Germany ended. Under the armistice, the commission's work should have changed by then. Crane reported that nothing had changed at all.

The Russians still controlled every American plane and person entering Bulgaria, officials included. Americans stayed confined to Sofia unless a Russian officer escorted them. Crane called the position most embarrassing, and said he could not even learn what was done in the commission's name. His protest went up the Army chain days before Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d408:
London and Paris chose concession in Winant's cable of July 7, 1945, about the disputed sentence in the French zone report. The British and French delegations to the European Advisory Commission had weighed the Soviet proposal of July 6. That proposal would omit the final sentence. Both delegations recommended that their governments agree to the omission.

Their reasoning was practical. It mattered more, they felt, to conclude the agreement on the French zone in Germany. They would leave open the method of fixing France's Berlin area. Forcing a decision in the Commission at that point, they judged, was worth less. Both delegations expected final word from their governments on Monday morning. Winant repeated the message to Murphy.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d508:
Poland's outstanding questions are sized up in Thompson's memorandum to Assistant Secretary Dunn, written at Babelsberg on July 15, 1945. The British, he notes, apparently contemplate asking for some assurance of the right of Polish political parties to take part in elections in Poland. Thompson advises against raising the election question at this meeting.

The American ambassador is expected in Warsaw shortly, he argues. On the basis of Lane's reports, Washington may later make concrete proposals to the Soviets. Raised here in general terms, the matter would almost certainly draw a strong Soviet rebuff and arouse suspicions. One useful step, he adds, would be pressing for early consulates in Poland, to observe conditions there.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d608:
Extracts from the White House meeting of June 18, 1945, form document 608 in the Potsdam papers. The memo by the Joint Chiefs' secretary, McFarland, stresses the invasion of Kyushu. Editors note that the extracts come from a debate that weighed the landings and the losses they would bring.

President Truman heard the same Joint Chiefs digest that the fuller minutes record. General Marshall said every weapon was being brought to bear on Japan. Bombardment and blockade would go on at full force while invasion plans were pressed. The extracts keep the focus tight on one question. Could a landing on Japan itself, backed by blockade and bombing, force a yield? The fuller record of the meeting, with the cost debate in context, is printed earlier in the volume as document 598.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d708:
An extract from James Dunn's Potsdam memo of July 14, 1945, covers Turkey. It is document 708 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers, drawn from his long talk with Sir Alexander Cadogan. Dunn was taking the measure of Britain's line before the conference opened.

Dunn told Cadogan the U.S. liked London's message to its Moscow ambassador on Turkey. Washington had sent no message of its own, for two reasons. It never signed the Montreux Convention, and the Turks had not approached it directly. Cadogan assumed Stalin's aim was free passage for warships through the Straits in wartime. The main Russian objection, he felt, was to Turkey's right to close the Straits under a mere threat of war. He also asked whether any Soviet bases should be placed under the new International Organisation.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1008:
Edwin Pauley wrote to President Truman on July 19, 1945, about Stalin's wish to split the German fleets. Stalin proposed a third of the naval and merchant tonnage for each big power. Most of that tonnage, Pauley notes, sits in British hands. Under the American definition, warships count as war booty, not reparations, while merchant ships count as reparations.

Giving Russia a third of the navy would thus be an outright gift. Pauley does not object, but he sets conditions. Definitions of booty, restitution, and reparations must first be agreed. No ships should be delivered before the Japanese war ends. The Soviets should also supply oil from Hungary and Rumania to ease the tanker burden.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1108:
America's top military chiefs sent this message to President Truman on 17 July 1945, the day the Potsdam Conference opened. The Joint Chiefs of Staff led the armed forces and advised the president on war matters. Their channel to him stayed open through the whole summit.

While envoys in Germany bargained over the peace, the war against Japan was still being fought. The chiefs kept Truman supplied with the armed forces' view of the questions before him. A message of this kind put the soldier's outlook in front of the commander in chief at the start of the talks. It links the summit table to the war still under way.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1208:
John McCloy wrote to the War Department on 26 July 1945, his second cable of the conference. The assistant secretary of war kept the Pentagon posted as the summit's military questions shifted. His post joined the talks to the department that would hold Germany.

The day of this cable, the British government changed hands in London. Work in Germany went on through the drama. McCloy's messages gave Washington the view from inside the room on the army's concerns. This dispatch keeps his running report home going. It shows a senior civilian hand on the link between sword and pen.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1308:
Stimson answered Harrison on 21 July 1945, writing from the summit to the acting chairman of the Interim Committee. The reply direction shows the channel working both ways. The war secretary directed the atomic file from Potsdam while the committee's work went on in Washington.

A secretary's note to his acting chairman could carry rulings, questions, or word of the talks that bore on the bomb. Stimson held the whole thread in his own hands that week. This message is his end of it. It shows the atomic policy being run by letter between two men who shared its full secret.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1408:
Caffery's run of cables to Secretary Byrnes continues with a third dated 6 August 1945. Paris was then pressing Washington on France's role in the German settlement. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Three cables to the secretary in a single day is the mark of a post that believes its hour has come. The Potsdam powers had drawn Germany's zones without France; Paris wanted in, and Caffery carried that want to Washington. His cluster of cables lets readers feel the weight of paper a determined embassy could pile on a secretary's desk. The volume's French section turns on days like this one.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-108: This note from the volume's editors appears unnumbered after document 710 in the second Potsdam volume. Foreign Relations editors used such notes to supply what a document leaves unsaid. The note might identify a writer, give a source, or link the paper to a wider file. For readers it is a small act of guidance inside the July 1945 record.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d808:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff wrote to the State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee on July 23, 1945. Document 808 is the chiefs' second letter to that body in this run. The committee joined military and civil planning in Washington. The letter was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Repeat letters show a channel in constant use. The chiefs fed the committee the military side of live questions. Readers see the American system processing the summit's demands. War plans and peace terms had to be kept in step. The document shows that alignment being done in writing, at speed, while the leaders sat in Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d908:
Collado drafted this American working paper on July 22, 1945. It suggests a position on economic questions touching Germany, Poland, and reparations. The paper argues the Moscow Reparations Commission has done its main work. Future handling should pass to the Control Council and the zone commanders.

It urges adopting a definition of restitution, with Allied teams free to hunt their property in all zones. It drops any split between war booty and reparations for capital equipment inside Germany's 1937 borders. Soviet and Polish claims would, in practice, be met from the eastern zone. Exports must be set aside to pay for needed imports.
gao-gaoreports-b-297508: The MIL Corporation doubled its January 2006 protest — two case numbers, one defense-services fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-298408: WareOnEarth Communications took its July 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Telecom firms get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-299108: SEI Group took its February 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Short names get the same long, careful hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-299408: Dellew Corporation took its May 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the protest against bid law. Every protest gets the same careful reading, whatever the trade.
gao-gaoreports-b-310108: This 2008 GAO ruling is about apportionment Limitation for Aviation Resources at Forest Service. GAO's legal decisions tell agencies what federal funding law allows. Agencies follow these rulings when spending federal funds. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-b-310708: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by T. F. Boyle Transportation, Inc. Decided January 29, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-b-310808: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Daylight Tree Service & Equipment, LLC. Decided January 29, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-b-311308: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Advanced Seal Technology, Inc. Decided June 5, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-308: Public health IT initiatives faced challenges in 2005, and GAO's report says federal agencies struggled to implement the programs. The findings demand the fixes. The report warns that the patients deserved modern systems. The challenges had to be faced. The patients deserved modern systems.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-108: Welfare-to-work strategies needed better data in 2006, and GAO's report says more information was needed to assess promising approaches. The findings demand the evidence. The report warns that the parents' incomes deserved proven strategies. The information had to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-408: The SEC's cyber program needed work in 2006, and GAO's report says the commission had to keep improving its information security. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the market watchdog's own vault needed locking. The program had to be hardened.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-708: Top officials' pay trends got a GAO look in 2006, and the report tracks executive and judicial compensation. The findings do the counting. The report shows the public's top servants' paychecks were being watched. The trends had to be faced. The paychecks were being watched.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-908: The Air Force's space troops needed better management in 2006, and GAO's report says actions were required to identify, track, and train the personnel. The findings demand the system. The report warns that the guardians of the high frontier needed proper tending. The space force had to be built right.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-408: The VA's hospital-building choices needed a scorecard in 2007, and GAO's report says the department should track how its asset decisions played out. The findings demand real follow-through on the plans. The report's point is firm: the blueprint is a promise, not a result.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-708: Modernizing the FHA was a budget riddle in 2007 — GAO's report says the reform ideas carried real program and dollar consequences for taxpayers. The findings price the proposals in plain terms. The report warns Congress to read the fine print before rebuilding the housing agency.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-808: The pension backstop needed better bosses in 2007 — GAO's report says the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation's governance needed repairs. The findings target the leadership of the insurer of last resort for retirements. The report warns that the safety net's own safety needed attention.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-408: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at defense Acquisitions: 2009 Is a Critical Juncture for the Army's Future Combat System. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
guazzo-compendium-maleficarum-latin-1608:
Francesco Maria Guazzo, a Milanese priest, published the Compendium Maleficarum in Latin at Milan in 1608. Three books gather the lore and practice of witchcraft into one compendium, a summary of the whole dark subject. This text is the Latin original from which the library's 1929 English translation was made.

Guazzo describes the pact with the devil, the sabbath, and the marks left on witches' bodies. He draws on trial records and on the demonologists before him. Woodcuts in the original printing show the sabbath in grim detail. The compendium served priests and judges as a reference work. Having the Latin source lets readers check the famous translation against its original voice.
hardy-dynasts-1908:
Thomas Hardy spent five years writing The Dynasts, his vast verse drama of the Napoleonic Wars. It appeared in three parts between 1904 and 1908, and this text holds the complete work. Hardy never meant it for an ordinary stage; he called it a drama for mental performance.

The action sweeps from London drawing rooms to the fields of Trafalgar and Waterloo. Above the human struggle, spirit figures debate the blind Immanent Will that drives history. Kings, generals, and common soldiers all move inside a pattern they cannot see. The Dynasts is Hardy's strangest and most ambitious work, part epic poem, part philosophy of history.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: Volume eight of Carlyle's Frederick the Great: Prussia against all Europe in the Seven Years' War. Battles, sieges, and the king's iron will fill these pages, narrated in Carlyle's most prophetic voice. The heart of the great work, where heroism meets history. Demanding, but the drama is real.
hodgson-house-on-the-borderland-1908:
A lone man finds a house on the edge of a vast pit in William Hope Hodgson's novel of 1908. Swine-like brutes besiege the house by night. Time then speeds up. Years fly past in days, and stars wheel fast in the sky.

The tale leaps from siege horror to a view of the end of the world. Few books of its time reach so far in scale. Lovecraft took it as a model for the long weird novel. Its mix of dread and vast time still shocks. A found log frames the tale, which adds grit to its wild leaps. Few peers match its blend of house siege, time flight, and last suns.
hyslop-psychical-research-resurrection-1:
James Hyslop turns test lore to the church's core claim in Psychical Research and the Resurrection, out in 1908. Hyslop led the field's chief band in the United States. His ask is bold. If sittings prove the self lives past death, the old claim gains new aid. That aid comes from the lab, not just from faith and old texts.

He weighs the best cases with his strict hand. Creed and lab meet in these pages in rare peace. The book is his field's word to the church. It seeks a bridge.
ibn-tufayl-hayy-ibn-yaqzan-1708:
Ibn Tufayl wrote Hayy ibn Yaqzan in Spain in the 1100s. Simon Ockley gave the tale English dress in 1708 as The Improvement of Human Reason. The hero grows up alone on an isle with beasts for kin. No man teaches him a word or a creed.

Hayy works out the world by his own sharp thought, step by step. In time he finds God by pure reason and by a deep inner light. A guest from a peopled isle then tests his lone faith. The tale is a jewel of Islamic thought on reason and faith.
io-bap-portae-neopolitani-de-distillatio: Io, bap. Portae Neopolitani de distillatione, 1608, the distillation books. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
j-p-jacobsen-niels-lyhne-1908:
J. P. Jacobsen's Niels Lyhne, given here in the 1908 English version, follows one Danish idealist through a hard life. Niels loses love, a child, and at last the faith he was raised in. Still he refuses to bend or pretend belief he cannot feel.

Jacobsen tells the tale in prose of rare beauty and care. Doubt becomes a kind of honor for his hero, a dignity kept at great cost. The book taught many young Scandinavians how to face loss without lies. Rilke loved it deeply, and it stands near the source of Danish modern writing.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-08:
Jean de Brébeuf and his work among the Hurons anchor Volume 8, from 1897. Thwaites pairs Quebec reports with Huron letters in this part of the set. Brébeuf's first full reports show a gifted linguist hard at work in the field.

He learned the Huron tongue and wrote down customs with great care. Towns, councils, feasts, and beliefs appear in close, patient detail. Later readers prize the volume as a full account of Iroquoian life. A tragic end waits far ahead for Brébeuf and his hosts. These early pages let readers meet both saint and people first.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lyon-george-lew:
George Lewis Lyon, an English journalist and communal worker, receives an entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Portsea on December 11, 1828, he began as secretary of the Portsmouth Hebrew Benevolent Institution. In the early 1850s he moved to London. There he became secretary of the Jews' and General Literary and Scientific Institution. He died in London in 1904.

The article follows his turn to financial journalism. He served as city correspondent for many London and provincial newspapers. In February 1873 he founded and edited the Jewish World, though it later passed to other hands. He also worked as secretary of the Jews' Infant School and of the Jews' Emigration Society. The short entry records a man who served Anglo-Jewish life through both the press and its charities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-major-solomon-i:
Solomon ibn Major, a Turkish rabbi of Salonica, is the subject of a short 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He flourished toward the end of the sixteenth century. At Salonica he headed the yeshivah, the rabbinical academy. His standing drew distinguished pupils to study under him.

The article names three of those pupils. Joseph Florentin and Abraham Falcon studied with him, and so did his own son, Moses ibn Major. Solomon's own writings were responsa, legal answers to questions sent by other communities. None appeared as a book of his own. Some were printed inside the responsa of Hayyim Shabbethai at Salonica in 1651. Others appear in Shabbethai's Torat Hayyim and in Judah Lerma's work at Venice. The entry preserves a teacher whose rulings survive scattered through his students' and colleagues' books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-may-laws-10508:
The May Laws of 1882 were the “temporary” rules that hemmed in the Jews of Russia for a generation. Herman Rosenthal prints and examines them in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. Count Ignatiev proposed them, and the czar sanctioned them on May 3, 1882. The regulations forbade Jews to settle anew outside towns and boroughs. They blocked Jewish mortgages and leases on country property and closed Jewish businesses on Sundays and Christian holidays, all within the Pale of Settlement.

The article quotes the four clauses in full. Then it turns to the gap between promise and practice. The rules were sold as a stopgap until a general revision of Jewish legal status. A commission under Count Pahlen finished that revision. But no action followed, so the stopgap simply stayed in force, hardening into the framework of Jewish life in the Pale.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mels-alfred-pse:
Alfred Mels was the pen name of Martin Cohn. Cohn was a German author with a soldier's past. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Berlin in 1831. In 1848 he ran away from the university to join the French Foreign Legion in Algiers. He was badly wounded on the road to Oran. Paris then gave him literary work under Alexandre Dumas. Soldiering came again, against Denmark in 1850 and in Spain, where he rose to captain; journalism in Madrid, Berlin, and Vienna filled the gaps.

War reporting made his name. In 1870 the London "Times" sent him with the German army. After Sedan he resigned to go with the captive Napoleon III. His lasting success was the stage comedy "Heine's Junge Leiden" of 1872, played more than two thousand times. He died at Summerdale, near Chicago, in 1894.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mesha-me-asha-1:
Mesha, also written Me'asha, was a Palestinian amora of the third century at Lydda. Solomon Schechter and A. S. Waldstein remember him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They remember him less for doctrine than for a childhood tale. Orphaned young, he was raised by his grandfather, the great haggadist Joshua ben Levi. The grandfather loved to hear the boy recite the week's Torah portion on Fridays. He marked the boy's fine intelligence early.

The Midrash tells a strange tale. Once, ill, the child lay in a trance three days. On recovering, he said he had been in a world turned upside down. There, those held in honor here were disgraced. The entry then returns to scale. Only a few of his legal rulings and sayings survive in the Talmud. Heilprin gathered them. Bacher gathered them too, in his work on the Palestinian amoraim. A brief entry, and a haunting one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-modigliani-elia:
Elia Modigliani was an Italian naturalist and traveler born at Florence on June 13, 1861. Isidore Singer and Vittore Castiglione profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He graduated at Pavia in 1883, with natural science already his bent. Travel turned the bent into a career of collecting expeditions.

From the Malay Peninsula he came home with a very rich haul of specimens. He presented them to the museums of Genoa, Florence, and Rome. His books report the work. They include studies of the Bergeggi cave and, above all, the island of Nias. Nias is described in his 1890 book, Un Viaggio all'Isola di Nias. A further volume, L'Isola delle Donne, followed. A compact entry for a museum-filling life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-b-shab:
Mordecai ben Shabbethai, called he-Aruk, the Tall, was a liturgical poet of the thirteenth century. He was a native of Italy or of Greece. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach give him a paragraph in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Almost nothing of his life is recorded. What survives is the work, and the work traveled.

His penitential prayers, the seliḥot, are praised for both their form and their clear, flowing language. They were taken into three rites that rarely agree on anything. Those rites are the German, the Roman, and the Karaite. Zunz's history of synagogue poetry is the entry's single source. That is fitting, since Zunz mapped poets like this one back into view.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-b-joseph-: Moses ben Joseph of Rome was a liturgical poet and rabbinical authority of the thirteenth century. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach give him a two-line entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Only one fact about his work is recorded. One of his liturgical poems was taken into the German ritual, and was prayed far from his native Rome. Nothing more of his life survives in the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mule-11208:
The mule, in Hebrew pered, is treated in this Jewish Encyclopedia article by Emil G. Hirsch, Solomon Schechter, and I. M. Casanowicz. The animal is a hybrid of ass and horse, first mentioned in the Bible in David's time. Kings rode mules, and Solomon's tribute included them.

Jewish law forbade breeding mules, under the ban on mixing kinds, yet the mule stayed a favorite for its sure feet and endurance. The article tracks mules as royal mounts, war animals, and beasts of burden, with Togarmah as their market. Talmudic notes add that the creature cannot breed and was among the last things created.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naomi-11308:
Naomi was the wife of Elimelech and the mother-in-law of Ruth, and Emil G. Hirsch with M. Seligsohn tell her story in the Jewish Encyclopedia. She had gone with her husband and two sons to live in Moab. When husband and sons all died there, she set out home for Bethlehem. Ruth, her widowed daughter-in-law, refused to leave her.

Poverty and grief had changed Naomi so much that her old neighbors asked, Is this Naomi? She answered that she should be called Mara, bitter, not Naomi, pleasant. She then guided Ruth toward marriage with Boaz, the family redeemer. The article ends with her nursing their child, her bitterness turned to honor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nebushasban-114:
Nebushasban was a Babylonian officer named in Jeremiah. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and Ira Maurice Price for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He heads the four chief officers in Jeremiah chapter thirty-nine. Nebuzar-adan sent them into captured Jerusalem. Their task was to free the prophet Jeremiah.

They were to take him from the court of the guard. Then they were to deliver him into safe hands. Nebushasban's own rank and office stay unknown. His name in Babylonian form is Nabu-shuzibanni. It means, in prayer form, Nabu, save me. A son of Egypt's Necho I bore the same name. Name lists in old inscriptions confirm the Bible's form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-newman-leopold-:
Leopold Newman was an American soldier of the Civil War. Cyrus Adler wrote his brief entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He entered as captain of Company B. His regiment was the 31st New York Infantry. He rose in time to lieutenant-colonel of that regiment. His term of service was nearly out in 1863.

Days before Chancellorsville, Newman's term expired at last. He chose to remain at the front regardless. On May 2, 1863, he was fatally injured there. He died shortly after, in Washington city. President Lincoln visited him at his bedside there. Lincoln brought a commission making him brigadier-general. The honor reached him before death took him. His story is told in Simon Wolf's book of Jewish patriots.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-novgorod-syever:
Novgorod-Syeversk is a town in Russia's Chernigov government. Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The town traces its start to the eleventh century. Jews lived there in the sixteenth century. They paid taxes on a footing with burghers.

Street repairs drew their contributions like all others. Jewish butchers faced one sharp limit there. They could not rival Christians in selling meat. Their meat sold only in the synagogue yard. Cossacks stormed the town in 1648 cruelly. Jews and Poles alike were put to the sword. Today 2,700 Jews live among 9,185 souls. Artisans among them number 318 by count. Two charities serve its poor and its sick.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-onan-11708: Onan was a son of Judah, in the book of Genesis. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. When his elder brother Er died, Onan would not wed the widow. That kind of wedlock, with a dead brother's wife, was a duty then. It kept the dead man's name and line alive in Israel. For this refusal, the text says, the Lord slew Onan as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-parenzo-asher-b: Asher ben Jacob Parenzo was a Hebrew printer at Venice. Joseph Jacobs and Ismar Elbogen wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked at Venice from 1580 to the year 1600. His brother Meir ben Jacob was a printer as well. Asher worked for Giovanni Bragadin on a host of Hebrew books. They held notes on the five books of Moses and a Bible. His kin and forebears were printers before him, he states.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-penso-abraham-1:
Abraham Penso was a rabbinical writer in Ottoman Bosnia. He lived at Sarajevo near the end of the eighteenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He had studied under David Pardo. His books were printed at Salonica in his lifetime.

Penso wrote a book on the laws of Passover. Appe Zutre came out at Salonica in 1798. He also gathered his sermons in Tola'at Shani. That volume followed in 1805, from the same city. He edited Azulai's notes on the Shulhan Aruk as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phillips-12108:
Phillips is an American family of New York and Philadelphia. Cyrus Adler, L. Hühner, and David Sulzberger wrote the article. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The line starts with Jonas Phillips, who reached America in 1756. Jonas had left Germany for England five years before.

Henry Phillips the younger won fame as a coin scholar. His books on colonial paper money were the first of their kind. The Supreme Court even cited them in a famous case. Henry Mayer Phillips took a different road to honor. He sat in Congress in the late 1850s.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-plessner-solomo:
Solomon Plessner was a German preacher who defended Orthodoxy. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Breslau in 1797. He died at Posen in 1883, famed for sermons. Berlin heard him preach on alternate Saturdays for years.

Orphaned young, Plessner worked in trade and studied alone. At seventeen he took up Wessely's Apocrypha work. His Hebrew Esther additions appeared in 1819. Reform foes had police bar his preaching. In 1825 Posen banned Talmud teaching in schools. Plessner's defense won the decree's repeal within a year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-posner-meir-cal: Meïr Posner, also called Munk or Meïr Pinner, was a Prussian rabbi born in 1735. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. From 1782 he served the Schottland congregation at Danzig. He held that pulpit until his death there in 1807. His one book is Bet Meïr, a note on the Shulhan Aruk. It treats the part called Eben ha-Ezer. His fresh notes on that part were printed with the book. It came out in 1787 and again in 1836.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-proverbs-midras:
Midrash to Proverbs is an old Jewish note on the Book of Proverbs. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was first named in the eleventh century. Hananeel ben Hushiel cites it as Midrash Mishle. Nathan of Rome calls it Agadat Mishle in his word book.

The work has not come down to us in full. Whole chapters of Proverbs lack any note in it. Chapters three, seven, and eighteen are such gaps. Other chapters are handled only in part. Men once called it by a wrong name, Shoher Tob. That name in truth belongs to a midrash on Psalms. The article traces the book's remains and its prints.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-psalmomancy-124:
Psalmomancy is the use of the Psalms in charms and spells. Joseph Jacobs and Ludwig Blau wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Use of the Bible in magic is treated in a sister article. The Psalms held a pride of place in such use. Next to the Torah, no book was so loved by the folk.

The Psalms formed the true book of the people, they say. Folk knew them by heart as prayers of their own. In old thought, prayers held a strange power in themselves. A prayer could be bent to work as a charm. The article tells which psalms were used for which needs. It names cures, guards, and wins sought by such means.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabinovich-leon:
Leon Rabinovich was a Russian physicist and journalist, born in 1862. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Brestovitz in the Grodno government. His house traced its line to famed rabbis of old. Heller on his father's side and Eisenstadt on his mother's, he claimed.

The boy learned first in a heder in his town. His mother taught him German at home as well. At fourteen he went to the yeshivah of Mir. From there he moved to the great yeshivah of Volozhin. His path then bent from the study house toward science. The entry tells how the physicist grew from the Talmud boy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reading-12608:
Reading is a city in Berks County, Pennsylvania. Cyrus Adler and Julius Frank wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A few Jewish settlers arrived before 1847. That year Reading became a city.

The article says a cemetery plot was bought in 1864. Congregation Oheb Sholom was founded that same year. It had about fifteen founding members, mostly South Germans. The congregation bought a church building in 1884. Isaac M. Wise dedicated it the next year. Orthodox Jews formed Shomre Habris in 1887. A Hebrew free school stood beside that congregation. By 1905 about eight hundred Jews lived in Reading. Most worked in trade, the writers say.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rothenburg-mose: Moses ben Mordecai Süsskind Rothenburg was a German rabbi born about 1665. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Bernhard Friedberg wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He served as rabbi at Tykoczin, then at Brest-Litovsk, and finally at Altona. There he first shared the post with Hakam Zebi, and from 1710 he held it alone. He died at Altona on January 12, 1712. Some of his novellae were printed by his widow in his father's responsa in 1747.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sarphati-samuel:
Isidore Singer and E. Slijper wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Samuel Sarphati. He was a Dutch physician and economist. Sarphati was born at Amsterdam on January 31, 1813. He died there on June 23, 1866. After medical studies at Leyden, he took his degree in 1838. He then practiced as a doctor in Amsterdam.

Sarphati spent his energy improving his city. He founded a society to farm land enriched by town sewage. At his urging, Amsterdam opened its first school of commerce. After a trip to London in 1852, he planned a palace for industry shows. The Palace of Industry opened in 1864. A new quarter grew around it, with streets and a park named for him. He also founded a company for cheap bread. The Amstel Hotel rose at his initiative in 1866.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schossberger-de:
Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Simon Wolf Schossberger de Torna. He was a Hungarian merchant and estate owner. Schossberger was born in 1796 at Sasvar. He died at Budapest on March 25, 1874. His trade, factories, and farms brought him wealth and honor. His work in tobacco solved a Hungarian economic problem.

Before 1861 Schossberger twice led the Jewish community of Pesth as its president. In 1862 Emperor Francis Joseph raised him to the nobility. He was the first Hungarian Jew so honored. He took the name De Torna with the title. His son Sigmund was made a baron in 1885. Sigmund was the first Jew in Hungary to hold that rank.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-selihah-plural-:
Selihah, plural Selihot, names the penitential prayers of the synagogue, and Wilhelm Bacher, M. Seligsohn, Cyrus Adler, and Francis L. Cohen wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on them. The word comes from a root meaning he forgave. Such prayers first belonged only to the Day of Atonement.

Over time the prayers spread to New Year, the days between, and other fast days. The entry traces that growth and the services built around the prayers. Readers learn how Jews asked God for mercy after sin, and how set days of repentance took shape. It remains a clear guide to an old part of Jewish worship.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sharon-13508:
Sharon is a large coastal plain in Palestine, once famed for pasture and flowers. Joseph Jacobs, Immanuel Benzinger, and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Mount Carmel bounds it north and Jaffa south. The sea lies west and hills rise east.

Its rich soil earns it the name garden of Palestine. Red and white lilies and anemones color the plain. David's herds grazed there in Bible times. Isaiah pictured Sharon turned to wilderness as utter ruin. He also pictured it as a fold for flocks in better days. The beloved in Canticles calls herself the rose of Sharon. The entry blends geography with the plain's rich biblical poetry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-of-mizpa:
Simeon of Mizpah was a tanna of the first generation. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this short Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He lived in the time of Gamaliel I. With Gamaliel he went to the court in the hall of hewn stone. They went to learn a ruling on the corner of a field.

He is also said to have made a set of rules for the Temple rite. Those rules dealt with the service on the Day of Atonement. The piece is brief, yet it places a minor sage inside early rabbinic life. It also shows how Temple practice was kept after his time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-slucki-david-13:
David Slucki was a Hebrew scholar of Warsaw who died there before 1880. Isidore Singer and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He edited works by David Franco Mendes and by Pappenheim. To both editions he added notes of his own. He also edited the Megillat Antiokus in 1863.

His chief work was Hokmat Yisrael, in eight parts. It gathered Jewish religious and philosophic classics with his notes. Part one held works by Bedersi, Ibn Gabirol, and Maimonides. Later parts held Saadia, Judah ha-Levi, and Bahya. He prefixed lives of the authors and full indexes. The set made hard texts far easier for Hebrew readers to use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steinbach-josef:
Josef Steinbach was an Austrian physician born at Fünfkirchen in 1850. Isidore Singer and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Hungary on January 3 of that year. He studied at the gymnasium there and at Vienna University. He took his medical degree at Vienna in 1875.

He served briefly as assistant physician at the university hospital. In 1876 he became a surgeon in the Austrian navy. He resigned that post in 1881 for further study at Vienna. He then settled as a gynecologist at Franzensbad in Bohemia. He published verse and translations of Kiss's poems as well. Since 1886 he has coedited a spa medicine journal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sulzberger-1410:
Sulzberger is an American family named for Sulzbürg in Bavaria. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. The town sits near Ratisbon in the Bavarian Palatinate. The first known member lived in the early 1600s. His great-grandson Ezra was rabbi and advocate at Sulzbürg.

Ezra Sulzberger founded a charity there that still exists. His ethical will survives in print today. Some descendants took the names Bayersdorfer or Löwenmaier. Reform leader Kaufmann Kohler descends from this family. Four branches emigrated to the United States over time. Ferdinand Sulzberger headed a New York packing firm. Solomon Sulzberger led Temple Beth-El in New York. The entry traces one family's spread across two continents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-talkar-ezekiel-:
Ezekiel Talkar was a Beni-Israel soldier born at Ahmedabad in 1848. Joseph Jacobs and J. Hyams wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He joined the Bombay Rifles in September 1864. He climbed the native officer ladder over decades. By 1890 he held the rank of subahdar-major.

Talkar taught musketry theory to his regiment's officers. The regimental school owed its shooting skill to him. He served in Kathiawar from 1865 to 1868. The Afghan war of 1879 and 1880 followed. Burma brought active service and two more clasps. In 1893 he retired from the army. He then inspected police at Dhrangadhra and Bhavnagar. The maharaja moved him to command in his state regiment. The entry honors a marksman who became an instructor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-temple-in-rabbi:
Rabbinic tradition about the Jerusalem Temple fills this long article. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. It gathers what the Talmud and later rabbis taught about Mount Moriah. Tradition links that mount to Adam, Noah, and Abraham.

The rabbis held that the world rested on a foundation stone under the Ark. They split Mount Moriah between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. David bought the site and planned the Temple, the article says. God barred him from building it, since he had shed blood in war. Solomon, a man of peace, built it instead. A plan drawn from Talmudic sources shows the layout.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-triennial-cycle:
The triennial cycle spread the Torah reading over three full years. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Palestine followed that slow cycle in ancient times. Babylonia read the whole Pentateuch in one year instead. Modern practice follows the Babylonian custom. Egyptian congregations still used three years in 1170.

Public Torah reading dates to at least the second century B.C. Festival passages were read on their own feast days. The Masoretic divisions called sedarim number 154. That count likely matches the cycle's Sabbath lessons. Other counts run to 161, 167, or 175 divisions. A Sabbath portion should hold at least twenty-one verses. The cycle's second year began at Exodus 12.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-virginia-14708:
Virginia is one of the thirteen original American states. Cyrus Adler and A. M. Hofmann wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jewish names appear in Virginia records as early as 1624. Elias Lagardo, Joseph Moise, and Rebecca Isaacke are listed then. A lawsuit names one Seignor Moses Nehemiah in 1658.

Little is heard again until 1754. That year two Jews marched with Washington over the Alleghenies. Richmond's Beth Shalom is the state's oldest congregation. It existed before 1790. The entry then lists Jewish communities across the state. Alexandria, Charlottesville, and other towns each get a brief note.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weather-lore-14:
Weather lore collects folk signs that predict the weather. Isidore Singer and Joseph Jacobs wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Some of these sayings occur in the Talmud. Clear weather at Shabuot meant sow wheat. Altar smoke turning north at Tabernacles meant rain. A warm New Year promised a warm year.

Later signs watch the turning points of the seasons. A season change on certain weekdays meant famine or war. Some signs were borrowed from the Greeks. Others read the moon and the planets. A new moon near Mars meant a warm, rainy month. Large prayer books printed many such items. The entry shows folk wisdom mixed with star lore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wieniawski-henr:
Henri Wieniawski was a Russian violinist and composer. Isidore Singer and Julius Gottlieb wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Lublin on July 10, 1835. He died at Moscow on April 1, 1880. His talent showed itself very early. At age eight he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

At eleven Wieniawski won the conservatory's first violin prize. He toured Europe's capitals to great acclaim. In 1860 the czar named him his first violinist. He toured America with Anton Rubinstein in 1872. He later taught violin at Brussels as Vieuxtemps's successor. Illness cut his last tour short at Odessa. Critics rank him among the greatest modern violinists.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-woodbine-15008:
Woodbine is a New Jersey borough built as a farm colony for Jews. Cyrus Adler and J. G. Lipman wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The town was laid out in August 1891 on a large tract. Baron de Hirsch Fund trustees bought that land for the plan.

The plan joined farm work with town trade and shops. Farm homes would feed a town market in time. Shops would give jobs to the kin of the farmers. By the fall of 1892 some fifty farm homes stood full. A cloak shop that year gave work to more than one hundred hands. Most of those hands lived on farms near the town. Hard times in 1893 hurt the cloak trade badly. The shop shut, and some farm families left for big cities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-ben-tabl:
Yizhak ben Tablai was a scholar of Palestine in the fourth century. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a peer of Jacob ben Zabdai and of Helbo. The three were called to rule on a point of law.

A query came on the rule for a Syrian leek. He could not rule on that point by his own light. He sought the word of Rabbi Jose on the case. A query on the law of the writ came to him too. He sent that case to Eleazar for a firm rule. One old word came down in two forms by two men. The Babylon books once mixed him with five like names. Bacher showed that mix to be false in his study.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zedek-joseph-ko:
Joseph Kohen-Zedek (1827-1903) was a rabbinical scholar and preacher. Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Lemberg, he died at London at the end. His house claimed a line back to the exilarchs of old.

That line ran through Solomon Luria and Moses Isserles. He was taught by the chief rabbi of Lemberg in youth. At Lemberg he made Hebrew verse of a loyal cast. He made a book in honor of Sir Moses Montefiore. He ran three Hebrew journals in that town in his prime. In 1875 he went to London to live and work. There he brought out a book of his own sermons. More books on Torah and law came from his pen there. He made a set of court replies in that town as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zutra-mar-bar-m:
Mar Zutra, son of Mar Zutra, was a Palestinian scholar and official leader of its Jews. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. On the day he was born, his father was crucified, and his mother fled with him to Palestine. He later became archipherecite, a chief officer of the community.

Under his lead, the entry says, learned material gathered in Palestine was collected and examined. The Palestinian Talmud is said to have been completed in his lifetime. He probably lived at Tiberias. In his term, Justinian's order about reading Scripture in synagogue was issued. The first protest against that order is credited to Mar Zutra.
journal-of-discourses-vol-08:
Volume Eight, from 1861, opens as the Civil War tears the Union. Secession and first battles fill the news that reaches distant Utah. Young's counsel stays steady through the crisis in these Tabernacle talks.

While the nation bleeds, the desert kingdom grows and prospers quietly. Sermons press the gathering of converts and the strength of the Saints. Separateness serves as both doctrine and a plan for survival here. The prophet's voice stays calm amid America's worst storm in generations. Readers feel the odd peace of a people set apart by faith and desert. War news arrives like weather from a world they left behind.
kenelm-chillingly-volume-08:
Volume eight of Kenelm Chillingly opens Book Eight at the breakfast table of Sir Peter. Cecilia Travers and Chillingly Gordon sit opposite their host. Sir Peter recoils in horror at a letter from Kenelm, set before him by the servant. Cecilia cannot conceive what bad news the letter holds.

Sir Peter wonders whether Kenelm has disgraced the family name or worse. He reads aloud, and the talk turns to a farmer named Nostock. Sir Peter defends old Nostock, known for six generations, against Kenelm's sharp words. Gordon changes the subject to a Times article on cabinet changes. Then Sir Peter withdraws to his library to study the letter closely. This final volume opens the novel's closing reckonings.
kleist-broken-jug-1808:
Heinrich von Kleist wrote The Broken Jug in the first years of the 1800s, and it was staged in 1808. The text here is the German original, since no English translation is in the public domain. In a Dutch village court, Judge Adam tries the case of a jug broken in a girl's room at night.

Adam presses the young suspect hard while hiding his own part in the night's events. Witness by witness, his questions trap him deeper in his own lies. A visiting inspector watches the farce of justice judging itself. Kleist builds the comedy in brisk verse with a detective's logic. The play is ranked the masterpiece of German comic drama.
kleist-penthesilea-1808:
Penthesilea, Kleist's tragedy of 1808, is given here in the German original. No English translation of the play is in the public domain. Penthesilea, queen of the Amazons, must win a Greek hero in battle before she may love him, by the law of her people.

She fixes on Achilles, and their meetings in the Trojan War blur war and courtship. Signals miscarry, pride flares, and love turns to a frenzy that destroys them both. Kleist drives the verse at a fever pitch few German plays attempt. Goethe found the play too wild, yet later ages prized its extremes. It stands as the most intense drama of German Romanticism.
lamb-ulysses-1808:
Charles Lamb retold Homer's Odyssey for young readers in 1808, a year after the Tales from Shakespear. He followed the old Chapman translation as his guide. The contents divide Ulysses' voyage into short chapters, starting with the Cicons, the Lotus-eaters, and Polyphemus the Cyclops.

Circe turns men into beasts, the hero visits the dead, and the Sirens sing their deadly song. Scylla, Charybdis, the Oxen of the Sun, and Calypso's island all follow in clear order. Lamb's warm and plain prose gave generations of children their first trip with Homer's hero, long before they could read the epic itself.
loisy-gospel-and-church-1908:
Alfred Loisy was a French priest and scholar whose Gospel and the Church, in this 1908 English edition, defined Catholic modernism. He wrote the book as a reply to Adolf Harnack, the great German liberal historian of doctrine. Rome condemned Loisy's works and excommunicated him the same year.

Loisy argues that Jesus preached the kingdom, and what came was the church, a living body that grew by its own laws. Doctrine, in his account, develops under history's pressure rather than dropping whole from heaven. The short book's calm tone made its radical claim all the harder for churchmen to answer.
london-iron-heel-1908:
Jack London published The Iron Heel in 1908, his chilling manuscript from a future America crushed under an oligarchic heel. The founding text of the modern political dystopia imagines three centuries of the Brotherhood of Man's defeat and revolt. London framed it as a manuscript found, annotated by a future scholar.

Ernest Everhard, a socialist orator, warns a dinner of masters that labor will answer capital's heel with revolution in America. Avis, his wife and the narrator, records strikes crushed, militias loosed, and the Chicago Commune's streets running with blood. The oligarchy, a union of trusts and state, builds its wonder city and rules through spies, agents, and the mercenary army. Everhard vanishes into conspiracy and death, and the manuscript breaks off, its future notes promising liberation centuries hence. Orwell and later dystopians read this fierce, flawed prophecy with care.
lowell-mars-abode-of-life-1908:
Percival Lowell made his case to the broad public in this book of 1908. It sums up his years of work on Mars for the lay reader. The theme is plain in the title: Mars is a home for life.

He walks from the white caps at the poles to the dark belts that shift with the seasons. Each sign, he holds, points to air, water, plants, and at last to minds at work. The book is the full habit plea for the red world, in Lowell's best public voice. It marks the peak of the Mars craze in print for lay readers.
maeterlinck-blue-bird-1908:
Maurice Maeterlinck wrote The Blue Bird in 1908, a fairy play for the stage. Two children, Tyltyl and Mytyl, set out to find the Blue Bird of Happiness. A fairy sends them through strange lands on Christmas Eve. They visit the past, the future, and the homes of night and joy.

Along the way, their dog, cat, and household objects come to life and speak. Each land teaches them something about what happiness is. At the end, the bird they sought was at home all along. The play charmed audiences around the world. Its gentle lesson still suits family reading and school stages today.
margery-gred-a-tale-of-old-nuremberg-vol:
Volume eight of Margery opens in delay and disappointment. The maidens hoped to ride into the wide world for their lover and brother. That hope is not to be yet, and patience is hard. Their guide Kubbeling, a born wanderer, loses his mirth at the forest lodge.

Then Kubbeling falls sick of a fever and lies abed two weeks. He had never needed healing beyond his cattle-leech's art. The household awaits his tidings with much fear. Doctor Holzschuher, once a steadfast friend, gives no sign at all. Ebers slows the tale into suspense and waiting. Love and loyalty are tested by sickness and silence.
mcclure-s-magazine-vol-31-no-1-may-1908:
McClure's Magazine for May 1908 opens volume thirty one. A full contents page lists tales, lives, and reports for the month. Georgine Milmine writes on Mary Baker G. Eddy in this issue.

Carl Schurz tells of the first days of Reconstruction in the South. He treats the Freedmen's Bureau, Johnson's haste, and the South's deep want. Fiction comes from Edward S. Moffat, Lucy Pratt, and James Barnes. George Kennan reports on poverty and unrest in Russia, and Ellen Terry writes on stage plays. A play piece on Olivia and Faust at the Lyceum adds stage talk. Tales and reports share the issue in the McClure mix of that era.
medela-chymica-or-an-account-of-the-vert: Christopher Packe wrote Medela Chymica, dated 1708 in the record. Its title promises an account of the virtues and uses of chemical medicines. It also promises cures for chronic and stubborn diseases. The hosted sample for this entry is garbled scan text with no readable passage. Only broken marks and letter scraps can be made out in it. This note stays with the title, the author, and the year for that reason.
medical-and-alchemical-recipes-manuscrip: Denis de la Fontaine is named as author of Medical and Alchemical Recipes, a manuscript dated 1608. The record calls it one volume, with drawings, in a small octavo size. The hosted sample for this entry is garbled scan text throughout. No readable recipe or passage can be made out in it. This note stays with the title, the author, and the year for that reason. The contents cannot be described from the sample held here.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-08: Volume eight, etext 3558, continues Bourrienne's account of his master Napoleon. The head note pairs its title with the year 1805. Eleventh edition, English language, and Widger as producer are also listed there. Readers of the sample, however, meet only Gutenberg boilerplate from top to end. Not one line of the secretary's narrative is included. Any summary of this volume would have to come from outside the sample, so none is offered.
munro-palaeolithic-man-1908:
Robert Munro, a Scots doctor and digger, gave these talks on stone age man and the Terramara sites in 1908. The Terramara are mound sites in Italy, built by folk of the bronze age. Munro had dug lake dwells in Scotland and knew both themes at first hand.

He joins the deep stone age of France to the lake and mound homes of a later Europe. Tools, homes, and graves show how life grew from camp to town in slow steps. The book forms a bridge from man's first times to the prehistory of Europe as a whole.
my-novel-volume-08:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's eighth book opens with a blast at loud progress. Trumpets and drums hail the March of Enlightenment, he writes. Yet light is noiseless, so why does this march clatter? He asks where Enlightenment is marching to at all.

Six loud fans would give six poor answers, he wagers. One slave cries for the Charter's seven points. One young French type wants free love and no prejudice. One plain rich man hopes for less and fears his errand boy. The chapter mocks cant about progress from all sides. Lytton's satire cuts reformers and snobs alike with a cool, amused hand.
nicoll-three-voyages-of-a-naturalist-190:
Michael Nicoll sailed the world to study birds and beasts, and met a monster on the way. Three Voyages of a Naturalist, printed in 1908, gathers his trips as a ship's naturalist. Nicoll was a trained observer with a name in the science of his day.

Off Brazil in 1905, from the yacht Valhalla, he and a mate watched a great sea serpent at close range. He tells the sighting with a field man's care for size, shape, and motion. Rupert Gould and others weighed the report as one of the best of its kind. The monster sits at the heart of a fine travel book.
ocean-of-story-kathasaritsagara-tawney-1:
The eighth volume of The Ocean of Story, in Penzer's edition of Tawney's Somadeva from 1924, nears the Kathasaritsagara's final books. The hero's marriages, wars, and wanderings among the Vidyadharas gather force here. Around him the tale streams still run thick with merchants, demons, and clever queens.

Penzer, by now deep in his ten-volume labor, annotates with a comparativist's full toolkit. Tawney's English stays lucid even where the Sanskrit delights in compounds and wordplay. The result serves two readers at once: the one lost in story, and the one tracing stories across the world. Volume eight rewards both. Its tales of the Vetala, the vampire riddler, are a set favorite.
openalex-w1599923008:
Ana Pilar Betrán, Ahmet Gülmezoglu, and co-authors wrote this review. It appeared in Reproductive Health in the year 2015. In 1985 the WHO set a guide rate for caesarean births. Rates above that guide lacked justification, the WHO said. World rates have climbed for three decades since then.

The team searched four databases for population level studies. Thousands of citations narrowed to eight included studies. Most linked higher caesarean rates to lower death rates. That link held only up to a modest threshold rate. After adjusting for wealth factors, the link weakened or vanished. Rates above the threshold brought no further gains, they report.
openalex-w2088190208:
Brian Lehmann, Joshua Bauer, Johanna Schafer and colleagues tested drug pairs for a breast cancer subtype. Their paper appeared in Breast Cancer Research in 2014. The subtype lacks three common drug targets. One group within it carries the androgen receptor. Those cancers often carry a key gene mutation.

The mutation switches on a growth pathway called PI3K. The team checked mutation rates in patient samples. Mutations were far more common in receptor-positive cases. They treated cancer cells with pathway blockers. Adding an androgen blocker strengthened the effect. Mouse tumour tests showed the same added benefit. The pair may suit patients whom chemotherapy fails. Targeted trials are the next step.
openalex-w2122737708:
Ricardo Esper, Roberto Nordaby, Jorge Vilariño, and colleagues published this review in Cardiovascular Diabetology in 2006. They give a full account of endothelial dysfunction, a failure of the thin cell layer that lines all blood vessels. That layer, the endothelium, helps control vessel widening, clotting, and swelling.

The review explains how the healthy endothelium senses physical and chemical signals and releases substances that keep balance. It then shows how heart risk factors and oxidative stress damage that control and start vessel disease. The authors also cover ways to test endothelial health, which rest largely on how much vessels widen in response to nitric oxide.
openalex-w2124463708:
Gisela De La Rosa, Jorge Donado, Alvaro Restrepo, and colleagues published this trial in Critical Care in 2008. They asked whether tight control of blood sugar with insulin helps very sick patients in a mixed medical and surgical intensive care unit. Earlier trials in single-type units had shown benefits, but mixed units were untested.

About five hundred patients were assigned by chance to tight or standard sugar control. Death rates after twenty-eight days did not differ in a meaningful way between the groups. Infection rates in the unit also showed no clear difference. Low blood sugar was much more common under tight control, so the stricter plan carried a real added risk here.
openalex-w2136326608:
América Mederos, Zully Ramos, and Georgget Banchero published this short report in Parasites and Vectors in 2014. They give the first report from Uruguay of worm resistance to monepantel, a sheep deworming drug. On two farms, egg counts in dung failed to fall after routine treatment, and lambs died from the blood-feeding worm Haemonchus contortus.

The team ran a standard egg count reduction test on both farms. Treated lambs were compared with untreated controls about a week after dosing. Egg counts barely fell on the first farm and fell only partly on the second. The resistant worms belonged to the Haemonchus group. The drug showed poor efficacy on both farms.
openalex-w2145617208:
Humberto Lara, Vanesa Ayala-Nunez, Liliana Ixtepan-Turrent, and Cristina Rodríguez-Padilla published this study in the Journal of Nanobiotechnology in 2010. Silver nanoparticles were already known to block HIV at doses that do not harm cells. The team set out to learn exactly how the particles attack the virus.

Using a panel of lab assays, they found the particles act mainly at an early stage. They bind to a coat protein on the virus and block its grip on the CD4 receptor of immune cells. That stops binding, fusion, and infection for free virus and virus passed between cells. The effect held across lab strains, patient isolates, and drug-resistant strains, and later stages were also inhibited.
openalex-w2151276208:
