Lilian Bahia-Oliveira, Jeffrey Jones, Juliana Azevedo-Silva, and colleagues published this survey in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2003. Reports of eye disease consistent with toxoplasmosis prompted a study in northern Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil. They measured how common Toxoplasma gondii infection was and what raised the risk.

Blood from more than fourteen hundred people was tested in 1997 to 1999. Infection was extremely common and rose steeply with age. After age adjustment, about eighty-four in a hundred people in the poorest group carried the parasite. Rates fell to about sixty-two in the middle group and twenty-three in the richest. plos-pbio-0020008:
Elena Rebollo, Salud Llamazares, José Reina, and their team studied cell division in the fruit fly for PLOS Biology in 2004. When a cell divides, a spindle of tiny tubes pulls the chromosomes apart. In fly sperm-forming cells, some of those tubes grow without the usual organizing centers, called centrosomes.

The question was whether those extra tubes truly help build the spindle or are just bystanders. The study shows they do real work in getting the spindle into shape. That widens the standard picture of division, which gives centrosomes the lead role. Knowing all the ways a spindle can form helps explain why division is so robust, and why it fails in some diseases.
plos-pbio-0020108:
Eric Bair and Robert Tibshirani presented a statistics method in PLOS Biology in 2004. Doctors want to predict how long cancer patients will live using gene activity data. The catch is that such data sets hold thousands of genes but few patients, so plain methods often fail.

Their semi-supervised approach first finds gene patterns tied to outcome without using survival times, then links those patterns to survival. Splitting the task this way cuts the noise that swamps direct methods. Better survival forecasts help doctors sort patients by risk and choose how hard to treat. The paper is a good example of math built for the exact shape of a real data problem.
plos-pbio-0020408:
Linus T.-Y. Tsai, Roland J. Bainton, Justin Blau, and their team linked clock neurons to drug response in flies in PLOS Biology in 2004. Fruit flies with faults in a gene called Lmo behave oddly after cocaine exposure. The authors traced part of that effect to the pacemaker neurons that run the fly's daily clock.

Clock neurons were thought to keep time and little else. Here they also shape how strongly a fly responds to a drug. That overlap hints that time-of-day systems and addiction pathways share parts. It may help explain why drug sensitivity varies across the day. The fly gives a simple system for testing such links gene by gene.
plos-pone-0000008:
Maxim Kapralov and Dmitry Filatov studied evolution in one of its classic island settings for a 2006 PLOS ONE paper. Schiedea is a plant genus found only in Hawaii, where one ancestor split into many species suited to different niches. That rapid split is called adaptive radiation.

The authors read the plants' DNA for signs of molecular adaptation, changes in genes driven by natural selection during the radiation. Finding which genes changed, and how fast, shows adaptation at work at the level of molecules, not just shapes and habits. Island groups like Schiedea are natural experiments, and this study checks the experiment's results gene by gene.
plos-pone-0000108:
Nikos Oikonomou, Vaggelis Harokopos, Jonathan Zalevsky, and their team traced a lung disease step in PLOS ONE in 2006. Lung inflammation can heal cleanly or turn into fibrosis, stiff scar tissue that blocks breathing. The signal TNF is a known driver of inflammation, and it comes in a free-floating, soluble form.

The team shows the soluble form is the one that pushes inflamed lung tissue over into fibrosis. That split matters for therapy, since anti-TNF drugs exist but carry risks. Aiming only at the soluble form might keep the benefit and drop some harm. The finding gives lung fibrosis, a disease with few good treatments, a precise target to test.
plos-pone-0000208:
Gidske L. Andersen and Knut Krzywinski published this desert ecology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It tracks desert trees in a hyper-arid environment, among the driest places on Earth. The authors measure mortality, recruitment of young trees, and overall population change.

In a hyper-arid desert, a tree population can hang on rare rains or quietly die out. Long-term counts of deaths and new recruits show which way the balance tips. The work matters for predicting how extreme drylands and their sparse tree cover will respond as climates shift. Long-term records like this are rare in deserts this dry.
plos-pone-0000308:
Heather A. Piwowar, Roger S. Day, and Douglas B. Fridsma published this research policy paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It asks whether sharing detailed research data pays off for the sharer. The authors report, as the title says, that sharing is associated with an increased citation rate for the papers whose data are shared.

Citations are the currency of academic reward, so a citation boost is a real incentive. The study measured that association across a set of shared datasets. It became a frequently cited piece of evidence in the open science movement's case for mandatory data sharing.
plos-pone-0000408:
Mitsumasa Yoda, Kohei Eguchi, and Tomoki P. Terada dissected the protein clock that ticks inside cyanobacteria, in PLOS ONE in 2007. These bacteria keep a daily rhythm using just three proteins, with KaiC at the center, cycling through chemical states over about 24 hours. The team studied how KaiC units shuffle and switch shape.

They describe monomer-shuffling, where KaiC subunits swap between complexes, and an allosteric transition, a shape change that alters the protein's activity. Together these motions may keep the clock's period steady. A clock built from so few parts is a gift for physics-minded biology: every moving piece can, in principle, be accounted for.
plos-pone-0000508:
W. John Kress and David L. Erickson proposed a standard DNA barcode for identifying land plants, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. A barcode is a short DNA stretch that differs between species, letting a sample be named from a leaf fragment or seed. Their two-locus barcode pairs the coding gene rbcL with the non-coding spacer region trnH-psbA.

One locus alone mislabels too many plant species; the pair complements each other, one steady and one variable. A working plant barcode serves ecology, customs checks on traded timber and herbs, and the cataloging of unknown floras. The paper helped settle a practical standard that later global efforts built on.
plos-pone-0000608:
Olivier Delelis and colleagues studied how HIV's copying enzyme cuts DNA at a specific pattern, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. HIV-1 integrase inserts the virus's DNA into the host genome, a step drugs can block. The team showed efficient and specific internal cleavage of a retroviral palindromic DNA sequence by tetrameric HIV-1 integrase, the four-part form of the enzyme.

A palindrome reads the same both ways, and the viral DNA ends carry such patterns. Showing the four-part enzyme cuts there specifically clarifies the exact reaction integrase inhibitors must stop. Mechanistic detail of this kind underlies the design of a major class of HIV drugs.
plos-pone-0000708:
Yoshihito Niimura and Masatoshi Nei tallied the gains and losses of smell genes across mammal evolution, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Smell in mammals runs on a large family of olfactory receptor genes. Their number varies extensively among species. Most species also carry many pseudogenes, broken copies that no longer work.

The title reports extensive gains and losses in this family over evolutionary time. Lineages that live by smell keep or expand their receptor sets, while others let them decay. Comparing counts and pseudogenes across species turns the family into a record of how each mammal makes its living. It also sharpens questions about why humans kept the sense they did.
plos-pone-0000808:
Sébastien Gingras, Stéphane Pelletier, Kelli Boyd and colleagues characterized a new family of nuclear proteins first spotted in activated T cells. Gene array analysis had been widely used to find genes switched on during T cell activation. Their studies identified an immediate early gene strongly induced by IL-2 in mouse T cells, which they named CSRNP-1, for cysteine-serine-rich nuclear protein-1. A human counterpart followed.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE paper characterizes the whole CSRNP family. Proteins rich in cysteine and serine, sitting in the nucleus, and switched on within hours of activation look like regulators of the response program. Naming and mapping a family is the first step toward learning what it controls.
plos-pone-0000908:
Luciana Girao, Ariadna Lopes, Marcelo Tabarelli and colleagues studied how breaking up Atlantic Forest changes tree reproduction, in PLOS ONE in 2007. A forest's mix of working traits helps keep the whole system running. How human disturbance scrambles that mix was poorly known.

The team tested whether fragmentation shifts which reproductive traits dominate among trees. Fragmented edges favor some pollination and seed styles over others, thinning the range of strategies. A narrower range can leave a forest less able to recover from drought or disease. The study gives conservationists a trait based way to judge forest damage, beyond counting species alone.
plos-pone-0001008:
Luis Santamaria, Javier Rodriguez-Perez, Asier Larrinaga and colleagues predicted where new plants arise from how animals move, in PLOS ONE in 2007. For plants spread by fruit eating animals, recruitment patterns start with where parent plants stand. They are then reshaped by how the animal digests seeds, where it travels and how the land is laid out.

The team use animal displacement kernels, math descriptions of how far seeds are carried, to predict spatial patterns of new plants. Such predictions help judge whether a plant population can track a shifting climate. They also show how losing a seed carrier can quietly rewrite a forest map.
plos-pone-0001108:
Chiara Begliomini, Andrea Caria, Wolfgang Grodd and colleagues compared grasping in natural and constrained movements, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In monkeys, grasping relies on a circuit between a parietal area called AIP and premotor area F5. Single cell recordings there show how the brain turns sight of an object into a shaped hand.

Human studies often force unnatural, constrained grasps for the scanner. The team compare those with natural movements to find what changes. If the circuit behaves differently under constraint, scanner results need care when read as daily grasping. The paper is a methods check with direct bearing on brain imaging of hand control.
plos-pone-0001208:
Invasive species usually get blamed on trade and travel, which carry organisms around the world. Wen Lin and colleagues added a less obvious driver in a 2007 PLOS ONE article: fast economic development within a country. They tested the idea using China as their case.

Using principal factor analysis, the authors explored how development intensity relates to the pace of biological invasions. Indirect factors that raise invasion pressure had rarely been quantified. Their finding suggests that as economies grow and build, they open more doors to foreign species, a cost of development that planning rarely counts.
plos-pone-0001308:
Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 is a probiotic strain used for gut disorders. Sya Ukena and colleagues studied how it affects a leaky gut, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The intestinal barrier is formed by gut lining cells and the junctions between them, and it keeps contents where they belong. Disruption raises permeability. It is also a key mechanism in gut infections.

The authors report that the probiotic inhibits leaky gut by enhancing mucosal integrity. Probiotics are proposed to positively modulate this barrier, and their study tests one strain's mechanism directly. The result supports a specific claim for a widely sold probiotic.
plos-pone-0001408:
Jörn Scharlemann and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a new way to clean satellite data for ecology. Satellites track land cover, heat, and plant growth over time. Such series help model where plants and animals live, most of all those of farm or wild life value. Raw series are noisy, so they must be smoothed with care.

The authors present a fresh method based on wave like fits over time. It aims to keep true seasonal shifts while cutting noise. Clean data matter, since maps built from them guide land and health choices. Their method gives field teams a sharper tool for work that spans years and wide areas.
plos-pone-0001508:
Paolo Monaci and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on picking useful antibodies fast. Labs build vast antibody sets and must find ones that bind targets with a set pattern. The usual search needs facts that may not exist. The team built a tag based array method to screen the sets by gene chip.

Short DNA tags mark each antibody clone in the set. Chips then read which clones bind which targets in one pass. That speed lets teams mine huge sets without slow one by one tests. The method could cut the cost of finding antibodies for research and care.
plos-pone-0001608:
Rita Neres and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on malaria in pregnancy in mice. Malaria in pregnancy brings grave harm: sicker mothers, poor fetal growth, low birth weight, and infant deaths. Its course in women is hard to study in depth. The team infected pregnant mice with a rodent malaria strain.

The mouse course closely copied the harm seen in pregnant women, down to womb tissue changes. A close copy gives labs an ethical way to test drugs and shots for this group. Pregnant women are oft left out of trials, so a sound model holds extra value. It may speed guards for a group at sharp risk.
plos-pone-0001708:
Zoe Waibler, Linda Y. Sender, Camilla Merten, and their co-authors profiled powerful immune-activating antibodies in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Superagonistic CD28 antibodies switch T cells on without the usual co-signal from the T-cell receptor complex. In rodents they expand regulatory T cells and can treat autoimmune disease. In a human trial, though, such an antibody caused severe harm, making its signals a safety question.

The team mapped the signaling signatures and functional properties of anti-human CD28 superagonists. The full text gives the cell tests and which pathways fired. Knowing exactly what these antibodies do in human cells is a precondition for any safe return of the class. It is also a case study in how animal results can mislead.
plos-pone-0001808:
Michael B. Gill, Rachel Edgar, Janet S. May, and their co-authors studied how a herpesvirus spreads between cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Viruses cannot propel themselves. To move within multi-cellular hosts they must manipulate infected cells. Herpesviruses are a model for such manipulation, but most movement knowledge covered alpha-herpesviruses, leaving the gamma group understudied.

The team reports that a gamma-herpesvirus glycoprotein complex manipulates actin, the cell's internal scaffolding, to promote viral spread. The full text gives the cell imaging and the spread assays. A virus that remodels the cell's skeleton to travel is harder to stop with antibodies alone, which aim at free virus particles.
plos-pone-0001908:
Kelly Salter and co-authors built a way to pick breast cancer drugs per patient, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. A core problem in cancer care is choosing the drug most likely to work for one person. A drug that fails still costs time, health, and quality of life, so a test that sorts patients first has real value.

The team joined several kinds of patient data into one approach to forecast how a tumor would respond to chemotherapy. A sound forecast lets doctors skip drugs bound to fail and start with the best bet. The study is a step toward cancer care matched to each tumor, rather than one plan for all.
plos-pone-0002008:
Jorge Zavala and co-authors studied how a caterpillar's gut copes with a plant's chemical defense, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The plant, a wild tobacco, makes trypsin proteinase inhibitors, proteins that block the gut enzymes of insects that eat it. Past work had shown these blockers defend the plant, by changing their levels in the plant and watching the caterpillar suffer.

The team now looked inside the caterpillar, the hornworm Manduca sexta, at its midgut proteinases, the enzymes that digest food. If the worm answers blockers by changing its enzymes, the plant defense is a moving duel. The study maps both sides of that duel.
plos-pone-0002108:
Chit-Ming Wong and co-authors asked whether exercise guards against death in flu seasons, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Little was known about the effect of physical exercise on influenza-associated mortality, the extra deaths that come with flu waves. The team collected data on exercise habits, other lifestyle traits, and social and economic status.

Their data cover the underlying cause of death of twenty-four thousand six hundred fifty-six adults, most aged sixty-five or older. A link, if real, would add flu survival to the long list of exercise gains. The study gives a careful test in a very large group.
plos-pone-0002208:
Daniel Ramot, Brandon Johnson, Tommie Berry, and co-authors built a machine to watch worms move, described in PLOS ONE in 2008. The tiny worm Caenorhabditis elegans is a workhorse for studying behavior, nerve signaling, and muscle. Most studies of its crawling relied on a human observer's judgment, which is slow and hard to repeat.

The Parallel Worm Tracker films many worms at once and measures their speed automatically. It can also score drug-induced paralysis, a standard test in worm labs. Automating the watching turns a chore into clean data, letting genetics and drug studies run at a much larger scale.
plos-pone-0002308:
Andrew Pask, Kerry McInnes, David Webb, and co-authors tested a topical estrogen treatment on human foreskin tissue, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. With HIV still spreading, simple and cheap new prevention methods are badly needed. Male circumcision cuts a man's risk of infection by about 60 percent, probably because it removes tissue rich in Langerhans cells. This HIV uses to enter the body.

The team asked whether estrogen cream could keratinise the foreskin, thickening its surface layer, instead of surgery. A tougher surface may block the virus. Their tissue study tests a low-cost idea that, if it works in people, could widen HIV prevention options greatly.
plos-pone-0002408:
Research by Roberge and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Christian Roberge, Simon Blanchet, Julian J. Dodson, and others. Its subject is disturbance of Social Hierarchy by an Invasive Species: A Gene Transcription Study. Ecological and evolutionary changes in native populations facing invasion by exotic species are increasingly reported.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002508:
Abraham and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from John M. Abraham, Yulan Cheng, James P. Hamilton, and others. Its subject is generation of Small 32 P-Labeled Peptides as a Potential Approach to Colorectal Cancer Therapy. Cancers have been revealed to be extremely heterogenous in terms of the frequency and types of mutations present in cells from different malignant tumors.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002608:
Led by Togbe, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Dieudonnée Togbe, Paulo Loureiro de Sousa, Mathilde Fauconnier, and others. Its subject is both Functional LTβ Receptor and TNF Receptor 2 Are Required for the Development of Experimental Cerebral Malaria. TNF-related lymphotoxin α (LTα) is key for the development of Plasmodium berghei ANKA (PbA)-induced experimental cerebral malaria (ECM).

The pathway involved has been attributed to TNFR2. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002708:
Work by Asaf Madi and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with genome holography: deciphering Function-Form motifs from gene expression data. Authorship is credited in the record to Asaf Madi and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. DNA chips allow simultaneous measurements of genome-wide response of thousands of genes, i.e. The authors add a further point. System level monitoring of the gene-network activity. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002808:
Research from Thomas G. Kaye and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers dinosaurian soft tissues interpreted as bacterial biofilms. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Thomas G. Kaye, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. A scanning electron microscope survey was initiated to determine if the previously reported findings of “dinosaurian soft tissues” could be identified in situ within. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002908:
Fadi Bittar, Hervé Richet, Jean-Christophe Dubus and co-authors used molecular tests in 2008 to find germs in sputum from cystic fibrosis patients. Standard culture in the lab detects only a small share of the bacteria in these patients' airways. That leaves emerging pathogens easy to miss.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team applied DNA-based detection to sputum samples and found multiple emerging pathogens. Better detection matters because treatment in cystic fibrosis hinges on knowing which germs are present. The paper supports wider use of molecular methods alongside culture in routine care for these patients.
plos-pone-0003008:
Elizabeth Thompson and Andrew Travers studied a fly version of the Smyd4 protein in 2008. Smyd proteins, named for their SET and MYND domains, regulate transcription tied to cell growth and development in vertebrates. Their in vivo functions and mechanisms were poorly understood when the study began.

In Drosophila, the homologue acts as a muscle-specific transcriptional modulator involved in development, per the title. Using biochemical and genetic approaches together, the authors pinned down that role. Published in PLOS ONE, a defined fly model lets others dissect how this protein family steers muscle genes. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003108:
Debra Toiber, Amit Berson, David Greenberg and co-authors linked a variant of acetylcholinesterase to Alzheimer's features in 2008. Alzheimer's disease involves loss of cholinergic neurons and hyper-phosphorylation of the Tau protein. Both are hallmarks that any causal account should connect rather than treat separately.

Overexpression of an N-terminally extended synaptic variant, N-AChE-S, was causally involved in both phenomena in their tests, the authors report. Published in PLOS ONE, a single variant tying neuron loss to Tau change suggests a shared upstream step worth probing for therapy. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003208:
Paule Bénit, Sergio Goncalves, Emmanuel Philippe Dassa and colleagues study the Harlequin mouse as a disease model in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Despite progress in knowledge of the molecular bases of mitochondrial diseases, no effective treatments had been made. Faithful animal models would be very helpful for designing such treatments. The team had shown earlier that the Harlequin mouse carries just such a defect.

They report that variability of the Harlequin phenotype resembles that of human mitochondrial complex I deficiency syndromes. Readers learn why the model's uneven symptoms are a strength, since human disease also varies widely. A model that matches human variability can test treatments more honestly.
plos-pone-0003308:
Jana Sponarova, Sofia N. Nyström and Gunilla T. Westermark test transfer of amyloidosis by blood cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Spongiform encephalopathies have been reported to be transmitted by blood transfusion even prior to clinical onset. Experimental AA-amyloidosis shows similarities with prion disease, and amyloid-containing organ extracts can prime a recipient for the disease.

The title reports that AA-amyloidosis can be transferred by peripheral blood monocytes. Readers learn that mobile blood cells can carry amyloid seeding ability. That finding matters for transfusion safety and for how systemic amyloid disease spreads in the body.
plos-pone-0003408:
Stéphane Chavanas and co-authors studied far-off gene control in skin cells in this 2008 paper. Some DNA switches sit far from the genes they control. A loop in the chromosome can bring a distant switch into contact. The team studied one such switch for a gene called peptidylarginine deiminase 3.

The gene matters in skin cells that have matured, called keratinocytes. Its distant enhancer let a factor named AP-1 turn the gene on. The enzymes in this family change proteins in ways tied to disease. The study is a clear case of long-range control in human DNA.
plos-pone-0003508:
Thore Santel, Gabi Pflug, and Nasr Y. A. Hemdan studied a spice compound's target in this 2008 paper. Curcumin, from turmeric, is praised for anti-inflammatory and anti-tumor effects. Glyoxalase 1 is an enzyme that detoxifies a reactive sugar byproduct called methylglyoxal. Blocking such enzymes is one route to new drugs.

The team found curcumin inhibits glyoxalase 1 directly. That block offers a possible link to curcumin's reported health effects. One named target makes the spice's claims easier to test. The result gives follow-up work a concrete biochemical starting point. Turmeric has been used as food and folk medicine for a very long time.
plos-pone-0003608:
Yi Tan and co-authors mapped two virus infections among drug injectors in southern China in this 2008 study. Hepatitis C and HIV both spread through shared injection gear. Co-infection with both is a growing problem in this group. Rates and viral genotypes vary with geographic location.

The team studied injection drug users in Liuzhou. They charted HCV alone and HIV/HCV co-infection at the molecular level. Harm reduction access is opening chances for care in the region. A clear genotype map guides prevention where the epidemics overlap. Needle sharing drives both epidemics in many cities across Asia and beyond.
plos-pone-0003708:
Baxter P. Rogers and John C. Gore published this neuroimaging methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. fMRI connectivity studies judge brain networks by how signals in different regions move together. Labs compute those measures in varied ways. That variety makes the published literature hard to compare.

The authors ran an empirical comparison of where the variation in such analyses comes from. Method choices, they show, pull in different sources of noise and difference. Their head-to-head results tell imagers which approaches give the steadiest read on brain networks, and which to treat with care.
plos-pone-0003808:
Kristin L. Bishop, Anita K. Pai, and Daniel Schmitt published this animal locomotion study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Moving costs energy, and that cost is a large part of an animal's budget. How animals control muscular effort while walking shapes limb design and behavior. Cats are famous for quiet, stealthy movement.

The authors measured the whole body mechanics of stealthy walking in cats. Their analysis shows how the prowl keeps locomotion cheap and silent at once. The energy budget of a stalking cat turns out to be a lesson in efficient movement for any walking animal.
plos-pone-0003908:
Roland T. Ullrich, Thomas Zander, Bernd Neumaier, and co-authors tested early scans of lung cancer treatment in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns advanced non-small cell lung cancer. A drug called erlotinib blocks a growth receptor that some tumors depend on. Doctors need fast ways to tell whether the drug is working.

The team used PET scans with a tracer called FLT to watch tumors early. Changes in the scan can show tumor growth slowing soon after treatment starts. Early reads let doctors switch failing treatments sooner. The approach may spare patients weeks on a drug that brings no gain.
plos-pone-0004008:
Vladana Vukojević, Yu Ming, Claudio D'Addario, and co-authors watched alcohol and a drug meet at a receptor in 2008. Alcoholism is a widespread chronic disorder with heavy social costs. How ethanol acts at the molecular level remains poorly understood. Drug treatment for alcoholism is still in its early days.

Their PLOS ONE article studies naltrexone and ethanol at the mu-opioid receptor. They used light methods in live cells to watch the interaction. Naltrexone is already used to help people stop drinking. Seeing its receptor behavior may explain how it counters alcohol. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004108:
Shin-ichi Hashimoto, Wei Qu, Budrul Ahsan, and co-authors analyzed gene start sites with new sequencing in 2009. Tag-based sequencers like SOLiD generate huge expression data sets cheaply. They promise to transform whole-genome expression study. The start end of transcripts carries key control information.

Their PLOS ONE article gives high-resolution analysis of the 5-prime transcriptome. Mapping where transcripts begin reveals promoters actually in use. The method extracts that map from next-generation sequencing reads. It helps labs annotate genes beyond their coding regions. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004208:
Trupti Joshi and colleagues published this cancer immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Macrophages help clear tumour cells that have been coated with antibodies, a process called ADCC. The signalling pathways that regulate this killing were poorly defined.

Using human B cell lymphoma cells coated with the drug rituximab, the team traced the pathway in macrophages. They report that the PtdIns 3-kinase and Akt pathway regulates macrophage-mediated killing of the lymphoma cells. Knowing the control circuit could help make antibody therapies clear tumours more completely. Rituximab is a standard antibody drug for this cancer.
plos-pone-0004308:
Emma Nickerson and colleagues published this clinical study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most knowledge of invasive Staphylococcus aureus infection comes from cooler countries. In the tropics, basic facts about these infections were full of gaps: how they spread, how to treat them, and how patients fare.

The team tracked S. aureus bacteraemia, bacteria in the blood, in a tropical setting, following patients as they were treated. They tracked patient outcomes and the impact of antibiotic resistance. Their data give tropical hospitals evidence of their own, rather than borrowed numbers from cooler climates.
plos-pone-0004408:
In HIV, immune cells can be both highly active and less mature. Jason Barbour, Lishomwa Ndhlovu, Qi Xuan Tan, and co-authors study that pairing in this 2009 PLOS ONE article. High T cell activity and changed cell growth are each known marks of HIV-1 infection.

The team asked if drugs that stop the virus would change both marks at once. They found high CD8 activity marks a less mature HIV-specific response. That pattern did not change when viral growth was suppressed, as their title states. The result shapes how immune recovery is judged in care.
plos-pone-0004508:
Magnetic pulses to the brain's motor area change how people handle verbs, show Liuba Papeo, Antonino Vallesi, Alessio Isaja, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. A theory called embodied cognition holds that understanding action words involves the same motor areas used to act. On that view, word meanings are partly stored in the body systems they describe.

The team used transcranial magnetic stimulation, brief magnetic pulses through the skull, on the primary motor cortex. They timed the pulses to different stages of processing motor and non-motor verbs. If the motor cortex is just a bystander, the pulses should change nothing. The study's design lets the timing speak. Results of this kind decide whether the body truly helps build word meaning.
plos-pone-0004608:
A prostate protein switches on two signals that help tumors grow, report Marco Colombatti, Silvia Grasso, Alessandra Porzia, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The signals are interleukin-6 and the chemokine CCL5, both implicated in the development and progression of several tumors, including prostate cancer. The protein is PSMA, the prostate specific membrane antigen, whose expression rises in high-grade and metastatic tumors.

The team shows PSMA regulates the expression of IL-6 and CCL5 in prostate tumor cells by activating the MAPK pathways. That makes PSMA more than a passive marker used to find tumors on scans. It is an active driver of the tumor's signal environment. Targeting it might cut off chemical support the tumor gives itself.
plos-pone-0004708:
Bernhards Ogutu and colleagues tested a blood stage malaria vaccine in young children in western Kenya, for PLOS ONE in 2009. The vaccine used a piece of a protein from the malaria parasite surface. It was mixed with a strong booster to raise high levels of antibodies in the blood.

High antibody levels alone did not protect the children, as the title states. The trial result is a hard but useful lesson for vaccine design. It shows that the amount of antibody is not enough by itself. Future vaccines must raise the right kind of defense, not just more of it.
plos-pone-0004808:
Jesper Petersen and colleagues built a microfluidic device for creating ionic strength gradients over DNA microarrays, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Growth of DNA microarray assays is hampered because processing is done under a single stringency condition. Characteristics such as melting temperature are also difficult to predict for immobilized probes. Leading to uneven performance across spots on the same array in routine diagnostic use.

Gradients allow many stringencies in one test. Efficient melting studies become possible on a single chip. Assay growth can proceed faster and cheaper. The device addresses a practical bottleneck in array design. Replication in other settings will show how robust the findings really are.
plos-pone-0004908:
Jibin Wang and colleagues studied contact of coronavirus infectious bronchitis virus membrane protein with beta actin, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Coronavirus M protein is an essential virion component playing pivotal roles in assembly, budding, and maturation. The protein integrates into viral envelope with three transmembrane domains, and contact with host actin implicates cytoskeleton in virion formation, and Release from infected poultry cells in this economically key virus.

Host skeleton assists viral exit strategies. Actin contact may be conserved across coronaviruses. Blocking interfaces could yield antivirals. Poultry disease informs general virology. Further tests can show how widely the pattern holds beyond the cases studied here. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0005008:
The protein p63 is a master builder of skin. Without it, skin and other outer tissues fail to form. Silvia Pozzi and colleagues mapped its gene network in PLOS ONE in 2009. They worked in human keratinocytes, the main cells of the skin's outer layer. Their goal was the full set of genes p63 controls.

The network shows which genes p63 switches on and off. Together they govern skin growth and upkeep. The map reveals the control web behind skin development. It serves as a reference for skin disease research. Wound healing studies can also use it. Many conditions trace back to genes in this network.
plos-pone-0005108:
VEGF is the body's main grow-vessels signal. A soluble form of its receptor traps it like a sponge. Florence Wu and colleagues modeled that system in PLOS ONE in 2009. They built a compartment model of VEGF distribution in humans. The soluble receptor, sVEGFR1, acts as a ligand trap in the model.

The model predicts where VEGF goes in the body. It also predicts where the trap catches it. Angiogenesis must balance stimulatory and inhibitory processes. This trap is one of the inhibitors. The work guides dosing of VEGF-blocking drugs. Such drugs treat cancer and eye disease. A good model helps design trials. It also helps explain why doses that work in dishes fail in bodies.
plos-pone-0005208:
People with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder often vary a lot in how well they perform from moment to moment. That uneven performance is one of the most robust findings in ADHD research. Pouget and colleagues linked it to a brain circuit in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The circuit, in the front of the brain, runs on the calming signal GABA. Disturbing that circuit produced high swings in performance like those seen in ADHD. The result frames attention as a fragile balance, and it suggests why steady focus can fail even when ability is intact.
plos-pone-0005308:
Ebola virus spreads by direct contact with body fluids and can kill up to ninety percent of those infected. A vaccine based on a disabled adenovirus was already in early human testing. Richardson and colleagues tested an improved version in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The improved adenovirus-based vaccine gave enhanced protection against Ebola in their tests. Better protection from a vaccine platform already known to be safe is valuable progress. Outbreak response needs vaccines that work fast and strongly, and this work moves that goal closer. A strong vaccine for this virus must work in the field, where cold chains fail and care is far off. So each gain in strength gives outbreak teams a tool they can trust more.
plos-pone-0005408:
Birth defects are a major public health concern and a leading cause of infant death. Observational studies have linked air pollution to congenital anomalies, with mixed strength. Hansen and colleagues examined that link in Brisbane, Australia, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The study tested associations between ambient air pollution levels and birth defects across the city. Population data of this kind cannot prove cause, but consistent patterns guide deeper study. Expectant parents and city planners both have a stake in whether city air carries this risk. City air is a mix that shifts by hour. By street, so a whole-city study is the right scale to test a risk that no one family or one clinic could see on its own at all.
plos-pone-0005508:
John Paul SanGiovanni and colleagues linked mitochondrial DNA to an eye disease in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Age-related macular degeneration slowly destroys central vision and is the top cause of blindness in older people of European origin. The energy centres of cells, mitochondria, show wear in this disease.

The team found that certain DNA variants in mitochondria, marking one family line, raise the risk of the disease. Those variants sit in genes for a key energy machine. The link adds weight to the idea that failing energy supply helps drive the disease.
plos-pone-0005608:
Mahesh Yaragatti and Qi Wen presented a logic-based method for reading genome signals in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. To model how genes are controlled, workers first need to find the DNA sites where control is active. The authors treated DNA code as bits and applied a logic gate idea.

Their approach uses the XOR gate, a simple rule from computing, to infer active control modules in a genome. A new lens on the data can flag regions that standard searches miss. Such tools feed into models that predict how gene networks behave.
plos-pone-0005708:
Pavel Baranov, Maxime Venin, and Gregory Provan proposed in 2009 that the genetic code began with shorter code words. Today's code reads DNA in three-letter words called codons. The code is strikingly good at limiting the harm from small errors.

The authors suggest codons may have shrunk over time, settling at three letters. Their argument tries to explain the code's neat design without assuming nature planned ahead. Evolution has no foresight, so any neatness must grow step by step. A size-reduction path offers such steps. The idea adds a testable story to one of biology's oldest puzzles.
plos-pone-0005808:
Ammar Hawasli and co-authors examined in 2009 how an enzyme best known for brain development also tunes excitability and behavior. Cdk5 helps wire the hippocampus, a center for memory, and goes wrong in several brain diseases. Earlier work by the group showed that removing Cdk5 in adult mice sharpened some hippocampal functions.

The follow-up study mapped how Cdk5 sets the excitability of hippocampal circuits and related behavior. Too much or too little activity may each carry risks. That balance matters for drugs aimed at Cdk5 in disorders like Alzheimer's. The paper fills in dose and circuit details.
plos-pone-0005908:
Reyad Elbarbary and co-authors turned a bacterial RNA-cutting enzyme in 2009 into a tool for silencing chosen human genes. The long form of tRNase Z can cut any target RNA at a site picked by a guide RNA mimicking part of a tRNA. That programmability is rare among natural enzymes.

Using such guides, the team modulated expression of human genes on demand. A controllable silencer adds to the gene-knockdown toolkit alongside RNA interference. It may reach targets or cell types where other tools falter. The paper lays out the method and its effects on gene output.
plos-pone-0006008:
Clinics changed HIV test methods and suddenly more patients looked virus-free. Ronald Lubelchek, Blake Max, Caroline Sandusky and colleagues asked in 2009 whether the new test itself was the cause. Their PLOS ONE study compares two assays, RT-PCR and bDNA, at the low end of HIV measurement, using patients whose virus levels had been highly stable.

At very low amounts, the two tests do not always agree, so a switch can shift results without any change in the patient. Knowing how reliable each test is at its floor guides how doctors read a near-zero result. The work is a caution for any clinic that changes methods: the numbers may move because the ruler changed.
plos-pone-0006108:
HIV's copying enzyme is a prime drug target, and two of its building blocks hold the whole thing together. Hao-Jie Zhang, Yong-Xiang Wang, Hao Wu and colleagues proved that in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies reverse transcriptase, the enzyme that starts HIV-1 replication, and two amino acids in a turn of the protein, at positions two hundred seventy-one and two hundred seventy-four.

Changing either one wrecked the enzyme, earlier work showed, and this study traces the cause to protein stability. A spot that holds a drug target together is itself worth a drug designer's eye. The finding adds fine structure to one of medicine's most studied enzymes.
plos-pone-0006208:
Older antipsychotic drugs can leave patients stiff, slow, or frozen in posture. Jonathan Chetrit and colleagues recorded brain activity to find where those motor side effects arise, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Little was known about the electrical patterns behind the movement problems, called extrapyramidal symptoms.

The team traced changes through the basal ganglia, a brain network that helps control movement. Drug treatment disturbed the network's normal rhythms and coordination. Mapping the disturbance gives researchers targets for safer drugs. It may also help doctors spot side effects earlier. Patients gain when relief for the mind stops costing control of the body.
plos-pone-0006308:
Some men are sterile because their sperm-making stem cells fail early. Timothy Richardson and colleagues restored fertility in rats lacking the DAZL gene in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. About four percent of couples remain involuntarily infertile, and male factors contribute in almost half of cases.

Transplanting spermatogonial stem cell lines into the sterile testes restarted sperm production. The method also maximised transmission of donor genes to offspring. Sterile recipients thus served as vessels for donor fertility. The technique informs livestock breeding and future fertility research. Work of this kind may one day help men whose own stem cells fail.
plos-pone-0006408:
Honey bees tell their hive mates where food is by dancing on the comb. Moushumi Sen Sarma and her team read gene activity in bee brains during that dance in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They used three kinds of honey bee and took samples from set parts of the brain.

The dance shares the place, the way to go, and how good the food source is. Gene reads taken mid dance show which brain parts are at work in that act. Lines shared by all three kinds would point to the core parts of the bee's dance system. The work ties a famed act of animal talk to the genes that support it.
plos-pone-0006508:
Wei-Li Wu, Chih-Hung Wang, Eagle Huang, and colleagues used mice with hearing loss to study social development in PLOS ONE in 2009. Infant crying is an important cue that prompts mothers to respond adequately. Poor responses to crying can hinder infants' social development. In rodents, pup-mother communication also depends on sound.

The team used female mice lacking the Asic3 gene, which have a hearing deficit. They asked how that deficit affects the social development of pups. A mother's hearing shapes the care pups receive. The model shows how a sensory gap in the parent can alter the next generation's social growth.
plos-pone-0006608:
Jasimuddin Ahamed and co-authors tested a platelet protein's role in activating a growth factor in PLOS ONE in 2009. Thrombospondin-1 is contained in platelet granules and released with activation. It has been shown to activate latent TGF beta 1 in vitro. Its in vivo role was the open question.

The team present in vitro and in vivo evidence that thrombospondin-1 contributes to stirring- and shear-dependent activation of TGF beta. Shear is the force of flowing blood. Activation in flowing blood links clotting to tissue repair signaling. TGF beta controls healing and scarring, so its activators are drug targets.
plos-pone-0006708:
Maureen Miller and her team looked at a common germ in towns and cities in PLOS ONE in 2009. The germ is Staphylococcus aureus. Drug-proof strains of it caused far more illness outside hospitals. Yet the share of people who just carry it in the nose stayed flat. That gap raised a plain question for health work.

Can nose carriage rates stand in for illness rates when staff track spread? The team set carriage next to real illness in town settings. If the two do not move as one, plans built on carriage can mislead. Their work helps health teams pick fair gauges of risk. Fair gauges mean drugs and staff go where they help most.
plos-pone-0006808:
Neira Sáinz and colleagues gave a fat-related hormone to mice lacking it in PLOS ONE in 2009. The hormone is leptin. Mice without leptin, called ob/ob mice, grow obese. They also carry reduced skeletal muscle mass. The team examined how leptin affects pathways that build or break muscle.

Leptin administration favored muscle mass accretion, as the title reports. It lowered a breakdown driver called FoxO3a. It raised PGC-1α, a regulator tied to muscle building and energy use. Three leg muscles were examined for these effects. The results link leptin to muscle maintenance, not just appetite control.
plos-pone-0006908:
Karima Azdad and her team studied how striatal cells adapt when dopamine runs dry in PLOS ONE in 2009. The striatum is the chief gate of the basal ganglia. It picks which facts count as a beast acts. The dopamine cells that feed it die in Parkinson's disease. Acts grow clumsy and slow as a result.

Once dopamine was gone, striatal cells reset how keen they were to fire. That reset is the cell's bid to hold its own pace. The bid may guard some acts in the first phase of the disease. It may also twist signals in the late phase. Grasping the reset helps read why signs of Parkinson's shift with time.
plos-pone-0007008:
Ruth Johnson and Ross Cagan presented a measurement method for fly eyes in PLOS ONE in 2009. The Drosophila pupal eye is a favorite model for studying how tissues form patterns. Its units, called ommatidia, must be arranged in a neat array. That order needs cells to move, die, and change shape at the right times.

Their method turns that patterning into numbers researchers can compare. The eye's regular grid makes errors easy to score once a metric exists. A shared quantitative method helps labs compare mutations fairly. It strengthens the fly eye as a test bed for development genes.
plos-pone-0007108:
Vernon Lee, Mei Yin Tok, Vincent Chow, and others priced pandemic flu plans for Singapore in PLOS ONE in 2009. All national plans for a pandemic call for mass vaccination. Few studies had weighed what such campaigns cost against what they save. The team set vaccination beside treatment with antiviral drugs alone.

They modelled the money outcomes of each plan for Singapore. Costs, cases stopped, and lives saved all went into the count. Such work guides stockpile and campaign choices before a crisis hits. Money spent on the wrong layer of defense is money missing when it is needed most.
plos-pone-0007208:
Gerold Schmitt-Ulms, Sepehr Ehsani, Joel C. Watts, and colleagues traced the origin of prion genes in PLOS ONE in 2009. The prion protein had been known for more than twenty years by then. Yet both its evolutionary origin and its normal job in cells remained unclear and puzzling.

The authors study the protein's molecular neighbors inside cells for clues. They argue that prion genes descend from the ZIP family of metal ion transporters. Those proteins move metals such as zinc across cell membranes. Their claim links a disease protein to an ancient, useful transport system.
plos-pone-0007308:
Siew Hoon Sim, Yichun Liu, Dongling Wang, and colleagues studied lung cell responses to a dangerous bacterium in 2009. Burkholderia pseudomallei lives inside host cells and causes systemic infection. Human mortality is high, especially when infection starts through inhaled aerosols carrying the bacterium into the lungs.

Earlier work showed lung epithelial cells actively join the immune response. The authors examine innate immune responses of those cells during infection. Their PLOS ONE paper maps early signals from the lung surface. Those signals shape whether inhaled bacteria are contained or spread through the body.
plos-pone-0007408:
François Le Naour, Marie-Pierre Bralet, Delphine Debois, and colleagues imaged the chemistry of fatty liver tissue in 2009. Fatty liver, or steatosis, is a frequent tissue change. It is a precursor for steatohepatitis, which may progress to cirrhosis and sometimes to liver cancer if the underlying causes continue unchecked.

The authors address composition and distribution of biochemical compounds in tissue sections. They use synchrotron infrared imaging and ToF-SIMS microspectroscopy, two advanced chemical imaging tools. Their PLOS ONE maps show where fats and other compounds accumulate inside liver tissue. Such maps can reveal early disease patterns.
plos-pone-0007508:
Andrea Doeschl-Wilson and colleagues published a modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how farm animals handle infections with tiny parasites. Growth and immune defense compete for the same energy and protein. An animal's genes set its potential for both growth and resistance. Nutrition shifts the balance further. Predicting the outcome of infection from experiments alone is hard, so the team built a mathematical model.

The model combines growth potential, disease resistance, and feed intake for an individual animal. It then predicts how growth and immune response play out during infection. Such a model can explain why well-fed animals still sometimes lose ground. It can also guide breeding and feeding choices before disease strikes. The study treats the growth-versus-defense trade-off as a problem that can be computed, not just observed.
plos-pone-0007608:
Jay Joo and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Ewing tumors, aggressive cancers of children and young adults. These tumors are driven by a rogue fusion protein, EWS/FLI1, born from a chromosome mix-up. The fusion switches many genes on and off, but its central routes were unclear. The team traced the signaling downstream of the fusion. One mediator stood out: GLI1, a protein better known from other cancer pathways.

GLI1 proved to be a central mediator of EWS/FLI1 signaling in Ewing tumors. Much of the fusion's effect flows through that one factor. A central middleman is a promising drug target. Blocking GLI1 might blunt the fusion's program without needing to drug the fusion itself. For a cancer with a strong drive to spread, a new target is welcome news. The study redraws the tumor's wiring diagram around GLI1.
plos-pone-0007708:
Shelley Hough and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines human embryonic stem cells and the moment they start to specialize. Textbooks often draw that shift as a sharp either-or choice. A cell either stays pluripotent or commits to one lineage.

Close study of cell cultures told a different story. The authors found a smooth range of states between the two poles. Cells in a single dish sat at many points along that range. The finding changes how researchers should read stem cell cultures, and how they guide cells toward a desired type.
plos-pone-0007808:
Karim Ouattara and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It reports a language-like trick in the calls of Campbell's monkeys. These monkeys live free in African forests and give alarm calls. The authors describe how the monkeys add a suffix-like ending to calls.

Adding that ending changes what the call means. Human language does the same thing through affixation, adding prefixes or suffixes to words. Finding a working analogy in monkey calls is striking. It suggests that building meaning by small additions has deep roots. Those roots reach far back in the primate line.
plos-pone-0007908:
Melville Vaughan and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It shows what a cancer-linked gene does to skin grown in the lab. Ras proteins control cell growth and the release of collagen-cutting enzymes. Both processes matter in cancer progression.

Normal skin depends on orderly growth and layering of keratinocytes, its main cells. The team switched on H-Ras in immortalized keratinocytes. In cultured skin equivalents, the cells produced an invasive epithelium. The model lets researchers watch the first steps of skin invasion. It offers a test system for drugs that might halt that invasion.
plos-pone-0008008:
Sounak Gupta and colleagues studied a stress sensor in pancreas tumors of mice for PLOS ONE in 2009. The sensor, PERK, helps cells cope when protein folding goes wrong. It is also needed for the normal growth of insulin-making beta cells.

In tumors grown from those same beta cells, PERK helped drive growth and spread within the pancreas. The sensor thus serves health in normal cells and harm in cancerous ones. That double role makes it a tricky but tempting drug target, since blocking it may starve tumors that lean on it.
plos-pone-0008108:
Jessica Cole and Ann Jerse tested antibodies against a gonorrhea protein's loops in PLOS ONE in 2009. Gonorrhea has no vaccine, partly because the germ keeps changing its surface. Its opacity proteins vary, but each carries one loop that stays much the same across strains.

Antibodies raised against those loops were checked for what they can actually do, not just what they can bind. A loop that stays the same and can be usefully attacked is a rare gift in this germ. The work helps vaccine makers choose which loop to build around.
plos-pone-0008208:
Scott G. Kitchen and colleagues built virus-fighting T cells in mice in a PLOS ONE study from 2009. Chronic viral infections still lack effective therapies for many patients. A strong immune response controls most viral infections in healthy people. Restoring that control could be a powerful treatment strategy. The team started from human blood-forming stem cells.

They genetically modified the stem cells so they would grow into antigen-specific T cells. These are immune cells tuned to one target. The work was done in immunodeficient mice that can host human cells. Success there is an early step toward engineered immune therapy.
plos-pone-0008308:
Barbara Jung and colleagues studied colon cancer signaling in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Activin signaling is often disrupted in colon cancers with unstable DNA. In those tumors, the activin receptor gene is commonly mutated. Protein loss then disrupts signaling and tumors grow larger. Whether the same disruption occurs in microsatellite stable cancers was unknown.

Using a population-based sample of stable colon cancers, they found disruption there too. It arose from a mix of genetic and epigenetic mechanisms. So activin loss matters beyond the unstable tumor type. That widens the group of patients this pathway could affect.
plos-pone-0008408:
Laia Ribas and her team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about a fungus that kills frogs round the world. The fungus, Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, has spread in a wave of disease on a world scale. Not all frog kinds face the same risk from it. Heat and cold shift that risk a lot from place to place. The team read which genes switch on or off in frogs that meet the fungus.

They set gene reads from frogs kept warm next to reads from frogs kept cool. The gene sets show how a frog fights back, or fails to. That split by heat may show why the disease hits hard in one place and spares the next. Such facts can guide work to save frog kinds now in fast fall.
plos-pone-0008508:
Thomas Cremer and co-authors compare two tularemia germs in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Francisella tularensis causes tularemia and evades host defenses. A milder relative is called F. novicida. Past work found a defense path involving PI3K, Akt, and SHIP. That path helps the host resist the germ. The team ask why the virulent form provokes a weaker response. They track a small RNA called miR-155.

The milder germ induces miR-155, but the virulent one does not. MiR-155 drives SHIP levels down in their system. Lower SHIP allows a stronger pro-inflammatory cytokine response. The virulent germ's failure to induce it may help it hide.
plos-pone-0008608:
Jeffrey Wells and co-authors compare endangered bird lists in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Setting species priorities at state or regional scale poses a paradox. Local lists may draw greater interest and resources to nearby species. But they may divert focus from species most endangered globally. US state agencies maintain endangered bird species lists. The team ask if those lists focus on global or local risk. They compare state priorities with global conservation status.

They find a mix of global versus local focus across states. Some state lists favor locally rare but globally secure birds. Aligning local lists with global risk could improve outcomes. The study informs how agencies set conservation priorities.
plos-pone-0008708:
Natarajan Singaravelan, Tomas Pavlicek, Alex Beharav, and colleagues studied mouse coats in a steep Israeli valley. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper comes from Evolution Canyon, a spot where two slopes differ sharply. Spiny mice living there blend with local rock and soil. Coat color in mammals is set by two pigments, dark eumelanin and reddish pheomelanin.

The team measured the pigment mix in mice from different spots. Mice tuned the ratio of the two pigments to match their ground. That fine tuning helps each mouse stay cryptic to hunters. The canyon works as a natural lab for watching selection act fast.
plos-pone-0008808:
Remo Frei, Johanna Steinle, Thomas Birchler, and colleagues found teamwork between two immune systems. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. MHC class II molecules show foreign scraps to helper T cells. That display drives the adaptive arm of immunity. Toll-like receptors, by contrast, drive the fast innate arm. The two arms were often studied as separate worlds.

Class II molecules boosted the innate responses triggered through Toll-like receptors. The enhancement links presentation machinery to first-response alarms. Crosstalk like this may tune how strong a vaccine response becomes. It also suggests new angles for immune disorders.
plos-pone-0008908:
Aarthy Vallur and Nancy Maizels compared two cutting enzymes at the folded DNA of chromosome ends. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Telomeres cap chromosomes with G-rich repeating DNA. That DNA can fold into knots called G4 structures. Two related enzymes, EXO1 and FEN1, trim DNA during copying and repair. Both also help maintain telomeres. How each handles a G4 knot was unclear.

The enzymes acted quite differently at telomeric G4 DNA. One cut where the other stalled or skipped. Distinct handling explains their separate jobs at chromosome ends. Telomere upkeep, tied to aging and cancer, gains mechanistic detail.
plos-pone-0009008:
Christopher Batters, Hannah Zhu, and Julian Sale built a way to watch a DNA repair signal live, in PLOS ONE in 2010. When DNA copying hits damage, the clamp protein PCNA gets a single ubiquitin tag. That tag tells the cell to use a damage-bypass route. Seeing the tag appear inside living cells was the hard part.

The team paired two glowing proteins whose light changes when they come close. With spectral imaging done in a single pass, the microscope caught the tagging event. Cells could then be filmed as they switched PCNA into bypass mode. A live view of this switch helps explain how cells survive DNA damage.
plos-pone-0009108:
Fleur Lejeune and co-authors showed that babies born early can feel shape differences with their hands, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Newborn grasping was long dismissed as a simple palm reflex. Recent work showed full-term babies actually detect and remember shapes by touch. The team asked whether preterm infants can do the same.

The babies were 33 to nearly 35 weeks in conceptional age. They held objects by hand and grew used to one shape. A new shape renewed their interest, proving they told the shapes apart. Touch learning is already working weeks before the due date.
plos-pone-0009208:
Nicolas Langer, Gian Beeli, and Lutz Jäncke published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. About one person in four sneezes, or feels a prickling nose, when hit by bright light. The quirk is called the photic sneeze reflex. Despite being so common, it had never been examined scientifically.

The team used EEG, which records electrical activity from the scalp, while showing light to sneezers and non-sneezers. Comparing the two groups let them spot the brain activity tied to the prickle and the sneeze. Their experiment is the first scientific look at this odd reflex. It opens a path to explaining why light alone can set off a sneeze.
plos-pone-0009308:
Alan Rorie and co-authors published this monkey brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A brain area called LIP helps decide where the eyes move next. Its neurons carry both what the eyes see and how good the outcome will be. How those two streams merge into one decision was unknown.

The team recorded single neurons in macaque monkeys making choices reported by eye movements. Each choice mixed sensory evidence with reward value. They traced how LIP neurons combine the two kinds of information. The result speaks to a basic question in decision science: how the brain adds up wanting and seeing before it acts.
plos-pone-0009408:
Shiro Mitsuya and co-authors published this plant stress study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Salt in soil is a major limit on farming worldwide. Plants answer stress by changing their inner machinery. One response is making more peroxisomes, small compartments that handle harsh chemistry.

In the model plant Arabidopsis, salt stress indeed caused peroxisomes to multiply. The team then forced extra peroxisomes without any salt present. That alone did not improve the plants' salt tolerance. The neat lesson is that a stress response can be a symptom rather than a cure, a distinction crop engineers must respect.
plos-pone-0009508:
Jeffrey Yao and co-authors studied blood chemistry in people with schizophrenia in PLOS ONE in 2010. All patients were in their first episode of illness. None had yet taken antipsychotic drugs. That clean state is rare and valuable for research. The team focused on purines, building blocks used in DNA and in energy transfer.

Measures of purine breakdown were out of balance in these patients. The authors link that upset to oxidative stress, a form of chemical strain on cells. The work adds a metabolic side to a disease often framed only in brain signals. Purine measures might one day serve as markers for the illness.
plos-pone-0009608:
Jing Kang, Hugh Robinson, and Jianfeng Feng cataloged rhythm coding in rat brain cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Neurons carry information in the rate and timing of their electrical spikes. Many cortex cells also have an intrinsic frequency, a rhythm they favor. The team recorded from rat cortical neurons and sorted their frequency patterns. They also probed what makes the patterns differ.

The variety of patterns was wide, even among like cells. Each pattern could suit a different coding job in the cortex. Mapping that variety helps modelers build more faithful brain networks. It also hints at how the cortex keeps many channels of information apart at once.
plos-pone-0009708:
People everywhere recognize faces, but cultures may train the eyes differently. Roberto Caldara, Xinyue Zhou, and Sébastien Miellet examined that question in PLOS ONE in 2010. They used a method called Spotlight to track which parts of a face people actually use.

Earlier studies had reported that viewers from different cultures scan faces differently. The new analysis found a shared core in how people gather face information. That core held across cultures, beneath the surface differences. The result reframes the debate about culture and face reading. The findings speak to readers in both psychology and neuroscience.
plos-pone-0009908:
Counting a gene's RNA copies is easy; knowing how fast those copies are made is harder. Brewster Hayles, Sailu Yellaboina, and Degeng Wang compared the two measures head to head. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Transcription rate is how fast a gene is copied into RNA. mRNA abundance is simply how much of that RNA is present. The two measures can tell different stories about the same gene. The authors weighed which measure serves biochemical pathway and network analysis better. Choosing the right measure changes what a network map seems to say.
plos-pone-0010008:
Najwane Saïd-Sadier, Eduardo Padilla, Gordon Langsley, and co-workers studied a dangerous lung fungus in PLOS ONE in 2010. Aspergillus fumigatus can cause invasive disease that kills people whose immune systems are weak. It is among the most common fungal causes of serious illness, yet much about the response to it stays unclear.

The authors showed the fungus switches on the NLRP3 inflammasome, a protein machine that drives inflammation. That route needs reactive oxygen species, harsh oxygen-based molecules, and an enzyme called Syk. Naming those steps gives drug makers clear points where a harmful immune response might be calmed.
plos-pone-0010108:
The authors were Jinwei Hu, Julia Ljubimova, Satoshi Inoue, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tackled drug delivery to brain tumors in mice. Most cancer drugs reach body tumors well enough. Brain tumors hide behind a blood-brain tumor barrier that keeps many drugs out, sharply limiting treatment there.

The team tested type 5 phosphodiesterase inhibitors, a known drug class, as helpers. In mouse models of metastatic brain tumors, those drugs raised transport of Herceptin, an antibody drug. They also improved how well that treatment worked, offering a route around the barrier.
plos-pone-0010208:
The authors were Paul Coppo, Michael Schwarzinger, Marc Buffet, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study drew on a French national reference center for rare blood diseases. The diseases, called thrombotic microangiopathies, involve small clots forming in tiny vessels. In some patients the cause is severe loss of an enzyme, ADAMTS13, attacked by the immune system.

Finding that deficiency early lets doctors start targeted therapy sooner. The team identified features that predict severe deficiency at presentation. Their experience-based guide can help hospitals triage these rare, dangerous cases faster. The report appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010308:
The authors were Yu-Sin Kim, Fei Ke, Xiao-Ying Lei, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study protected fish cells from a virus using tailored RNA. The virus family, iridoviruses, infects frogs and fish and can devastate aquaculture. One envelope protein, 53R, helps the virus assemble, and it comes from a frog virus used as the family model.

The team silenced the 53R gene with artificial microRNAs in fish cells. Highly specific silencing gave the cells resistance to iridovirus infection. A gene-based defense like this could protect farmed fish stocks from outbreaks.
plos-pone-0010408:
Devasahayam Christopher and colleagues measured tuberculosis infection among young nursing trainees in South India for PLOS ONE in 2010. Nurses in poorer countries spend long hours close to TB patients. That closeness puts them at high risk of catching the infection themselves. The team recruited trainees to gauge how common infection already was. They also sought the pattern of risk inside hospitals.

High rates among trainees would signal a workplace danger, not just a public one. Protecting health workers protects patients too, since sick staff can spread TB. The study gives hospital managers local numbers to act on. Screening, masks, and ventilation all cost money; data show where they matter most. Young nurses, the work implies, need guarding as much as patients.
plos-pone-0010508:
Christian Lienhardt and colleagues compared two tests for hidden tuberculosis infection in Senegal household contacts for PLOS ONE in 2010. Treating contacts of TB patients can prevent new cases, especially where TB is common. First, doctors must find who is silently infected. The old skin test is the classic tool, but it misreads people vaccinated against TB. A newer blood test, based on interferon-gamma release, promises cleaner answers.

The team judged whether the blood test predicted future disease better than the skin test. Prognostic value, not just detection, decides which test should guide treatment. Household contacts are the highest-value group to screen. This study supplies evidence from a high-burden African setting. It helps programs choose tests that prevent the most disease.
plos-pone-0010608:
Nidhi Tyagi, Krishanpal Anamika, and Narayanaswamy Srinivasan sorted a confusing family of bacterial proteins, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Kinases pass chemical signals by tagging other proteins. The standard kinase family tree was built for animals and fungi, not microbes.

Most bacterial and archaeal kinases fit none of the standard branches. The authors grouped them using sequence patterns and known shapes instead. Their framework placed many former misfits into sensible groups. A workable map of microbial kinases helps researchers compare species and spot drug targets that differ from human kinases. The scheme covers both bacteria and archaea.
plos-pone-0010708:
Wasila Dahdul and colleagues worked to free species trait data trapped in old papers, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Systematics journals hold a century of careful descriptions: fin counts, bone shapes, color patterns. Written as free prose, those traits stay invisible to databases that track genes and development.

The team built methods and shared word lists to turn prose traits into coded records. Curators tested the workflow on real literature. Coded traits can then be searched, compared, and joined with genetic data. Unlocking the archive matters because new fieldwork cannot re-collect rare and extinct species already described.
plos-pone-0010808:
Gerald Carter, John Ratcliffe, and Bennett Galef tested how two bat species re-find food, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The flower bat Glossophaga soricina drinks nectar, while Carollia perspicillata eats fruit. Both revisit known food sites night after night. Memory could lean on place, shape, or scent cues, and each diet favors different cues.

When cues were set against each other, both species trusted place most. Shape and scent lost out to spatial memory. Remembering where food was beats remembering what it looked like when feeders move or change. The result shows natural selection tuning the same basic memory system toward the cue that stays true.
plos-pone-0010908:
Adam Reid, Juan Ranea, Andrew Clegg and co-authors published this computational biology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Knowing which proteins work together is basic to understanding cells, and one clue is gene fusion: two separate genes in one species appear as a single fused gene in another. In complex genomes, big families of similar protein parts make that clue noisy.

Their method, CODA, scores fusions while accounting for how large each domain family is in the genome at hand. Tested on human data, it predicted functional links between proteins as accurately as the best existing methods, and different methods proved to catch different links. Reid and colleagues also used CODA's output as evidence in protein databases. The tool sharpens a classic inference trick for the genomes where it was weakest.
plos-pone-0011008:
Alice den Hertog, Dennis Visser, Colin Ingham and co-authors published this tuberculosis diagnostics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Growing TB bacteria remains essential for diagnosis and drug testing, and watching colonies under a microscope can speed answers in poor settings. The authors automated that watching, growing the bacteria as microcolonies on a porous support.

Repeated digital imaging followed individual microcolonies as they grew, which greatly simplified the computer vision problem. Existing public algorithms could then presumptively identify the colonies, and the setup also allowed the growth medium around them to be changed mid-experiment, opening the door to drug exposure tests. Den Hertog and colleagues present a simpler automated culture reader. Faster, cheaper TB culture matters most where the disease burden is highest and laboratories are thinnest.
plos-pone-0011108:
Ryan, Hoff, Driver and colleagues reported tuberculosis research in PLOS ONE in 2010. Inside the lungs, TB germs may not all behave the same way. Using tissue from infected mice and guinea pigs, the team applied two stains at once to tell germ types apart.

The double staining revealed several distinct forms of the germ living side by side in lung tissue. Mixed forms help explain why TB is so hard to clear with drugs. Some forms may resist treatment while others do not. Seeing that mix clearly could lead to drug plans that target every form, not just the most common one.
plos-pone-0011208:
Kachhap, Rosmus, Collis and colleagues studied prostate cancer drugs in PLOS ONE in 2010. A class of drugs loosens packed DNA, changing which genes are active. The team found these drugs also switch off genes that repair broken DNA by copying from a matching strand.

The shutdown ran through a single gene control factor. Turning off repair leaves cancer cells less able to survive DNA damage. That gives a clear logic for pairing these drugs with DNA damaging treatments. Such pairs could hit prostate tumors harder than either drug alone, a strategy now open to testing.
plos-pone-0011308:
Shah and Gilchrist questioned RNA heat sensors in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some bacterial RNAs change shape with temperature and act as thermometers that switch genes on in warmth. The authors asked whether that heat sensing property is truly unique to this special class of RNA.

Their analysis explores whether ordinary RNAs might show similar behavior under some conditions. If heat response is widespread, the special status of RNA thermometers needs rethinking. The physics matters for molecular biology because cells sit at shifting temperatures. It also affects engineers who design heat switches for synthetic biology, including ones meant to respond to fever.
plos-pone-0011408:
Kylie Gorringe and co-authors scanned ovarian cancer genomes in 2010 for chunks of DNA gained or lost across tumors. Ovarian cancer is hard to treat in part because its genome is so heavily rearranged, and single-study samples had been too small to sort signal from noise. The team pooled genome-wide copy data from four collections to gain power.

Beyond listing single gains and losses, they found new interactions between distant regions, pairs of changes that turn up together more than chance allows. Cooperating pairs suggest the cancer needs both changes at once, which single-gene views miss. That pairing logic gives researchers fresh suspects to test in the lab. It may also explain why tumors with different-looking genomes behave alike, if they share the same cooperating pattern underneath.
plos-pone-0011508:
Simon van Gaal, Victor Lamme, and Richard Ridderinkhof showed in 2010 that the brain can adapt to conflict without ever noticing it. When a task contains clashing signals, people usually adjust and do better on the next try, a control process thought to need conscious awareness of the clash. The team masked the conflict so volunteers never saw it, then checked whether adjustment still followed.

It did: conflict adaptation was triggered unconsciously, with performance shifting after conflicts the person could not report. A supposedly high-level control thus runs in the automatic machinery of the mind. The finding blurs the textbook line between deliberate and reflexive thought. It also matters for how awareness itself is defined in brain science, since one of its supposed signatures turns out not to need it at all.
plos-pone-0011608:
Hyojoong Kim, Wonhoon Lee and Seunghwan Lee studied the aphid genus Aphis in PLOS ONE in 2010. Aphis holds more than five hundred species, many feeding on specific host plants. Despite their numbers, the species look much alike, because unrelated lines often evolve toward the same body forms.

The authors combined body measurements with family trees to test how shape and ancestry relate. Their analysis follows how key traits changed as species split. For biologists trying to sort this crowded genus, the work shows which visible features truly signal close kinship and which are misleading look-alikes.
plos-pone-0011708:
