Marc Sylvester and co-authors mapped a central hub in T cell signalling, in PLOS ONE in 2010. When a T cell is triggered, it sticks more firmly to other cells, among many changes. A protein called ADAP is rapidly tagged with phosphate after triggering and passes the signal on to adhesion molecules.

The authors charted the web of phosphate-linked interactions around ADAP. Their map places it at the centre of the network that coordinates the response. Knowing the switchboard wiring of immune activation could reveal new points for calming or boosting T cells in disease.
plos-pone-0011808:
Yoshihiro Fujiwara and co-authors studied bacterial partnerships in a deep-sea mussel, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Vent and seep mussels housing energy-making symbionts are thought to have evolved from shallow-water relatives without symbionts, by way of sunken wood and whale falls. Such associations have been well characterised in several species.

In the whale-fall mussel Adipicola pacifica, the team found symbiosis that is both extracellular and of a feeding-mixing type. Comparing it with relatives suggests an evolutionary trend from outside-the-cell toward inside-the-cell living. The shift shows partnerships moving house over evolutionary time.
plos-pone-0011908:
François Michaud and co-workers showed in 2010 how a common virus dulls an early immune alarm in blood cells. The virus, called Epstein-Barr, is tied to glandular fever, to some cancers, and to growths that form when immune control fails. Monocytes are blood cells that reach trouble spots early, and the virus changes much of what they do once it gets inside them.

The work shows the virus cutting off the build-up of a key alarm signal by turning on a brake protein named SOCS3. With the alarm held down, the virus can settle in with less fight from the host. Naming the brake gives labs a firm step to study when they ask how this virus stays in the body for life.
plos-pone-0012108:
Margarita Kunin, Natalia Dmitrieva, Morgan Gallazzini, and colleagues wrote in PLOS ONE in 2010 about how cells survive very salty conditions. When salt rises around a cell, a master switch turns on genes that stock the cell with safe molecules and stress guards. The team fished out the proteins that travel with that switch, looking for partners that help it respond.

One partner helps the switch react when salt levels climb. Kidney cells face exactly this stress every day as they concentrate urine, so the details matter beyond the lab dish. Each partner found adds a piece to the map of how cells keep their inner balance when the world outside them turns harsh.
plos-pone-0012208:
Fabrice Dumas, Richard Byrne, Ben Vincent, and co-authors studied how cells control where membranes fuse, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fusion joins the small bubbles that ferry cargo inside cells, and it also rebuilds the nucleus after division. The puzzle is targeting: with membranes everywhere, how does fusion happen at the right place and not elsewhere?

Working from studies of artificial membranes and theory, the authors point to chemical edits of the fat molecules in the membrane itself as a spatial control. Where those fats are modified, fusion is favored or blocked. A control based on the membrane's own chemistry would explain precision that protein locks alone struggle to give.
plos-pone-0012308:
Janet Wolford, Yasmin Chishti, Qiaoling Jin, and co-authors tracked zinc inside human embryonic stem cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. These cells' ability to become anything, pluripotency, is the trait that makes them priceless for development research and future cell therapy, yet its inner mechanism is still incompletely known. Zinc was already known to matter when ordinary cells specialize.

The team found that as the stem cells lose pluripotency, zinc levels in the cell nucleus rise in direct step. A measurable metal signal tied to the cell's state could become a simple marker for checking cultures. It also suggests the metal plays an active part in the decision to specialize, not just a bystander's role.
plos-pone-0012408:
Maria Veiga, Pedro Ferreira, Berit Schmidt and colleagues watched malaria parasites react to drug exposure inside red blood cells, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Drug-resistant Plasmodium falciparum is a growing barrier to malaria control. Parasites may dodge drugs by pumping them out, and the team asked how drug pressure changes the parasite's growth cycle and pump genes.

Exposure slowed the parasite's cycle inside red cells and switched on drug transporter genes. A slower cycle can buy the parasite time against short-lived drugs. Catching these early responses helps scientists spot resistance as it emerges and design drug pairings that close the escape routes.
plos-pone-0012508:
Eldad Saragosti, Dan Tchernov, Adi Katsir and colleagues measured reactive oxygen leaking around a reef coral, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Stylophora pistillata hosts algae, Symbiodinium, inside its tissue, and their partnership powers reef growth. Reactive oxygen species are blamed for coral bleaching and cell death, yet direct measurements in corals were rare.

The team tracked superoxide produced and broken down outside the cells of coral and cultured algae. The partners actively manage this dangerous chemical at their borders. Knowing who makes and who cleans it helps explain why some coral-algae pairs survive heat stress that bleaches others.
plos-pone-0012608:
Read, Phillipson, Serrano-Pedraza and co-authors studied depth vision in a patient known as D F. Her injury damaged the lateral occipital cortex, part of the brain's ventral stream for seeing form. Both brain streams hold cells that sense the slight mismatch between the two eyes, the basis of stereo depth.

Their 2010 tests asked how much stereo vision survives without that cortex area. The case shows which parts of seeing depth depend on the ventral stream and which do not. Rare single-patient studies like this one let scientists map vision in ways group scans cannot.
plos-pone-0012708:
Wei, Shi, Chen and co-authors offered a fresh view of a lopsided pattern in insect mitochondrial DNA. In animal mitochondria, one DNA strand tends to carry more of some letters than the other. Their 2010 study compared these strand biases across many insect genomes.

Explaining the bias means explaining the mutation steps that shape these small genomes over time. Mitochondrial DNA is a workhorse for tracing species history, so its quirks matter widely. A better model of the bias helps scientists read insect family trees with fewer errors.  Insects give the widest test set for that idea.
plos-pone-0012808:
Nobrega, Greebe, van de Kant and co-authors described the home base of sperm stem cells in zebrafish and moved them between fish. Spermatogonial stem cells found all sperm production for a male's life. They sit in a niche, a pocket of the testis that keeps them in stem form.

Their 2010 study mapped that niche in zebrafish and transplanted the stem cells into new hosts. A fish model that accepts transplants lets researchers test stem cell behaviour fast. The work aids fish breeding and the wider science of stem cell homes.
plos-pone-0328408:
Zhou and Qin built an augmented reality teaching system for medical training in a 2026 study. The system runs on smart glasses and pairs live overlays with a large AI model trained for medicine. A compression method shrank the model's memory needs greatly, so it could run on light glasses without losing skill.

During lessons, the glasses add labels and written feedback directly onto medical scenes. Responses came in about one second across image types, faster than a leading general AI baseline. Reported accuracy on the teaching tasks was also very high. Blending sight and text this way could make hands-on medical practice richer where expert teachers are scarce.
plos-pone-0335108:
Michaels and colleagues checked AI pose tools against true motion data for older adults' falls in a 2026 study. Falls injure many older people, and bending the knees may protect the hip, but knee motion in real falls is hard to measure. More than one hundred lab videos of sideways falls were analyzed by three pose tools.

The tools captured broad differences between fall styles, from stiff falls to tucked rolls. They missed finer differences between the two legs, especially in tuck-and-roll falls. This first validation gives fall researchers a usable, cheaper tool with known limits, and it points to fall-specific training as the way to sharpen accuracy.
plos-pone-0337508:
Luciana Guimaraes de Andrade and colleagues trial a DNA method for tracking ducks and geese. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Waterfowl shift range fast during migration. Counting them across a continent costs a lot. DNA shed into pond water could give a cheaper census. The test must be precise, though.

Old bird tests lit up other animals by mistake. So the team designed new primers for one gene region. The primers cover all known North American duck family species. Lab checks showed sharp targeting. Field teams then sampled a New York refuge in fall migration season. The DNA tracked how each species rose and fell as flocks passed.
plos-pone-0339708:
Lemeng Liu and colleagues measured how Zhangjiakou, a medium-sized Chinese city, changed while preparing to co-host the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics. Their 2026 paper builds a single urbanization score from population, economic, land use, and environmental measures, then tracks it across the city's districts from 2017 to 2022.

Overall urbanization rose by about a fifth, led by economic growth, more building, and population shifts. Environmental quality, though, rose and then fell back, ending the period in decline. Growth spread outward from the city centre toward the north. The authors argue that mega events can speed a smaller city's development while leaving uneven results and ecological strain behind.
plos-pone-0341108:
Yinyin Zhang and seven colleagues scan the whole genome for chemical tags that differ between people with and without osteoporosis, in this 2026 PLOS ONE pilot study. The tags, methyl groups attached to DNA, help switch genes off and on and may shape how bone is maintained or lost. Using whole-genome bisulfite sequencing, the team compared methylation patterns and looked for regions where the difference lined up with gene activity.

Differences clustered in gene-rich islands, and six bone-relevant genes showed consistent tag-and-activity patterns, including several from well-known bone-building pathways. The authors label the study hypothesis-generating: a first map of suspects, to be confirmed in bigger samples before anyone calls methylation a cause of weak bones.
plos-pone-0343608:
Mohsen A. Khormi and co-workers give the first full account of a parasitic flatworm found living in the nose of a prized food fish in the Arabian Gulf. These parasites are poorly known in the region. Their 2026 study checks more than twenty-five hundred groupers of nine species, then studies the worm's shape, tissue damage, and DNA to place it on the family tree.

Only one grouper species carried the worm, in about one in ten fish, always as golden cysts inside the nose. Host reaction stayed mild, with thin capsules around the cysts. DNA placed the worm in a known genus close to a relative from the same fish. Fish inspectors now know where to look for this hidden passenger.
plos-pone-0344408:
Albert Dayor Piersson and five colleagues surveyed mothers in a low resource setting about joining brain development research, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2026. Studies of how pregnancy shapes early brain growth need mothers willing to accept scans and give samples, yet willingness in poorer regions is rarely measured. Their survey asked three hundred mothers about brain testing, many kinds of samples, and storing material for ten years.

Most mothers agreed to brain health testing, including electrical recordings and magnetic scans, even for conditions with no treatment. Routine samples such as blood, stool, and urine won near universal acceptance, while intimate samples like breast milk, placenta, and vaginal fluid drew far lower consent. More schooling consistently predicted a yes. The pattern helps planners design studies that mothers will actually join.
plos-pone-0345208:
Taylor Eich and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One molecular study of how the Epstein-Barr virus's most important cancer-linked gene is spliced. Most adults carry this virus for life, and its LMP1 gene helps drive several cancers, yet the folded shapes of its RNA message were unknown. Using a drug that freezes the splicing machinery, the team probed the RNA's structure directly and fed the data into folding algorithms.

The models revealed eleven stable folded elements, several sitting near the splice points of one intron and appearing in alternative arrangements that could open or block splicing. Some elements coincide with mutations linked to patient survival in Burkitt lymphoma. The authors offer the structural map as a starting point for drugs that might disturb this viral gene's processing.
plos-pone-0345608:
James Collins IV and seven colleagues describe building Ethiopia's first pediatric cancer registry in this 2026 paper. Without a registry, children with cancer were invisible in national data, and care could not be systematically improved. Clinicians and implementation scientists from the University of North Carolina worked with all five of Ethiopia's pediatric cancer centers, studying a pilot database and each center's workflow.

Using a structured problem-solving approach borrowed from systems thinking, the team mapped barriers and facilitators, trained staff, and wrote shared standard procedures so every center collects data the same way. The result was the launch of a single national, hospital-based registry. The authors present the process as a template for other low-resource countries where childhood cancer has gone uncounted.
plos-pone-0345708:
Ari Probandari and seven colleagues map attempts to handle three big health problems as one package. Their 2026 scoping review covers TB alongside diabetes and high blood pressure. These conditions arrive together more and more, in poorer health systems. Joined-up care promises screening, diagnosis, and treatment under one roof. The team gathered studies from 2005 to early 2025 across four databases. Four team members screened and extracted data, using a standard form.

The review charts which integration models exist in practice. It weighs their potential benefits, from better treatment completion to simpler patient journeys. Barriers get equal attention: fragmented programmes, separate budgets, and staff trained for single diseases. Strategies that helped elsewhere are catalogued for implementers. Tuberculosis programmes cannot end the epidemic while ignoring the other long-term ills their patients also carry. This map shows where joined-up care has been tried, and what keeps it rare.
plos-pone-0346008:
Ana B. Vivas and a six-country team mapped how digital technology is used in non-drug therapies for people with dementia or mild cognitive impairment. Such programs aim to preserve thinking and daily function. Searching seven databases for studies since 2012, the 2026 scoping review gathered one hundred fourteen papers and sorted the technologies into eight families.

Games, apps, and web programs were studied most; virtual reality was the rising newcomer. Results on effectiveness varied wildly, as did how programs were built and measured. Most interventions were designed for live supervision by a professional, yet the most common formats are precisely those suited to home use. The authors call for more consistent designs and reporting.
plos-pone-0346308:
Nicolás Molano-González and Jaime Moreno-Chaparro published a review protocol on clinical research data systems, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Trials run on systems that capture, collect, manage, and store data, and the wrong choice can add cost and error for years. Their protocol sets out how they will map that crowded field.

The planned scoping review will chart what systems exist, what they do well, and where evidence about them is thin. Publishing the plan in advance keeps the review honest and lets others repeat it. Trial teams choosing software gain a future guide grounded in a full survey, not vendor claims. Good data systems are invisible when they work, and this review aims to show which ones do.
plos-pone-0346708:
Christopher Mai and colleagues built an automated eye for zipper factories. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Checking zippers for flaws is still mostly hand work. Skilled staff stare at each piece, which is slow and error-prone. Their system, DualFusionNet, scans fabric images for defects.

The design joins two kinds of image reading. One reads fine local detail, like a broken tooth. The other reads the whole pattern at once. Some flaws show only in the full view. Joining both views beat single-view systems on accuracy. For clothing and bag makers, machine checks promise speed. They also spare human eyes the strain.
plos-pone-0347008:
Seohyun Choi, Seon Min Lee, Young Jae Kim, Yong-Cheol Yoon, and Kwang Gi Kim published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It establishes normal values for femoral head coverage angles, measurements of how well the thigh bone's ball sits in the hip socket. The measurements come from three-dimensional computed tomography images.

Normal reference values are the yardstick that lets doctors call a hip abnormal. Without them, judging coverage in hip pain or early arthritis is guesswork. A 3D CT-based set of values gives orthopedic surgeons and radiologists a firmer basis for spotting hips at risk of wearing out, especially in younger patients.
plos-pone-0347208:
Seren Azad, Pavel Trtik, and colleagues imaged damaged concrete with neutrons in 2026 to watch it swell with moisture. Alkali silica reaction, a slow internal swelling, cracks concrete worldwide, but how its gel products respond to water at small scale was unproven.

Three concrete mixes of differing reactivity were scanned before and after three days in water, and image matching mapped local strain. The largest expansions sat in cracks within the cement paste, where the glassy form of the reaction product gathers. Cracks in stones, holding the crystalline form, barely moved. The direct images back the long held idea that the glassy product is the swelling culprit.
plos-pone-0347608:
Carmen Callizo and co-workers interview Catholic priests about feeling forgiven by God during confession. The sense of being forgiven by a higher power after wrongdoing is rarely studied, especially across cultures. Their 2026 study talks with ten Spanish-speaking priests from Spain, Mexico, Peru, and Chile, each both hearing confessions and giving their own.

Priests described confession as a moving encounter among the self, the wrong, God, and the priest who makes forgiveness feel real. The path ran through openness, sorrow, telling, making amends, and release. Guilt and shame could block it, while a kind priest and community support helped. Knowing one is forgiven and feeling it, they said, are not the same thing.
plos-pone-0347908:
Komsan Arramrak and colleagues tested whether calcitriol, the active form of vitamin D, can protect the liver against scarring. In their 2026 rat study, a chemical called diethylnitrosamine was used to trigger liver fibrosis, the harmful buildup of scar tissue that can lead to cirrhosis. Some rats also received low or high doses of calcitriol during the experiment.

Calcitriol reduced signs of cell damage in the liver and lowered blood markers of liver injury. It also quieted inflammation signals and the proteins that drive scar formation, and tissue samples showed milder scarring, with stronger effects at the higher dose. The results suggest vitamin D treatment deserves more study as a possible help against liver fibrosis.
plos-pone-0348208:
Feng Li and his team studied salt in the soil of a cotton field in Nanpi County, Hebei, China. The field sits near the coast, where salt can creep up and harm crops. The team asked how the depth of ground water steers that salt. They took field measures, then ran a soil model for ten years at three set depths.

The model matched the field data well. When the water table rose from five and a half metres to three, the soil held more water. But salt in the top layer doubled, from mild to a mid level of harm. The team says farms in such places must keep ground water deep enough.
plos-pone-0348508:
Siheng Zhang, Yan Xu, and Ying Xiao trained a deep learning system to recognise whooping cough from recordings of coughing. The disease's distinctive cough is a diagnostic clue, but computer listeners usually cannot explain their verdicts. Their 2026 framework fuses sound patterns across time and frequency, then steers its attention toward the parts of the sound doctors find medically meaningful, making its reasoning visible.

Tested on three small public datasets, the system scored near-perfect accuracy, a couple of points above the best rivals, and barely degraded when noise was added. Removing either main component hurt performance, confirming both contribute. The authors offer the design as a reusable pattern for medical sound analysis.
plos-pone-0348608:
Vincenzo Ronca, Gianluca Borghini, and co-authors introduced a brain-based index for measuring divided attention, tested in a driving simulator. Existing brainwave markers respond to effort or visual clutter generally, not to attention genuinely split between tasks. Their 2026 index instead measures how several brain signals modulate together, drawing on information theory, in twenty-five drivers handling a main driving task plus side tasks of different kinds.

Older single markers reacted partly but could not isolate split attention. The new index rose systematically whenever attention divided, even distinguishing city from highway driving under focused conditions. It tracked eye movements and drivers' own distraction ratings closely. Control tests that scrambled the signals' timing erased the effect, supporting the claim that the index captures real coordination, not noise.
plos-pone-0348708:
Kaijiao Zhang, Bingkang Qu, and Qizhi Huang mined a decade of discussion on Zhihu, a large Chinese question-and-answer platform, to watch how the public picture of climate change is built. Climate talk there mixes science, policy, and everyday worry. Using network and correspondence methods, they mapped which ideas sit at the centre of the conversation and which orbit at the edges, and how that arrangement shifted over ten years.

Scientific evidence formed a stable core throughout. Around it, the framing widened from scientific agreement toward risk management and economic paths, with the economic angle becoming the dominant public representation. The authors argue that policy signals keep quietly rebuilding what climate change means to ordinary readers, with real consequences for how risks are understood and acted on.
plos-pone-0348808:
Xiangjun Hu and colleagues hunted for the genes behind failed blood vessel growth in diabetic foot ulcers, wounds that refuse to heal and often end in amputation. Bulk gene data from ulcer tissue were crossed with known vessel-growth genes, a machine learning sieve narrowed the list, and single-cell data then showed which cells actually use the surviving candidates. A five-gene signature emerged.

Two genes stood out with clear addresses: one concentrated in fibroblasts and support cells that build tissue scaffolding, the other in similar matrix-handling roles. Both are known regulators of the material between cells, fitting the ulcer's tangled mix of poor circulation, chronic inflammation, and disordered repair. The authors nominate the pair as candidate markers and targets for restoring healing.
plos-pone-0348908:
Mohammadamin Moragheb and co-workers build a deep learning tool that predicts how pairs of drugs will act together at specific doses. Drug pairs can help more than single drugs, but the right dose of each is hard to find by trial alone. Their 2026 method blends one model trained on all known pairs with another that studies only pairs much like the one being asked about.

Tested on two large public collections of drug-pair results, the combined approach beat rival methods. Pulling in similar past cases sharpened each prediction beyond what the global model alone could do. Better dose forecasts could cut wasted lab work and point chemists toward pairings worth testing first in cancer and beyond.
plos-pone-0349108:
Toshiyuki Nakanishi and co-workers give a first clinical check of a newer throat airway device in Japanese patients. The device seals above the voice box during anesthesia and was shaped around Western anatomy, so fit elsewhere was unproven. Their 2026 study observes sixty-four adults at one university hospital, balanced across younger and older men and women, and measures the pressure at which air starts to leak.

Placement succeeded on the first try in more than nine of ten patients, and the vocal cords were visible in most. The leak pressure ran lower than values reported in European patients. Men showed lower leak pressures and fewer visible cords than women. The device works well, but fit clearly varies with the patient.
plos-pone-0349308:
Jannah M Wigle and co-authors interviewed patients and health workers at a Toronto primary care service about trauma-informed care. This approach assumes many patients carry past trauma and shapes care to avoid fresh harm. Ten patients and thirteen providers, from doctors to support staff, shared how they understand the approach and what it looks like in daily practice.

Both groups described such care as basic good medicine: whole-person, patient-led, and built on trust built over time. Everyone backed making it the universal default rather than a special service. Access to trauma-specific supports and wider pressures on the clinic shaped how well it worked. The authors call for a system-wide shift toward this stance, arguing primary care relationships make clinics the natural home for it.
plos-pone-0349408:
Yun Ji Lee and co-authors studied a growth factor receptor in a hard type of stomach cancer in 2026. The poorly cohesive form spreads diffusely and behaves aggressively, and any marker that splits patients by outlook is valuable.

More than two hundred surgically treated patients at middle stages had tumor staining and clinical follow-up. Receptor positive cases were commoner at the lower stage and linked with notably better survival, standing as an independent favourable factor. Gene sequencing of a few cases found no receptor amplification. A marker tied to better outcomes, against the cancer's grim reputation, may help sort who needs the heaviest follow-up.
plos-pone-0349508:
Md Koushik Ahmed and colleagues present a protocol for mapping how realist research methods have been used across the life of complex health and social programs. Realist work asks what works, for whom, and in what setting, looking for the hidden mechanisms that make a program succeed in one place and flop in another. Nobody had charted how often these methods guide a program's design and growth, not just its later evaluation.

The planned scoping review will follow standard mapping frameworks and search for studies applying realist ideas at the development, delivery, and scale-up stages. No results appear here; the document fixes the method in advance. Knowing where realist thinking is used, and where it is absent, should help program designers borrow its questions earlier, when choices can still change.
plos-pone-0349708:
Adel Alshammari and Glen Cooper built a model of a healing bone defect. The model tracks three things at once. Cells move and multiply. Stress spreads through the tissue. And the scaffold that guides growth slowly breaks down. No past model had joined all three. The team set the model in a rat leg defect held by a plate. They checked it in part against real implant data.

Shape changed the results a lot. Thick scaffold strands more than doubled new bone growth by day ninety. The thin design lagged far behind. More open scaffolds let cells roam about a third faster. The team says scaffold shape needs the same care as scaffold material.
plos-pone-0350008:
Katherine M Tezanos and colleagues ran a small pilot trial of a group class that teaches skills for noticing and growing positive feelings. Young adults face rising depression and suicide risk, and the class acts as an add on to usual care. Fifty two people aged eighteen to twenty six at a United States community clinic were split by chance into the class or stronger usual care.

Attendance stayed high and feedback was warm, so the group form looks workable and welcome. The pilot was too small to prove group differences. Still, class members gained positive feelings and showed clear drops in depression and suicidal thoughts after the course and later. Larger trials are now warranted to test real benefit.
plos-pone-0350108:
Mariane Pivard and co-authors separated the effects of a staph germ's signalling system from its family background in 2026. The system, called agr, controls toxin output, and its four types link to different infections, but type and lineage usually travel together.

Working with lab strains that share one background but carry each agr type, the team read gene activity at three growth stages. Types switched on at very different times, and that timing drove most gene changes. Early types fired toxins and capsule genes hard; later ones delayed. The clean design shows timing of one switch can reshape a pathogen's whole behaviour.
plos-pone-0350508:
Rania Sakka and co-authors pooled studies in 2026 on gene types in progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis, a group of inherited liver diseases of children that often end in transplant. Whether the exact gene fault should guide transplant decisions was unsettled.

Eighteen studies covering four hundred twenty patients across the first four disease subtypes were combined. Patients were split by whether their gene faults were null, wiping out the protein, or non null. Transplant events were compared between groups. No agreed gene based selection rule exists yet, and the pooled odds give transplant teams the firmest numbers so far for counselling families.
plos-pone-0350608:
Yo Ishigaki and colleagues investigated a February twenty twenty-five COVID cluster that jumped between rooms of a sealed, mechanically ventilated hospital ward in Japan. Seventeen people fell ill across several rooms, and some had no close contact with the first patient, pointing at the air itself. The team measured air change rates with tracer gas, released fog as a stand-in for virus-laden aerosol, and simulated the ward's airflow on computer.

Opening a patient room door measurably sped air exchange and let tracer escape into the corridor. Fog released in the index room turned up beyond it, showing a physical route room to room through shared air. For infection control teams, the case is rare hard evidence that sealed modern wards can ferry virus between rooms, and that door habits and ventilation settings are clinical decisions.
plos-pone-0350808:
Praitayini Kanakaraj and seven co-authors study a known scanner flaw in brain diffusion MRI. Magnetic field gradients are not perfectly even. That flaw slightly distorts the measures used to map brain wiring. The team used nearly nine hundred fifty scans from a Vanderbilt aging study. They measured how much results shift when the flaw is fixed.

The fixes changed key diffusion measures by a few percent. The change covered at least a fifth of the brain. Some structure measures shifted far more. Effects varied by head position and brain region. The flaw explained only a small slice of the gap between impaired patients and controls. Still, a power analysis shows such effects become visible in studies larger than about a thousand people. Big multi-site studies should fix the flaw, or at least measure it.
plos-pone-0351108:
Deciding whether to have a child is fraught for women with multiple sclerosis, who worry about pregnancy, relapse, and medicines. Lara S Stahl and colleagues piloted a web decision aid, with or without nurse coaching, across Germany, in this 2026 PLOS One trial.

Women aged eighteen to forty-five who had not decided were assigned to the aid alone or the aid plus coaching; recruitment trouble forced the team to rebalance the groups partway. Questionnaires tracked how conflicted women felt, what they knew, and what worried them, while interviews explored whether the help felt usable. As a pilot, the study tests feasibility first and treats decision measures as early signals.
plos-pone-0351208:
Abdulrahman Alsayegh and colleagues surveyed three thousand eight hundred active people across thirteen regions of Saudi Arabia about dietary supplements: who takes them, why, and what predicts use. Supplements are booming in the kingdom with little hard data for regulators. A structured questionnaire covered health status, knowledge, and habits, and the team modeled the web of influences statistically.

Nearly two thirds of these active respondents used supplements, a strikingly high share. Health characteristics, beliefs about effects, and knowledge all fed into the decision in the model. For health authorities, a user base this large argues for attention to labeling, claims, and safety rather than treating supplements as a niche hobby. The study also gives gyms and clinics a profile of the typical user to aim education at, instead of broadcasting warnings to everyone.
plos-pone-0351308:
Chiara Cipriani and colleagues report a small pilot study, published in PLOS ONE in 2026, on depression around childbirth and children's brain development. Ancient viruses embedded in human DNA can switch on or off, and earlier work linked some of them to autism. The researchers wondered whether these viral remnants behave unusually in mothers who had depression during or after pregnancy.

Blood samples from mothers and their children showed that children with autism and their mothers shared odd activity in two viral elements and one immune signal. In mothers, one viral measure also rose alongside current depression scores. The authors treat the pattern as an early clue, not proof, and call for larger studies.
plos-pone-0351408:
Mukti Khetan and six colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One qualitative study of children's health habits in Jodhpur district, Rajasthan, India. Diseases linked to smoking, poor diet, and inactivity are rising, and habits form early. Through group discussions and interviews with children, teachers, parents, and canteen staff in rural and city schools, the team explored what helps and what blocks healthy living.

Participants understood the basics of these diseases but knew little about programs meant to prevent them. Healthy choices were blocked by few places to play, easy access to unhealthy food, and family finances, while support from family, friends, and schools helped. The authors recommend better communication about health programs, more recreation space, rules on unhealthy food sales, and health lessons woven into the curriculum.
plos-pone-0351508:
Jasmine Ahmed and colleagues examined a little-studied set of immune cells living in the skin's outer layer and their part in psoriasis. Most psoriasis research watches deeper skin cells that make IL-17, a driver of the scaly inflammation. The team focused on resident gamma-delta T cells in the epidermis and on one of their receivers for the signal molecule TNF.

A distinct subset of these cells carried the receiver called TNFR2. When TNF stimulated the cells, they produced IL-17 family signals and chemical calls for other immune cells. The receivers were not needed for the cells to develop or reach the skin, but TNFR2 pushed them toward the IL-17-making state seen in psoriasis. That makes this skin-surface subset a plausible early trigger and a fresh target for calming the disease.
plos-pone-0351708:
Expression of Concern: PLOS One's editors warn readers that a published trial of ColdZyme mouth spray for the common cold reported its results in a misleading way. This 2026 notice explains the journal's doubts about the earlier paper, which tested spraying the product soon after users diagnosed their own cold.

Two editorial board members judged that the underlying data support most findings, but the write-up unbalanced them. The trial's main and secondary outcomes showed no statistically clear difference from placebo, yet the conclusions stressed benefits such as shorter colds that the data do not back. Some sentences were unsupported or wrong. Readers should treat the original claims with caution.
plos-pone-0352208:
Lauren Trent and Anna Zanotto asked what helps people feel their life is good after losing part of an arm. They looked at ego-resilience, the ability to bend with stress and recover, alongside basic facts like age and amputation level. Their data came from ninety patients of a national prosthetic provider in the United States, gathered through standard questionnaires.

People who scored higher on resilience also reported better health-related quality of life. The two moved together across the group, whatever the person's background details. For clinics, the link suggests that building coping strength may be as much a part of recovery as fitting a good prosthesis, and worth checking early in rehabilitation. The study is a snapshot, so it cannot prove resilience causes the better outlook.
plos-pone-0352508:
Robert Deissler and Robert Brown present this 2026 PLOS One theory paper on objects sinking through thick fluids. The study covers any object with three symmetry planes at right angles. Rods and boxes both qualify. The authors derive formulas for the fall of such an object. The formulas give both the downward speed and the sideways drift, at any tilt. They use drag values measured along each of the object's three axes.

The authors work through examples. One is a box whose axis-by-axis fall speeds others had measured. The formulas recover its motion at any angle. They then carry the frame over to long magnetic particles pulled by a magnetic field. That case matters for drug targeting and particle imaging. The result is one recipe for predicting particle paths in medicine and industry.
plos-pone-0352608:
Wenwei Zhu and co-authors examined a new type of foundation pile designed to stop buildings floating upward in high groundwater. The design uses specially coated steel bars whose grip develops slowly, letting piles be cast in place. Their 2026 paper presents the structure, a two-stage uplift test method, and computer analysis of prestress loss.

Tests showed prestress loss grows with pile depth, yet the loss barely affects the pile's lower section. The whole pile stayed under compression even when pulled up to its design limit. Zhu and colleagues judge the safety performance strong. They argue the piles are cheap, resist cracking well, and suit wide engineering use where uplift is a risk.
plos-pone-0352808:
Qizheng Dong and Zaidong Li analyse how nearly eighty thousand Boston Marathon finishers paced themselves, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study of split times from 2015 to 2017. Timing mats recorded each runner at nine points along the course. By comparing first-half and second-half speeds, the authors sorted runners into four pacing styles, from metronome-steady to wildly variable.

Steady pacers finished fastest in every age and ability group — on average nearly an hour ahead of those who slowed dramatically late. Erratic pacers were the most likely to hit the wall in the final stretch. Among runners finishing under three hours, steady pacing was the norm; among casual runners it was rare. The advice writes itself: start controlled.
plos-pone-0353108:
Wang and colleagues built a smart physics engine for a snakelike cable-driven robot arm in a 2026 study. Such arms bend through many joints, which makes motion math slow and hard. The team first wrote exact motion equations, then built a large database of poses by random sampling.

A learning network, tuned by a search method, learned to predict poses quickly from that database. Speed matters because flexible arms are meant for tight spaces like disaster rubble and inside machinery. A fast, accurate engine lets controllers plan bends in real time rather than pausing to compute. The approach blends classic mechanics with learning instead of replacing one with the other.
plos-pone-0353308:
Go Bae, Jinyoung Lee, and colleagues explore in 2026 how family caregivers in urban South Korea take part in medical choices for long term illness. Focus groups covered relatives of people with high blood pressure, diabetes, kidney failure on dialysis, or heart disease. Western models often assume a two person choice between patient and doctor, which fits Korean family practice poorly.

Caregivers felt strain and doubt, searched for information themselves, and faced ranked talk with doctors. Split care routes and fixed information sheets limited guidance. Cultural respect for doctors and a sense of family duty framed their role as owed, not formally recognised. The authors argue the role needs clearer support.
plos-pone-0353408:
Goldsbury and colleagues measured health system costs of melanoma in New South Wales in a 2026 study. Australia has the world's highest rates of this skin cancer, and newer treatments for advanced disease are raising both survival and spending. Records linked a large adult cohort's surveys with cancer, hospital, and claims data over more than a decade.

More than eight thousand five hundred people with melanoma were compared with matched people without cancer to isolate extra costs. Costs and treatments were broken down by how far the disease had spread at diagnosis. Stage-by-stage figures help planners see where money goes and which patients drive spending, as costlier drugs spread into earlier stages of care.
plos-pone-0353608:
Wang, Zhang, and Koura studied how topics and feelings shape online behavior in a 2026 analysis of Chinese social media. More than fifty thousand posts discussed Japan's plan to release treated nuclear wastewater. The team sorted posts into four topics and scored seven feelings in each.

Global impact talk dominated the posts, while trade in Japanese seafood drew the smallest share. Posts spread through two routes: careful thinking about facts and quick emotional reaction. A poster's credibility changed how strongly each route drove likes, comments, and shares. The findings help explain why some claims race ahead during public disputes while careful posts lag.
plos-pone-0354108: Yang and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on tunnel boring machines cutting through wet, weak sandstone. The focus is the center cutter, a spinning blade at the head of the machine. The team studied how the blade wears and fails, and how its width changes that wear. Better blade design means fewer costly stops to swap tools mid-tunnel.
plos-pone-0354508:
Tafese and colleagues, in a 2026 study, measure cervical cancer screening in Eswatini, the country with the world's highest rates of this cancer. It is the most common cancer and the top cancer killer of women there, yet recent national screening figures were lacking. The team drew on a large 2021 household survey tied to an HIV assessment.

Among more than three thousand women aged twenty-five to fifty-nine, just under half had ever been screened, below global targets. Screening was more likely for women living with HIV, who meet the health system more often, for women in their late thirties and early forties, and for the better-off. It was less likely for unmarried women, women without schooling, and women who had not visited care recently or used family planning. The authors urge community awareness, work on stigma, and folding screening into services women already attend.
plos-pone-0354608:
Brendler and colleagues present a study protocol, published in 2026, for a trial called NUTRI-GUT-PD. The plan tests whether advice from a dietitian can ease constipation in people with Parkinson's disease. Constipation is a common symptom of the disease that is not tied to movement, and usual care leans on general tips or laxatives.

Under the plan, fifty-four outpatients without dementia will be split at random into two groups for ninety days. One group gets usual care, while the other gets a personal diet plan, one visit in person, and phone calls every two weeks. Topics include fiber, fluids, healthy eating, and how food interacts with levodopa. The team will track bowel habits, gut microbes, diet quality, and body strength, so the trial can show whether expert diet help beats routine advice.
plos-pone-0354808:
Bogdan Budnik and five colleagues published this 2026 diagnostic study asking whether a urine sample can reveal many diseases at once. Urine is cheap and painless to collect, but most protein studies chase one illness. Using samples from a Ukrainian biobank, they profiled thousands of proteins in cancer, multiple sclerosis, and fatty liver patients plus healthy controls.

Multi-protein panels separated most diseases from healthy samples with very high accuracy, and a few proteins mattered across several illnesses. Budnik cautions that these are upper-bound results from an exploratory study, and fresh patient groups must confirm them before clinical use.
plos-pone-0355108:
Michael Antonov and colleagues announce in 2026 version one of a long lived software library for network analysis, used across the sciences to study linked data. The library pairs a fast core, written in the C language, with friendly interfaces in several languages. After twenty years of growth it now serves more than a million downloads each month.

The release can handle billions of links, plot interactively, convert to and from other libraries, and offers many layout and community finding methods. Stronger testing, hundreds of bug fixes, a community forum, and documentation in several languages add robustness. Efforts to widen participation by underrepresented groups are highlighted as well.
plos-pone-0355408:
Ayodeji Babatunde Oginni analyzes child stunting in Nigeria through the overlap of wealth, place, and household leadership, in this 2026 study. Stunting in young children reflects long-term undernutrition, and the author asks which kinds of households stayed most at risk across four national surveys spanning fifteen years. Households were sorted by combining wealth level, rural or urban residence, and the gender of the household head.

Children in poor, male-headed rural households faced more than four times the odds of stunting compared with children in rich, female-headed urban homes, the reference group. Poor rural households led by women and average-wealth rural homes also stayed consistently worse off across every survey year. Because the same household types kept appearing at the top of the risk list, the author argues nutrition programs should target those combinations directly rather than treating poverty alone.
plos-pone-0355508:
Yacob Mohammed Yusuf and co-authors mapped drug-proof Proteus mirabilis germs from an Ethiopian hospital that serves military patients. This germ, tied to urine and wound ills, shrugs off more and more drugs. Gene-level data from sub-Saharan Africa stay scarce. Their 2026 study tested ninety-nine samples from sick folks and sequenced a picked subset in depth.

Near all samples fought at least one new-wave drug, and near all counted as proof against many drugs at once. Tests proved wide spread of enzymes that chew up those drugs. Sequencing listed proof genes, strain types, and the small DNA rings that ferry proof genes between germs. Yusuf and colleagues urge routine gene watch in area hospitals.
plos-pone-0355608:
Jonathan Chávez-Iñiguez and co-authors follow in 2026 hospital patients whose heart and kidneys fail together, asking whether infection makes clearing fluid harder. Their forward looking study covered a few hundred people at a large referral centre over two years. Infection meant clinical suspicion plus antibiotic treatment, and success was judged by symptoms, blood markers, and bedside ultrasound.

Patients with infection arrived more congested, yet cleared fluid at about the same rate as others. Infection also showed no clear link to major kidney harm or death in the month after care. The authors say strong fluid removal remains feasible even when infection triggers the crisis.
plos-pone-0356008:
Jing Feng and co-authors hunted for immune targets in a serious liver disease where gut microbes may help drive harm. Primary biliary cholangitis slowly destroys bile ducts, and high-risk cases progress fastest. Their 2026 study combined liver gene data with databases linking gut microbe chemicals to human genes.

The overlap produced six core candidate genes. One signalling gene ranked highest, tied to several common gut chemicals including the short fatty acids made when fibre ferments. It ran more active in high-risk liver samples and sat in immune-relevant cell types. Checks in a second dataset supported the shortlist. Feng and colleagues present the genes as ranked starting points for laboratory study of gut-liver links.
plos-pone-0356108:
Jan-Ole Hesselberg leads a team of six dissecting why grant reviewers disagree, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The stakes are large: peer scores steer research money, yet two experts often rate the same proposal differently. The team analyzed nearly one hundred thirty-five thousand reviews from four Norwegian funders.

Most effects were real in tests but small in size. Reviewers of the same gender split slightly less. Reviewers given in depth charge of one bid also converged a little more. Reviews bought in for narrow know-how, and certain research areas, split a bit more. Only about three percent of the split came from stable personal tendencies of single reviewers. The bulk of the noise lives in the encounter between one proposal and its readers, which limits how far picking reviewers alone can fix things.
plos-pone-0356508:
Lee Jia Hui and a Malaysian team built and validated a questionnaire. It measures what hospital pharmacists know and do about preventive antibiotics for cancer patients. Weakened immunity makes infection a constant threat for these patients. Their 2026 study drafted fifty-three items. Expert review and a Delphi process refined them. The survivors were then psychometrically tested on survey responses, using item response theory and factor analysis.

The final tool holds forty-three items, twenty-nine on knowledge and fourteen on practice. Eight weak knowledge items were cut for poor discrimination. One practice domain fell away for unreliability. The remainder showed strong internal consistency. A validated instrument lets hospitals audit prophylaxis practice properly. It lets them target pharmacist training where the gaps actually are.
plos-pone-0356608:
Opeyemi Atanda and colleagues published a 2026 evaluation in PLOS ONE of staff experience of relational care in youth mental health services in England. The study sat inside a trial comparing an Intensive Community Care Service, treating young people with flexible, relationship-first support, against usual inpatient or standard community care. The authors interviewed thirty-four staff about engagement and recovery.

Three themes ran through the accounts. Trust had to be built before treatment could work, often through informal visits and personalized contact rather than clinic routines. Flexibility in how long support lasted and how workers engaged was described as essential, yet systemic pressures constantly squeezed it. Staff described a web of trust linking worker, young person, and family, fragile when any strand failed. Protecting flexible, family-centered relational models inside systems rewarding throughput is their recommendation, since recovery in complex cases grows from relationships, not appointments.
plos-pone-0356808:
Rory Lambe led a team of eight authors testing the accuracy of a smartwatch, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The Google Pixel Watch 3 promises lab-grade fitness numbers, including heart rate, energy expenditure, and VO2 max. The team checked those outputs against trusted reference measures.

Lambe's validation tells athletes and coaches exactly what to trust on their wrist and what to treat with caution. Watches guide training decisions for millions of people, so overstated accuracy can mislead at scale. Honest error ranges let users weigh watch data against how they feel and perform. Independent testing like this, done outside the maker's lab, is how consumer health claims get sorted from consumer health facts.
plos-pone-0356908:
Abeeha Fatima, Anum Ashraf, and Muhammad Azzam Khan translate and validate a quick language test for aphasia into Urdu, for stroke care in Pakistan. The original English battery gives a broad language profile fast, but no checked Urdu version existed. Their work ran in three phases: careful translation with back-checking and pilot testing, validation with stroke patients with and without aphasia, and reliability testing across raters and repeat sessions.

Expert ratings judged the content strong, and every subtest separated patients with aphasia from those without by wide margins. A screening cutoff sorted cases with high sensitivity and specificity, and scores stayed steady across raters and repeats. Fatima and colleagues say Urdu-speaking clinicians now have a tested tool instead of ad hoc translation at the bedside.
plos-pone-0357008:
Solmaz Bohlouli and colleagues surveyed 302 immigrant parents in Edmonton, Canada. They asked about mental health, social media habits, and their children's dental routines. Their 2026 cross-sectional study focused on mothers of children aged two to twelve. It tested whether heavy social media use explained the link between a mother's mood and her child's oral care. It also tested whether that use changed the link.

More anxious or depressed mothers were less likely to have children who brushed regularly. The odds dropped noticeably as symptoms rose. Anxious and depressed mothers also scored higher on social media addiction. But that habit neither explained nor altered the brushing link. The authors argue dental services for immigrant families should screen for parental mental health. A struggling mother can quietly become a child's dental risk.
plos-pone-0357108:
Michele Garagnani and Nitin Yadav validate a laboratory task. It pits two ways of showing number against each other. Dots show amount directly. Digits name it. People estimate amounts at a glance, yet most choices in modern life compare written numbers. In the task, digit and dot count sometimes agree and sometimes clash. Volunteers must follow one rule while ignoring the other. One study ran online. The other ran in person.

Clashing displays slowed and confused people in an uneven way: ignoring the digit to count dots proved harder than ignoring dots to read the digit. Garagnani and Yadav say the validated task can now probe a basic question. How does the brain blend felt amount with symbols? The answer matters for math learning and decision research.
plos-pone-0357408:
Bilaal Wilson Matola, Juliet Charity Yauka Nyasulu, and Edward Nicol set out a research plan, published in 2026, for closing the HIV care gap among children in Malawi. Malawi nears its adult treatment targets, yet only about half of children with the virus have it fully controlled, far below the adult share. Their plan mixes four studies guided by models of social influence and care steps.

One part re-reads a decade of national program data, and another reviews what worked elsewhere in the region. Experts then shape a tailored service package, which a final part tests for fit at a community hospital with staff and caregivers. Matola and colleagues intend the package to be practical enough for Malawi's health system to adopt.
plos-pone-0357608:
Anna Coleman led a team of seven authors describing an inclusive research strategy in Manchester, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Medical studies too often exclude the very people they aim to help, through narrow sign-up rules or hard-to-reach sites. Manchester's Biomedical Research Centre, together with the city's Clinical Research Facility, set out to fix that in their own work.

Coleman's paper describes how the strategy was built and what it requires in practice. The aim is studies that reflect the diverse public they serve, so results apply to real patients. Other centers can borrow the approach. Inclusion is not charity; it is sound science, since treatments tested on narrow groups may fail the wider public.
plos-pone-0357708:
Qiyuan Lu published a study on smart home voice control in PLOS ONE in 2026. For a home system to act on speech, it must first classify what the speaker intends, such as turning off the kitchen lights. Lu built a deep learning model for that intent step and worked to improve its accuracy.

The model was tuned so commands are understood more reliably in daily dialogue. Fewer missed intents mean fewer moments when a resident repeats a command or gives up on the system. Work like this sits behind the smooth voice assistants people expect. It also matters for older residents who may rely on voice control when switches are hard to reach.
plos-pone-0357808:
Ranjdar Mahmood Talabani published a 2026 dental imaging study in PLOS ONE on a hidden root canal that causes many root canal failures: the second mesiobuccal canal in upper molars. Miss it, and infection survives. Using cone-beam CT scans from an Iraqi dental center, Talabani measured the canal layout in first and second upper molars. Machine learning models were then trained to predict the extra canal from anatomy, age, sex, and side.

The extra canal was common, present in about two-thirds of first molars and just over a third of second molars. A sex difference appeared only in second molars, where women showed it more often. Simple logistic regression beat the fancier models, scoring strongly for both tooth types, and feature analysis showed the distance between two canal openings mattered most. Such prediction could flag teeth needing extra search time or three-dimensional imaging before treatment starts.
plos-pone-0357908:
Eden Amir led a team of five authors who studied corneal donation decisions in an Israeli hospital, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Corneal transplants can restore sight, but tissue comes only from donors whose families agree, often within hours of a death. The team studied what shapes that hard choice at a hospital eye bank.

Amir's group identified factors that move families toward or away from saying yes. Their findings can guide how staff raise the request, what information they stress, and what support they offer. Small gains in consent mean more patients regaining sight. The study also respects the family's side: consent grows when people feel informed and unpressured at a painful moment.
plos-pone-0358008:
Bente Raafs and four colleagues published a treatment study protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. The therapy in view, called T-ScEmo4ALL Plus+, aims to help people who lost social skills after brain injury. Such patients may misread faces, tone, or jokes, and some also live with mental health problems.

Raafs and her team set out a single-case design, in which each patient is tracked closely through treatment. That design suits a group whose needs vary a lot from person to person. The protocol spells out who will be treated, what will be measured, and how change will be judged, so the later results can show clearly whether the therapy rebuilds social understanding.
plos-pone-0359108: Khademioore and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a review on eye surgery outcomes. Surgeons repair full-thickness macular holes, small breaks in the center of the retina. The planned review will test whether features seen in eye scans before surgery predict how well vision recovers. Forecasts of this kind help surgeons set honest hopes and pick the right cases for surgery.
plos-pone-0359208:
Qiong Wang, Huimin Li, and Guanlong Ren wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on industrial safety. A Christmas tree, in oil and gas work, is the assembly of valves that controls a well. The authors present a method for analyzing how reliable that equipment is while operating.

Their method combines FEMCA and fault tree analysis, two structured ways of listing failure modes and their causes, with numerical simulation. Together these tools estimate where a wellhead assembly is most likely to fail and what follows if it does. Engineers responsible for well safety are the audience for a reliability method built this way.
plos-pone-0359308:
Wanyang Zhou, Leo Manansala, Alice Valerio, and Xiaoting Sun published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies last-mile delivery services, the final leg that brings parcels to customers' doors. The authors examine value co-creation, how customers and companies build the service experience together, and its effect on customer satisfaction.

Two roles are weighed inside that relationship: digital accessibility, how easily customers can use the delivery apps and tracking, and delivery service quality. As online shopping grows, the last mile is where loyalty is won or lost. Delivery firms and retailers can use this evidence to decide where service investment pays off.
plos-pone-0359408:
Sarah Lisa Schütte, Benjamin Heidrich, Heiner Wedemeyer, Benjamin Maasoumy, and Tammo Tergast wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on liver disease care. Their patients have cirrhosis with refractory ascites, fluid in the belly that no longer responds to standard treatment, managed with peritoneal catheters. The new catheters carry silver particles.

As the title reports, the novel catheters show lower rates of peritonitis, a dangerous infection of the abdominal lining. Infection is the main hazard of long-term drainage, so a catheter that resists it could change care for these very ill patients. Liver specialists are the readers watching this device evidence.
pmc-10475008:
Jomova, Raptova, Alomar, and co-authors review reactive oxygen species, often called ROS, and their double role in health. At low levels, these reactive molecules act as useful signals that help run normal cell chemistry. The authors call this mild state good stress, since cells need some of it to stay balanced.

Problems start when levels climb too high for too long. Excess reactive species can damage cells and feed long-term disease and aging. The review weighs that harm against the protective role of antioxidants, the compounds that keep reactive levels in check. It suits readers who want both sides of a much-debated topic.
pmc-13217208:
Perera Molligoda Arachchige, Schmiliver, and Patel review how to image broken bones and joint injuries in children. A child's skeleton is still growing, and that changes everything about trauma pictures. Open growth plates, forming bone centres, and more springy bone produce injury patterns adults never show, and normal growth can mimic a fracture.

The review walks through age-specific traps and choices, from plain X-rays to scans for complex cases. Reading a toddler's elbow is not reading a teenager's, and the authors stress checking each image against the child's stage of growth. For emergency and radiology teams, the paper serves as a guide to fewer missed injuries.
pmc-13241508:
Kim and colleagues at Pusan National University trace how a tumor signal remakes natural killer cells in ovarian cancer. Epithelial ovarian tumors are often cold, with few immune cells inside. The team focused on growth differentiation factor 15, a stress protein tied to poor outlook. They asked how it interacts with a chemical-sensing receptor pathway in killer cells.

Tumor-derived Gdf15 boosted aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling inside natural killer cells, especially after chemotherapy and at relapse. Killer cells first fought tumors low in the protein, yet long signaling pushed them toward exhaustion. Their surveillance markers faded and tumors resisted attack. Mouse transplant and chemical exposure models echoed the clinical pattern, marking the axis as a warning sign for progression.
pmc-13241608:
Negret and colleagues in Colombia comment on trial evidence for JULIETA, a portable bioimpedance device for breast screening support. The letter stresses that the device cannot diagnose cancer or replace mammography. Its proposed role is triage: flagging which women should reach imaging sooner. Several authors work for the company developing the device.

The underlying multicenter study tested the device against mammography in four Colombian cities. It covered six hundred seventy-three breasts from four hundred sixty-nine women. The algorithm reached moderate sensitivity and specificity, with a negative predictive value above eighty percent. The device is painless, radiation-free, and quick, though the letter calls for validation beyond urban diagnostic centers.
pmc-13241808:
Iqbal and Osman in Dhaka report a young electrician whose lens clouded months after a high-voltage shock. The 21-year-old took current through his face from a power line, taking extensive burns. Five months later his left eye blurred more and more. Exams found flower-shaped cloudy spots typical of electric cataract.

Lens surgery with an implant proceeded without complications. Imaging then checked the back of the eye: retinal layers, nerve fibers, and optic capillaries all proved intact. His visual field tested normal. Vision reached perfect sharpness and held through twelve months, backing the guarded outlook.
pmc-13242108:
Elshouny's team surveyed nearly four hundred healthcare providers at a Saudi hospital about exhaustion and safety habits. The survey ran in Saudi Arabia. A burnout inventory scored personal, work, and client burnout. Patient safety work formed the main outcome yardstick. Survey data were gathered across 2023 and 2024.

Forty-one percent of those surveyed met burnout marks. Night-shift staff burned out sharply more than morning-shift staff, while the youngest fared best. Burned-out staff complied worse with infection control and knew standard precautions less well. Depression and work setting further dragged safety practice down.
pmc-13244508:
Wei-Syun Hung and colleagues examined whether a second viral infection worsens outcomes for intensive care patients fighting Pneumocystis pneumonia. Their study appeared in Annals of Medicine in 2026. The series covered 132 adults without HIV who needed ventilators in a Taiwanese ICU between 2017 and 2022 and had the fungal pneumonia confirmed by lung washings. Twenty-six of them also carried cytomegalovirus.

The co-infected fifth arrived sicker, with clearly worse oxygen levels and higher infection markers. Their ICU death rate ran three times the others' in a simple comparison. Yet once illness severity was modeled properly, the virus no longer independently predicted death. The authors read this as CMV marking the frailest patients rather than driving the outcome itself. Their management advice stays focused: start anti-Pneumocystis therapy early, keep it sustained, and protect the lungs of patients sliding toward ARDS.
pmc-13247308:
Wang and co-authors tested an antibody against sepsis inflammation in this 2026 Human Mutation study. Sepsis is a runaway immune reaction to infection, with macrophages at its center. A surface protein called podoplanin rises on inflammatory macrophages, so the team treated bacteria-toxin-stimulated mouse macrophages with SZ168, an antibody blocking podoplanin, and checked inflammation, cell fate, and signaling.

The antibody cut the release of three major inflammatory messengers, nudged macrophages toward a calmer, anti-inflammatory state, and reduced cell death, working through the ERK signaling pathway. Silencing podoplanin confirmed the pathway's dependence on the target. Added experiments in a mouse sepsis model and a preliminary patient cohort supported the effect. The authors propose podoplanin as a drug target for calming sepsis without shutting immunity down.
pmc-13248108:
Mejia and co-authors managed a hormone emergency in this 2026 Case Reports in Endocrinology article. A sixty-five-year-old woman had severe ectopic Cushing's syndrome: a small lung tumor was secreting ACTH, driving her adrenal glands to flood her body with cortisol. She arrived with dangerous low potassium, resistant hypertension, worsening diabetes, muscle weakness, and rapid weight gain, and a silently perforated colon forced emergency bowel surgery and a colostomy.

Cortisol control swung between two drugs: osilodrostat tablets when she could take them, and intravenous etomidate in intensive care when she could not, alternating as her condition demanded. Surgeons then removed the lung lobe holding the low-grade carcinoid tumor. Afterward her cortisol, electrolytes, and blood sugar all normalized. The authors highlight flexible, alternating therapy for patients too unstable for a single steady regimen.
pmc-13248208:
Song and co-authors present a forecasting tool for flight safety in PNAS Nexus in 2026. Sudden wind shear near an aircraft can change its energy fast and put a flight at risk. Older physics-based warning scores miss often and raise many false alarms, so the team blended physical rules with deep learning.

Their TwinTransformer model learned flight dynamics alongside data patterns and predicted several flight measures at once. Tested on real flight records, it beat leading comparison methods. It also gave pilots dependable warnings about fifteen seconds before a windshear hazard. The authors present the mix of physics and learning as a practical aid for cockpit decisions.
pmc-13249608:
Lavanya, Vats, and Shanwal explored what helps women with borderline personality disorder want to change, in a 2026 qualitative study. Five patients, aged twenty to thirty-five, at a mental health hospital in Ahmedabad, India, received six to eight motivational interviewing sessions, a counseling style built on gentle questioning rather than pressure. Interviews afterward were analyzed for shared themes.

Six linked themes emerged, tracing a path from emotional turmoil toward making meaning of their lives. Hope and helplessness wrestled throughout, and small supported steps acted as catalysts. The interviewing experience itself stood out as the strongest driver. The authors describe the method as a therapeutic bridge that can prepare patients for deeper therapy.
