Cane, O'Connor, and Michie test the validity of the theory domains framework for behaviour change and rollout research. The framework gathers theory about why behaviour happens into a set of domains, such as knowledge, skills, and setting. It had already been used in a wide range of clinical cases.

Their study asks experts to judge whether the framework's structure holds up. Sorting sample behaviours into domains checks whether the groups are clear and complete. A validated framework gives intervention designers confidence that they are spotting behaviour problems with a sound map.
pmc-4201108:
Italiani and Boraschi wrote in 2014 about how monocytes become macrophages of different kinds. Monocytes are blood cells that move into tissues and mature into macrophages. These tissue guards keep organs sound by clearing damaged cells and matrix, and by repairing harm.

The authors contrast two lenses on this change: what the cells look like and what they actually do. In one mode, often called M2-like, macrophages calm inflammation and promote healing. In another, they attack and inflame. The authors argue that function matters more than surface labels. That view helps immune studies describe these flexible cells with more honesty.
pmc-4516908:
Burgess, Scott, Timpson, and their co-authors gave a blueprint in 2015 for Mendelian randomization with published data. Finding individual-level data for a well powered analysis can be hard. At the same time, large research groups were publishing more and more summarized genetic association data.

Using those public summaries is an attractive option, and the paper shows how to do it efficiently. It sets out how to identify causal risk factors from data already in the open. That lowers cost and speeds work, since no new samples must be gathered. The blueprint helped teams turn public genome data into causal evidence for prevention and drug targets.
pmc-5383908:
Bakdash and Marusich presented repeated measures correlation in 2017, a statistical technique for a common design. Many studies measure the same people on two or more occasions, for example before and after training. Simple correlation is often applied to such data, but the observations are not independent, which breaks its assumptions.

Repeated measures correlation, shortened to rmcorr, finds the common within-individual association between paired measures. It asks whether, as one measure rises within a person, the other tends to rise too. That focus fits psychology and health data, where each person serves as their own baseline. The method gives a cleaner answer than pooling all points as if they were strangers.
pmc-6030908:
Jean-Paul Concordet and Maximilian Haeussler presented CRISPOR, a web tool for CRISPR guide choice, in 2018. CRISPR editing needs a short guide RNA that matches the target DNA. A poor guide can cut at the wrong places or barely work.

CRISPOR searches a pasted sequence, lists candidate guides, and scores each for off-target risk and likely activity. It covers many genomes and offers primer designs for checking the edit. The plain layout suits bench scientists who do not code. Careful guide choice at this stage prevents wasted weeks of lab work later.
pmc-7054408:
Manli Wang, Ruiyuan Cao, Leike Zhang, and coauthors tested two existing drugs against the new coronavirus in early 2020. The virus had just emerged, and no proven treatment existed. Screens of known drugs offered the fastest hope.

In cell culture, the antiviral remdesivir and the malaria drug chloroquine both blocked the virus at low doses. Remdesivir had already been through human safety testing for other viruses. The authors urged clinical trials to follow at once. The short report helped launch the first wave of treatment trials in the pandemic. Both drugs had published human safety records, which made rapid trials ethically plausible.
pmc-7547708:
Juliane Winkler and co-authors set out key concepts in 2020 for how tumors reshape the material around them as they grow and spread. Healthy tissue is held in a scaffold called the extracellular matrix, and cells constantly talk with that scaffold in both directions. Tumors exploit this remodeling, loosening and rebuilding the matrix into surroundings that favor their own growth.

The authors explain the main ways tumors rework their scaffold, and how those changes help cancer cells break away and seed new sites. They also discuss the enzymes and signals involved, several of which are drug targets. Their framework helps readers see metastasis not just as rogue cells, but as a whole neighborhood remade for escape.
pmc-7778908:
The UniProt Consortium described in 2020 the state of UniProt, the universal protein knowledgebase, as it stood entering 2021. The knowledgebase aims to give anyone free access to protein sequences paired with rich notes on what each protein does. It is one of the most heavily used reference resources in all of biology.

The article reports the significant updates made over the previous two years, covering new data, improved annotation, and better ways to search and download. It explains how the consortium keeps quality high while the flood of new sequences grows. For many researchers, UniProt is where a question about a protein starts, so these updates describe infrastructure that quietly supports work worldwide.
pmc-8116208:
Stephen Nayfach and co-authors presented CheckV in 2020, a pipeline for judging the quality of viral genomes recovered from metagenomes. Environmental sequencing had uncovered millions of new viral sequences, but those fragments vary greatly in completeness and accuracy. A partial genome can mislead studies of what a virus is and what it can infect.

CheckV automatically spots genomes that are complete, estimates how complete each fragment is, and trims away host DNA mistakenly attached to viral sequences. The authors test it against known references to show how well the estimates hold. With virus discovery running far ahead of manual checking, an automated quality gate like this keeps large catalogs honest.
pmc-8482308:
Kathryn Skivington and colleagues presented in 2021 a new framework for developing and evaluating complex interventions in health research. Complex interventions, such as programs that change clinician behavior or whole care pathways, cannot be tested like a single pill. Guidance from the United Kingdom's Medical Research Council had shaped this work for years, and this document replaces it.

The framework was commissioned jointly by two major British research funders and reflects recent advances in methods and thinking. It guides researchers through developing an intervention, testing whether it can be delivered, evaluating it, and putting it into practice. The authors stress context and the involvement of those affected. Trials of health programs worldwide are designed against this guidance.
podcast-joerogan-EoFniMSMj08:
Conservationist Paul Rosolie joins Joe Rogan for episode 2441 to defend the Amazon rainforest. Rosolie has spent years in the Peruvian jungle protecting wildlife from poachers and loggers. His books and films brought the fight to a wide audience, and Rogan is a keen listener.

Rosolie tells tales of giant snakes, jaguars, and the armed patrols that guard the forest. He explains what is lost each time another stretch of jungle falls. Rogan asks how outsiders can help without ruining what they save. Green and brave listeners get a modern jungle defender's stories from the front line.
podcast-joerogan-SmGbhtyfY08:
Jackie Gleason's UFO house is the hook for a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience on the ongoing alien fascination. Gleason, the great TV comic, was a serious UFO collector who built a home shaped like a flying saucer. Rogan uses the tale to open a wider subject.

The talk moves from Gleason's library of saucer books to the stars and soldiers who shared his obsession. Rogan asks why the subject draws such unlikely believers. The segment is light on its feet but real in its detail, a reminder that UFO culture was built by famous, curious people long before podcasts.
podcast-tuckercarlson-cxe_Da7OF08:
Commentator Matt Walsh joins Tucker Carlson as fights split the American right. Carlson praises how Walsh has handled the drama as a man. Walsh knows most of the figures involved in person.

The title says Walsh refuses demands to disavow his allies. The pair discuss how a civil war inside a movement can end. They weigh loyalty, honesty, and public pressure. Carlson leaves room for views that differ from his own. The episode offers a calm, personal take on a feud that plays out daily in angry posts online. Walsh stays even-toned while the feud rages on.
podmore-naturalisation-of-the-supernatur:
Frank Podmore was a lead hand in the Society for Psychical Research. His Naturalisation of the Supernatural came out in 1908. Podmore spent years at seances and in the hunt for fraud. The book is his calm sum of what the whole field had found.

Ghosts, spooks, and knocks all get a fair but hard test here. Podmore finds fraud, self deceit, and tricks of the mind in most tales. A few hard cases stand fast at the end of his sieve. The book is the great cool sum of the field at its prime.
popol-vuh-spence-1908:
Long before print, the K'iche' Maya of Guatemala kept the tale of how the world was made. The Popol Vuh, in Lewis Spence's English rendering of 1908, gives that book of creation in full. Spence's version is the classic public-domain rendering of the Maya text.

The gods shape the earth, fail with mud men and wood men, and at last make men of maize. Then the Hero Twins dive into the dark land of the dead and outwit its lords. No native book of the Americas stands higher than this one. Its tales still anchor Maya pride and study.
rasmussen-people-polar-north-1908:
Knud Rasmussen grew up in Greenland and spoke its tongue, and this book of 1908 was his first great Arctic tale. He wrote from trips among the Inuit of the far north. The text came out with drawings by Harald Moltke. His mixed roots gave him a rare place in both worlds, Danish and Inuit.

Rasmussen tells of hunts, camps, and long dark months, told close to the people who lived them. He gives much space to shamans and to the spirit world as the Inuit knew it. Few books of its time show Arctic life from so near at hand.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: In volume eight the valet's memories reach the middle of the imperial years. Constant recalls court routine, travel, and the emperor's private moods. The great man appears in slippers as well as in uniform. A close, human view of power behind the scenes.
royce-philosophy-loyalty-1908:
Josiah Royce published The Philosophy of Loyalty in 1908, his best-known work of ethics. Royce defines loyalty as devotion to a cause larger than the self. A good life, he argues, is built by choosing such a cause and serving it fully. Yet causes conflict, and bad causes can claim loyalty too.

His answer is loyalty to loyalty itself: choose causes that let others be loyal as well. The beloved community is his name for a world bound by shared devotion. The book offers a uniquely American moral philosophy. It influenced thought on community, service, and identity. Its central idea still sparks debate.
scheible-das-kloster-vol08:
Cells twenty-nine through thirty-two fill band eight of Das Kloster, issued in 1847 under Johann Scheible's editorship. The set had become the place where lost German print came back to light. Scheible bought, borrowed, and reprinted texts that most scholars of his day had never seen.

Folk magic leads again: grimoires, conjuring books in the Faust line, and the dreaded Höllenzwänge. Folk charms for house, field, and body keep company with chapbook tales. Taken as a whole, the band reads like a fair stall of the old print world. Its value lies in breadth: high sorcery and kitchen lore preserved in one binding.
schoetensack-unterkiefer-homo-heidelberg:
Otto Schoetensack, a German scholar, published his monograph on the Mauer jaw in 1908, in German. A workman had found the massive jawbone in sand pits near Heidelberg in 1907. Schoetensack named its owner Homo heidelbergensis.

He describes the jaw's size, teeth, and primitive features in careful detail. The fossil was then the oldest human remain known in Europe. It proved that humans had deep antiquity on that continent. Later finds across Europe and Africa filled out the species Schoetensack announced. The Mauer jaw still anchors the species name in museum collections and textbooks today.
shahnama-warner-vol-3-1908:
Volume 3 of the Warner brothers' Shahnama of Firdausi appeared in 1908, the third of nine volumes in the first complete English version. Firdausi wrote the Persian Book of Kings around 1000, drawing on older chronicles and oral tales. Arthur and Edmond Warner turned the long poem into English verse and prose summary.

Heroes, kings, and demons move through battles and feasts as the epic's early ages unfold. The translation notes names, places, and variant tales for careful readers. Taken with its companion volumes, this part keeps the long chain of Persian kings unbroken in English. It shows the scale of the task the Warners took on and sustained for two decades.
shahnameh-warner-vol3-1908:
English verse by the Warner brothers carried Ferdowsi's Shahnama to new readers in 1908. Their version was the first full one in English verse. Book three holds the mid part of the vast poem. Persia's kings, both famed and flawed, march through its pages.

Old tales tell of quests, duels, and courts where fate turns on a word. The poem blends myth with what looks like early past fact. Ferdowsi aimed to keep the Persian tongue and its old glory alive. The Warners' steady verse lets the long tale hold an English reader to the end.
shakespeare-king-lear-1608:
William Shakespeare's King Lear first reached print in 1608. Many call it his bleakest tragedy, a tale of madness and ingratitude. Old Lear divides his realm by which daughter claims to love him most.

Cordelia, the honest one, is cast out, and the flatterers take all. Lear ends up mad on a storm-torn heath, stripped of power and kin. Gloucester's plot mirrors Lear's, with a loyal son and a false one. The end is stark, yet love and service shine in the wreck. The storm scene alone secures its place on any stage in the world, even now, for new crowds.
simmel-soziologie-1908:
Simmel's Sociology, published in German in 1908, is his masterwork, subtitled studies on the forms of association. Simmel spent years as an underpaid lecturer in Berlin while his fame grew across Europe and America. The big book gathered the essays and lectures in which he had built a new way of seeing society.

He analyzes the forms of social life: the stranger who is near and far at once, the secret society, the pair and the trio, rule and subordination. Content varies endlessly, but the geometry of relations repeats, and that geometry is his subject. The book founded formal sociology, the branch that studies patterns of interaction rather than institutions. Its chapters on the stranger and the metropolis are still assigned wherever sociology is taught.
southey-chronicle-of-the-cid-1808:
Robert Southey published Chronicle of the Cid in 1808, the first English version of Spain's national epic tradition in full. The Cid, Rodrigo Díaz, was a Castilian warrior of the 1000s, famed in poem and chronicle. Southey, poet and historian, gathered the Spanish sources into one English narrative.

Exile, battles against Muslim and Christian foes, and the winning of Valencia fill the chronicle. Southey mixed the epic Poem of the Cid with later prose accounts and ballads. His preface and notes explained Spanish history for English readers new to it. The book fixed the Cid in English imagination and helped spark British interest in Spanish literature and history.
spr-proceedings-vol22-1908:
Part fifty seven stands alone as volume twenty two of the Proceedings, dated 1908. The Society for Psychical Research devoted single parts to its largest inquiries. Mediumship investigations dominate this era of the journal. Sittings are reported with sitters' names, dates, and tests against fraud or guessing.

Telepathy work continues in the background of society business. Apparition cases, checked against death records and letters, appear in support. The society's critics, inside and outside, get their say in print. Volume twenty two is a focused sample of the archive at work. It shows how one year's evidence was built. The file remains open to any reader's judgment.
steiner-way-of-initiation-1908:
Steiner's Way of Initiation, in this 1909 edition, is his practical manual on attaining knowledge of the higher worlds. Where his other books describe the unseen, this one tells the student how to train for seeing it. It became the working handbook of Anthroposophy.

He gives exercises in attention, reverence, and the control of thought, with warnings against haste and vanity on the path. The student is told to keep ordinary duties faithfully while the inner senses slowly open. Followers of Steiner still use the book as their first guide to his meditative discipline. His counsel is strict: slow growth, clean motives, and no hunger for power.
stronsa-beast-wernerian-society-1808:
A great carcass came ashore on Stronsa in the Orkney Islands in the autumn of 1808, and men argued over it for years. Doctor John Barclay told the Wernerian Society of Edinburgh what the sworn witnesses had seen and measured. His account, with its affidavits, appeared in the years 1808 and 1809.

The beast was long, maned, and finned, by the tales told of it, and some called it a sea serpent. Later study of the bones and form named it a basking shark, huge and rotten past knowing. The papers show science at work on a monster in the open. Error and care sit side by side in the record.
suess-face-of-earth-vol3-sollas-1908:
Volume 3 of Sollas's translation of Suess's Face of the Earth appeared in 1908. Eduard Suess devoted this volume to the structure of Asia and the Pacific rim. His synthesis drew on reports from surveyors, travelers, and colonial geologists across a vast region.

Mountain chains, plateaus, and island arcs of Asia are laid out as one connected system in Suess's account. He traced great lines of fracture and folding around the Pacific's edge. The Pacific rim's ring of volcanoes and quakes takes shape in such surveys. Sollas, himself a field geologist, rendered the dense German with care. The volume continues a global geology built almost wholly from paper evidence.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau: The eighth volume of Rousseau's Confessions covers his English exile. The unhappy philosopher quarrels bitterly with his kind host Hume. Growing paranoia and pride poison old friendships. A sad and lonely chapter of a great life.
the-taming-of-the-shrew-pg1508: The battle of Petruchio and Katherina in this edition: wit, slapstick, and one of comedy's great sparring matches. Audiences have argued for centuries about whether it is farce or something darker. Either way, it is irresistible theater.
the-wandering-jew-volume-08: Eugène Sue's Wandering Jew, volume eight: toward the climax. The Renneponts' fate nears. Melodrama's grand finale. The serial's late act, sue's serial nears its climax, grand melodrama, the late act, toward the climax, Sue's serial.
thompson-semitic-magic-1908:
R. Campbell Thompson, a British Museum curator, published Semitic Magic in 1908. He surveyed magical practice across the ancient Near East and traced its growth. Assyrian, Hebrew, and Arabic traditions all pass through his account.

Thompson draws on cuneiform tablets that few Western readers knew existed. Exorcisms, charms, and folk rites show traditions borrowing from one another. He asks where practices began and how they traveled between peoples. The survey pioneered a map of Semitic magical traditions as one connected field. Later scholarship corrected details but kept his broad frame. Thompson's museum work with tablets gave the book unusual firsthand authority.
tob-0108:
A further copy of Basil Valentine's Twelve Keys preserves the same set of alchemical emblems held elsewhere in the library. Twelve gates of image and riddle stand for twelve stages of the work that ends in the philosopher's stone. A wolf devours a king; lovers meet as sun and moon.

The Benedictine monk of legend writes in parables on purpose, to keep the art from the unworthy. Printers loved the keys and spread them across Europe. Verified from a pre-1930 public-domain edition, this copy keeps the full sequence intact. Few picture books of any century hide so much claimed knowledge in so few images.
tob-10008:
Virgil wrote the Aeneid to give Rome a founding epic, and John Conington rendered it into clear English prose. Aeneas, a Trojan prince, escapes as Troy burns and sails the seas in search of a promised new home. His fate points toward Italy and the birth of the Roman people.

Along the way Aeneas loves Dido, queen of Carthage, and leaves her, with tragic results. He visits the underworld, then wages hard war in Italy against those who resist Rome's rise. Duty pulls against private feeling on nearly every page. Poets for two thousand years have treated the Aeneid as the model epic.
tob-12908:
Helena Blavatsky cast The Key to Theosophy as a dialogue, fielding hard questions about her movement from an imagined inquirer. Its aims, its mahatmas, and its views on God, the soul, and life after death are all put to her directly. She answers in a direct and sometimes combative tone.

Correcting popular misunderstandings is the book's engine: Theosophy is not Buddhism, not spiritualism, and not, she insists, a new religion. The question-and-answer structure makes this the friendliest doorway into a demanding system. V1 evidence advises reading it before the big books, and its clarity about terms like karma and reincarnation explains why the advice has lasted.
tob-13508:
Pliny the Younger, a Roman lawyer and official who lived from about 61 to 112, left the most charming correspondence surviving from ancient Rome. The first series of his letters includes his famous eyewitness account of the eruption of Vesuvius, which killed his uncle, Pliny the Elder, who sailed toward the disaster to observe and rescue.

Villa life, courtroom cases, literary friendships, and provincial administration fill other letters. His inquiry to the emperor Trajan about what to do with Christians, and Trajan's reply, remain key documents for early church history. Witty, humane, and beautifully written, the letters let ancient Rome speak in its own urbane voice about ordinary and extraordinary days alike.
tob-13808:
Gertrude Lowthian Bell translated poems from the Divan of Hafiz, the fourteenth-century Persian master of the ghazal. Bell knew the Middle East as traveler, archaeologist, and mapmaker, and she loved Persian poetry. Her selection gathers some of Hafiz's best-loved lyrics in English verse.

Wine, roses, nightingales, and the absent Beloved return from poem to poem. Persian readers have sung and quoted these lines for six hundred years, hearing in them both earthly love and love of God. Bell strains to keep the music and wit of the originals. Her Hafiz remains a graceful first meeting with Persia's favorite poet.
tob-14508:
Under Max Müller's full name, the same beloved rendering of the Dhammapada presents 423 verses in short chapters on anger, craving, and wisdom. Each verse lands like a polished stone: brief, smooth, and meant to be carried in memory. Müller's translation has been many readers' first meeting with the Buddha's voice for over a century.

Because this entry duplicates the Müller edition cataloged nearby, it serves readers who search by the translator's full name. The substance is identical: a disciplined path taught through contrasts between the heedless and the heedful. Comparing this cataloging with its twin shows how library records, like scriptures, travel under variant titles.
tob-4008:
Giordano Bruno paid with his life for thoughts like those in On the Infinite Universe and Worlds. The Italian friar turned philosopher argued that the stars are suns, each perhaps with its own worlds, in a cosmos without center or edge. Rome burned him in 1600.

Bruno wrote in dialogues that mock timid scholars who cling to Aristotle's closed sphere. His infinite universe has no outside and no favored place, a vision far ahead of the telescopes. The evidence notes no Gutenberg translation exists and no text is attached to this entry. The work stands as philosophy's boldest early cosmology.
tob-4108:
James Legge's Chinese Classics, a seven-volume project, opens with volume one containing the Confucian Analects, the Lun Yü, and related texts. Legge prints the Chinese original beside his English rendering, with critical and exegetical notes, prolegomena, and copious indexes. Two thousand years of Chinese commentary stand behind his choices of meaning.

For readers who want the Analects with its full scholarly apparatus, rather than a pocket translation, Legge's learned edition remains the reference. Western Confucian studies rested on it for a century. The volume demands shelf space and patience, and repays both for students comparing translations, checking a saying's context, or tracing how Victorian scholarship built sinology.
tob-4208:
Yoga Sastra presents an 1897 examination of Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, with the Sanskrit text analyzed in detail. The Victorian-era study works through the eight-limbed path: restraints and observances, posture, breath control, withdrawal, concentration, meditation, and absorption. Commentary tests the root text line by line.

The author treats yoga as a serious system of philosophy and practice, not a curiosity. Comparisons with Indian schools of thought fill the notes. Verified from the 1919 edition, the volume shows how learned readers studied yoga's root scripture in the 1890s. They worked in India and the West together, before the modern yoga boom reshaped its meaning.
tob-9108:
Gwilt's Vitruvius returns in this record of the Ten Books on Architecture, the Roman handbook verified from the 1919 scan. Temples, houses, theaters, aqueducts, and machines fall under the architect's care. Vitruvius wrote under Augustus and meant his work to order the whole art of building.

Proportion rules the design chapters: a temple, like a body, must agree in all its parts. Water supply and war engines get equal respect at the back. Renaissance builders rebuilt classical Europe from these pages. The entry keeps the only ancient architectural treatise to survive in the version English builders long used.
topsell-historie-serpents-1608:
Edward Topsell followed his book of beasts with The Historie of Serpents in 1608. The two volumes belong together as his great survey of the animal world. This one covers snakes and everything his age counted as a serpent, real or rumored.

Dragons and basilisks share the pages with vipers and common adders. Topsell gives each creature's look, its poison, its cures, and the morals it teaches. Drawings show winged serpents as calmly as garden snakes. The book is a cabinet of scaled wonders from Renaissance England. Readers learn as much about the fears of 1608 as about snakes.
un-sc-res-108:
Talks meant to calm the Egypt-Israel armistice line broke down in 1955, and fighting flared up along the line drawn on 24 February 1949. Resolution 108, adopted without dissent on 8 September 1955, responds to a report from the Chief of Staff of the UN Truce Supervision Organization in Palestine.

The Council notes with approval that both sides accepted the Chief of Staff's call for a cease-fire with no conditions. It tells both sides to restore order, keep the cease-fire in full force, and pull their forces clearly apart, as he proposed. UN observers must be free to move in the area, and each side must name people to work with him.
un-sc-res-1308:
HIV and AIDS came before the Council as a peace and security issue for the first time in 2000. The pandemic was sweeping the world, and Africa was hit hardest. In January that year, the Council had met on the impact of AIDS on peace and security in Africa. A report from UNAIDS followed in July. Resolution 1308 was adopted unanimously on 17 July 2000.

The Council warned that the disease could damage the stability of states and make emergencies worse. The health of peacekeeping troops was also at risk. States that had not done so were urged to build national programs against the disease. UNAIDS and other partners could help with that work. The Secretary-General was asked to add training on HIV prevention to the preparation of peacekeepers. The training would run before deployment and during service. Work on testing, counseling, and wider access to care was encouraged.
un-sc-res-1408:
Resolution 1408 gave the Council's ruling on Liberia, adopted on 6 May 2002. An expert panel had found that Liberia's government still bought arms in breach of earlier sanctions. The panel also linked the government to rebel fighters who kept the region unstable. The illicit diamond trade played a key part in that picture.

The Council finds that Liberia has not fully met its demands. The sanctions stay in force for twelve more months, from 7 May 2002. Liberia must build a clear, checkable scheme for certifying its rough diamonds. Income from shipping and timber must serve public needs, not banned arms deals. A fresh expert panel gets three months to test compliance.
un-sc-res-1508:
Sierra Leone's United Nations mission was extended on 19 September 2003 for six months from 30 September. Security in the country was growing more stable. The Council still pressed for stronger Sierra Leone police and armed forces that could keep order alone. It tied the country's calm to peace in the subregion, above all in Liberia, where war had just ended.

The Council thanked the states supplying troops, police, and support to UNAMSIL. It praised the mission's progress in adjusting its size, shape, and deployment under resolutions 1436 (2002) and 1492 (2003). Building the government's own capacity, above all a sound police force, was named the key to a smooth exit. Freetown was urged to tighten control of diamond mining. The Council voiced serious concern at the Special Court's shaky finances and renewed its appeal for funds, and it praised the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's work.
un-sc-res-1608:
MINUSTAH was extended and reinforced for Haiti's elections on 22 June 2005. Free and fair polls had to be held in 2005, with elected leaders taking office on 7 February 2006. The Council's own mission had visited Haiti in April. Human rights abuses, long pretrial detentions, and impunity drew condemnation. Poverty was named a root cause of the unrest.

The Council extended MINUSTAH's mandate, as set by resolution 1542 (2004), until 15 February 2006. For a temporary period the mission would grow, to a military strength of 7,500 and a police strength of 1,897. The Secretary-General had to share his plan for the mission's work and for reform of the Haitian police. MINUSTAH was told to focus its resources on building a secure setting for the vote. The mission and the Haitian authorities had to act together to stop violence and protect civilians. The increase covered the tense electoral season.
un-sc-res-1708:
Côte d'Ivoire's sanctions experts gained more time under a Security Council decision of 14 September 2006. The Group of Experts had sent its final report on the arms embargo and related measures set by resolutions 1572 (2004) and 1643 (2005). The Council judged that Côte d'Ivoire still threatened peace and security in the region. The peace process between the government and the Forces nouvelles remained stalled.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the group's mandate to 15 December 2006. The Secretary-General was asked to make the needed administrative arrangements. The group had to send a brief written update to the Council, through the sanctions committee, before 1 December 2006. The update would cover how the embargo and the diamond and travel measures were being applied, with recommendations. The short renewal kept expert eyes on arms flows while the larger sanctions regime ran to its December review.
un-sc-res-1808: From 2008 comes Resolution 1808, a Security Council decision kept in official-record form in this collection. The text's authority flows from its adoption by fifteen members under the Charter. Its form is the familiar one, preamble then operative paragraphs, and the entry preserves both in full through the Wikisource transcription of the record.
un-sc-res-2008: Security Council Resolution 2008 is held in this collection as a transcription of the official record from English Wikisource. The members who adopted it acted within the Council's standing charge over peace and security. Their complete text is the entry: the shared account of the matter first, then the shared decision that followed from it.
un-sc-res-208: A seat on the International Court of Justice fell vacant when Judge Abdel Hamid Badawi died on 4 August 1965. The Security Council noted his death with regret on 10 August 1965. The vacancy covered the rest of his term and had to be filled under the Court's Statute. Article 14 of the Statute leaves the election date to the Council. It decided that the election would take place during the twentieth session of the General Assembly.
un-sc-res-2308:
Liberia prompted the Council to adopt Resolution 2308 on Liberia on 14 September 2016. Liberia's own police and army had just taken over full control of security from United Nations peacekeepers. The vote came near the end of a mission that began in 2003, after a long civil war.

The text extends the United Nations Mission in Liberia, called UNMIL, until 31 December 2016. It keeps the mission's caps at 1,240 soldiers and 606 police. It warns that land disputes, graft, and fights over natural resources still threaten calm. The Council says it may withdraw the mission after a December review and move to a smaller United Nations presence.
un-sc-res-308:
Addis Ababa hosted the Security Council under a decision taken on 19 January 1972. The Organization of African Unity had asked the Council to meet in an African capital, and the General Assembly passed the request on. Ethiopia, Guinea, Senegal, and Zambia had all offered to host. A Council committee weighed the costs and the practical plans and reported back.

The Council decided to hold meetings in Addis Ababa from Friday, 28 January to Friday, 4 February 1972 at the latest. The sessions would take up the questions on Africa then before the Council and the carrying out of its resolutions on them. Ethiopia was thanked for offering facilities at no cost to the United Nations. The Secretary-General was told to negotiate a conference agreement with Ethiopia at once. The Addis sitting remains a rare case of the Council meeting away from New York.
un-sc-res-408:
The Golan observer force was renewed in a short sitting on 26 May 1977. The Secretary-General had reported on the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force. Efforts toward a durable and just peace in the Middle East needed to continue and grow, the Council said. Tension in the area still caused concern. The force had watched the Israeli-Syrian disengagement line since 1974.

The Council called on the parties to carry out resolution 338 (1973) at once. That text demanded a cease-fire and talks on the basis of resolution 242. The Council renewed UNDOF's mandate for six months, until 30 November 1977. The Secretary-General had to report at the end of the period on how the situation stood and on the steps taken to apply resolution 338. The spare formula of this text became the pattern for the Golan renewals that have followed twice a year ever since.
un-sc-res-708: Judge Taslim Olawale Elias of Nigeria died in August 1991. His death left a vacancy on the International Court of Justice. On 28 August 1991 the Security Council fixed the date to fill it. The election would be held on 5 December 1991. It would take place at a Council meeting and at a General Assembly meeting. The Assembly was then in its forty-sixth session. The one-paragraph text performs that scheduling act alone.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 108, adopted unanimously on 8 September 1955, concerns renewed violence along the armistice demarcation line between Egypt and Israel. The Council notes with grave concern that talks begun by the Chief of Staff of the Truce Supervision Organization had broken down. It welcomes both parties' acceptance of his appeal for an unconditional cease-fire. It calls for order and tranquillity. It endorses separating the two armies as he proposed. It insists that United Nations observers be given freedom of movement.

On 17 July 2000, the Security Council took up a disease as a security issue. It adopted Resolution 1308 without dissent. The topic was HIV and AIDS. The Council voiced deep concern at the scale of the pandemic. Africa faced the worst of the crisis. A January 2000 Council meeting on AIDS and security in Africa set the stage.

The text focuses on peacekeepers. Troops on duty abroad could catch the virus. They could also spread it. So the Council asks the Secretary-General to expand HIV training for peacekeeping staff. It urges member states to build national programs for their troops. Those programs cover teaching, prevention, testing, counseling, and care. Later Council action on AIDS built on this start.

Liberia's defiance keeps sanctions alive in Resolution 1408, adopted on 6 May 2002. The Panel of Experts had found that Liberia's government was still breaking the measures in Resolution 1343 (2001), above all by acquiring arms. Its backing for armed rebel groups, including former RUF fighters from Sierra Leone, was judged a threat to regional peace.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council decides Liberia has not complied with its demands and keeps the measures from Resolution 1343 in force for 12 more months from 7 May 2002. They will end at once if Liberia is found to comply, with reviews before 7 November 2002 and every six months after. Liberia must build a transparent certificate-of-origin regime for rough diamonds and audit shipping-registry and timber revenue so the money serves social and development ends. A new Panel of Experts will check compliance and report by 7 October 2002.

Sierra Leone's calm was still young when Resolution 1508 passed on 19 September 2003. All members backed it. The UN force there, UNAMSIL, had guarded the peace since 1999. Its work was nearly done, but not quite. The Council kept it for six more months.

In that span, Sierra Leone had to grow its own strength. Its police and troops must learn to keep the peace alone. State rule had to reach the diamond fields, where war had fed on gems. Ex-fighters needed homes in civil life. Those who fled had to come back in safety. Calm at home also hung on calm in Liberia, next door, where war had just ended.

Haiti's road to elections in 2005 is the concern of Resolution 1608, adopted on 22 June 2005. The UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti, MINUSTAH, supported a transitional government. The Council insisted that free and fair votes, open to all parties that had given up violence, be held on time, with elected leaders taking office on 7 February 2006. Poverty, long pretrial detentions, and weak courts fed the unrest.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MINUSTAH until 15 February 2006. For the election period it adds 750 troops for a rapid reaction force around Port-au-Prince, 50 staff for a sector headquarters, and 275 civilian police. Total strength rises to up to 7,500 troops and 1,897 police. It asks for an overall election plan, a police reform plan, and a step-by-step drawdown plan for after the vote.

Resolution 1708, adopted on 14 September 2006, keeps a team of sanctions detectives working in Côte d'Ivoire. A group of experts had been checking how well the arms embargo and other measures against the divided country were holding. Their final report, covering diamond and weapons flows, had just reached the Council.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the experts' mandate until 15 December 2006 and asked the Secretary-General to handle the administrative arrangements. The group had to send a short written update, through the sanctions committee, before 1 December, judging how the measures from resolutions 1572 and 1643 were being carried out and offering recommendations. Expert panels of this kind became the Council's eyes inside embargo regimes.

Georgia's observer mission, UNOMIG, is extended on 15 April 2008. Geneva-format meetings had become the main forum for talks between the Georgian and Abkhaz sides, and both had renewed their commitment to the process. Still, the primary duty to use that support and move the talks forward rests with the parties themselves.

UNOMIG's mandate is extended for a new period, and both sides are urged to finalize the long-discussed document on the non-use of force without delay. More direct bilateral contacts and real steps on refugee return and confidence building are called for. The Secretary-General is asked to use the mandate actively to push the settlement process, whose core remained the division of powers between Tbilisi and Sukhumi.

Resolution 1908, adopted unanimously on 19 January 2010, sends reinforcements to Haiti one week after a devastating earthquake. The quake of 12 January had killed huge numbers of Haitians and many UN staff, and the stabilization mission there, MINUSTAH, was itself a victim. The Council expressed its deepest sympathy and gratitude to the mission's troops and to other international workers.

Acting on the Secretary-General's recommendation, the Council raised MINUSTAH's ceilings to support recovery, reconstruction, and stability. The force ceiling rose to eight thousand nine hundred forty troops, with police capped at three thousand seven hundred eleven officers. The new levels were to stay under review as conditions changed.

Liberia was weeks away from presidential and legislative elections when the Council adopted Resolution 2008 on 16 September 2011. The resolution extends UNMIL, the United Nations Mission in Liberia. Planning had begun for Liberia's own forces to take over security duties from the peacekeepers in time.

The Council extended UNMIL's mandate until 30 September 2012. The mission could keep helping with the 2011 elections. Its help covered transport, reaching remote areas, and coordinating international election support. Free and peaceful elections were treated as a key test for later withdrawal of the force. After the new government took office in 2012, a team would visit to assess the situation. Its report would help plan the next stages of the drawdown.

Resolution 208, adopted unanimously on 10 August 1965, fills a seat on the International Court of Justice. Egyptian judge Abdel Hamid Badawi had died on 4 August, leaving a vacancy for the rest of his term. Under the court's statute, the Council's job in such a case is narrow: fix the date of the election to choose a replacement.

The Council decided the election would be held while the Assembly sat for its twentieth session, which opened that autumn. Texts like this one show the Council's quieter housekeeping powers, separate from peace and war. The General Assembly and the Council vote independently in court elections, and this resolution simply set the shared timetable for filling Badawi's place.

Liberia's own forces take full charge of security in Resolution 2308, adopted on 14 September 2016. The UN Mission in Liberia, UNMIL, had handed over all security duties on 30 June 2016. The Council praised the police, immigration service, and army for taking on that role. It still worried about land and natural resource disputes, corruption, and slow growth of sound state institutions ahead of the 2017 elections.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends UNMIL until 31 December 2016, keeping its ceilings at 1,240 military and 606 police staff. It says it is ready to weigh pulling UNMIL out and moving to a new UN presence, based on a review by 15 December 2016 of Liberia's ability to keep stability. It recalls its request for an assessment mission to report with advice by 15 November 2016.

Resolution 308, adopted on 19 January 1972, agrees to take the Security Council to Africa. The Organization of African Unity had asked the Council to meet in an African capital, and the Assembly echoed the invitation. Ethiopia, Guinea, Senegal, and Zambia all offered to host; a Council committee studied the offers and the costs, and reported back.

The Council decided to meet in Addis Ababa from Friday 28 January to no later than Friday 4 February 1972. The sessions would cover African questions already before the Council and how its resolutions on them were being carried out. Thanks went to Ethiopia for hosting and supplying facilities without charge. The Addis meetings remain a rare case of the Council sitting outside New York.

Resolution 408, adopted on 26 May 1977 by twelve votes to none, is another six-month renewal for the Golan observer force. The Secretary-General's report on UNDOF was considered, along with efforts to build a lasting, fair peace in the region. The Council said the area's prevailing tension remained a concern, as it did in nearly every renewal of the era.

The parties were called on to carry out resolution 338 of 1973, the ceasefire-and-negotiations text, immediately. UNDOF's mandate was renewed for six months, until 30 November 1977. The Secretary-General was asked to report at the end of the period on developments and on the measures taken to put resolution 338 into practice.

Nigeria's best-known judge died in August 1991. Taslim Olawale Elias passed away on 14 August. He had led the world court as its president in past years. His seat on the bench fell vacant at once. Resolution 708 passed with no dissent on 28 August 1991.

The Council set the poll to fill the gap. It would fall on 5 December 1991. Votes would run side by side in the Council and in the Assembly's forty-sixth session. Court rules fix this joint method. The new judge would serve only the rest of Elias's term. Elias had shaped law in Nigeria and far past its shores. The text marks his loss with spare, formal grief.
valens-anthologiarum-1908:
Vettius Valens was a Greek astrologer who worked in the second century, in the age of the Roman Empire. He wrote a practical handbook of astrology drawn from his own case work. Wilhelm Kroll edited the Greek text for the Teubner series, and that edition appeared in 1908. The work is presented here in Greek.

Valens explains how to cast and read a birth chart, judging health, wealth, marriage, and length of life. He fills the books with real example charts from his practice. Because so much ancient astrology is lost, his handbook is the most important one that survives. Scholars use it to rebuild Hellenistic astrology.
vinogradoff-english-society-eleventh-cen:
Vinogradoff's English Society in the Eleventh Century appeared in 1908, built from his Ford Lectures at Oxford. The eleventh century brought the Norman Conquest, when England's society was remade by invasion. Vinogradoff set out to paint that world whole, from the king's court to the peasant's furrow.

He describes thegns and ceorls, priests and reeves, and above all the manor, the cell of social life where lord and tenants met. His evidence is the Domesday survey of 1086 and the manor rolls, read with a lawyer's care. The lectures remain the classic portrait of Conquest England. Vinogradoff, a Russian writing England's past better than the English, shows what the new discipline of social history could do. The eleventh century is made visible, field by field and rank by rank.
vivekananda-complete-works-vol2-1908:
The second volume of Vivekananda's Complete Works appeared in 1908, continuing the record of his lectures and writings. Its center is Jnana Yoga, the path of knowledge, drawn from his talks in London and New York. Writings on the Vedanta societies he founded fill out the volume.

Jnana Yoga teaches that the soul is already divine, and that ignorance alone hides that fact from us. Vivekananda presses the point with stories, sharp questions, and direct appeals to his hearers' own reason. The volume shows the teacher at work, building institutions while preaching freedom of the soul.
voltaire-charles-xii-todhunter-1908:
Charles XII of Sweden rode from victory to ruin faster than almost any king, and Voltaire made his life a new kind of history. Winifred Todhunter's Everyman translation tells the meteoric tale: a teenage king beating Danes, Russians, and Saxons, then broken at Poltava and stranded among the Turks.

Voltaire worked from witnesses and documents, writing history as clear narrative rather than chronicle. The book made philosophical history a genre and its author a historian of Europe-wide fame. Charles stands here as both hero and warning, a conqueror whose gifts served no lasting end.
wallas-human-nature-politics-1908:
Human Nature in Politics, published in 1908, is Graham Wallas's founding text of political psychology. Wallas, a Fabian socialist and teacher, argues that political theory had pictured man as a calculator. In fact, he says, man is a creature of impulse, instinct, and suggestion.

Elections, parties, and symbols work on feeling long before they reach argument. Democrats must reckon with that fact, or be beaten by those who do. Wallas writes from committee rooms and campaigns, not from theory alone. The book began the modern study of voting and propaganda. Its warnings about the irrational in politics have not dated.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol08:
Volume VIII of the Journal of Discourses, printed at Liverpool in 1861, gathers another round of Utah sermons for the record. Brigham Young leads the speakers, with his counsellors and the Twelve Apostles beside him on the stand. Reporters' careful shorthand turned frontier preaching into print that crossed the Atlantic to waiting readers.

The discourses teach, warn, and comfort in turn, always in the direct voice of men who ruled as well as preached. Reading them in order shows doctrine settling into habit across the settlements, year by year. The volume continues the running record that makes the Journal of Discourses a first source for the period.
zohar-de-pauly-french-vol-3-1908:
The third tome of Jean de Pauly's Zohar came out in 1908. The Book of Splendor, ascribed to the circle of Moses de Leon in medieval Spain, is the fountainhead of Kabbalistic teaching. De Pauly's French edition, in six tomes, is the only complete public domain translation of the work in a Western tongue.

In its pages the companions of Rabbi Shimon wander and dispute, drawing the inner sense out of each verse of the Torah. Creation, exile, prayer, and the life of the soul are read as one drama inside God. The Aramaic original hides its terms in symbol and tale. De Pauly renders the whole with steady patience. Tome three stands midway in his labor.
